### Use Spring Cloud to develop

**applications**

#### Spring Cloud overview

EDAS supports the native Spring Cloud microservice framework. You can deploy your applications to Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS) without changing your code or configurations. This lets you use enterprise-level features such as application hosting and microservice administration. These administration features include service search, canary releases, outlier ejection, and graceful shutdown. You also have access to monitoring, alerting, and application diagnostics. These features help improve the stability and security of your applications.

**Introduction**

Spring Cloud provides standards and specifications that simplify application development. These include service discovery, load balancing, circuit breaking, configuration management, message-driven event handling, and message buses. Spring Cloud also builds on these specifications to provide service gateways, distributed tracing, security, distributed task scheduling, and distributed coordination. Popular implementations of Spring Cloud include Spring Cloud Netflix, Spring Cloud Consul, Spring Cloud Gateway, and Spring Cloud Sleuth. Spring Cloud Alibaba, which was recently open-sourced by Alibaba Middleware, is another highly regarded implementation. evelopment If you develop applications with Spring Cloud components such as Spring Cloud Netflix or Spring Cloud Consul, you can deploy them directly to EDAS. Your applications will run and benefit from application hosting capabilities. Without changing any code, you can also use advanced monitoring features from EDAS. These features include distributed tracing, monitoring and alerting, and application diagnostics. If you want to use the service administration features of EDAS for your Spring Cloud application, you can deploy it directly to EDAS. No code or configuration changes are required. You can then use the comprehensive microservice administration capabilities.

**Compatibility**

EDAS currently supports Spring Cloud Greenwich, Spring Cloud Finchley, and Spring Cloud Edgware. The following table lists the Spring Cloud features, open-source components, and compatibility with EDAS.

| Spring Cloud feature |   | Open source implementation | Compatibility with EDAS |
|---|---|---|---|
| General features | Service registration and discovery | Netflix Eureka Consul Discovery | Compatible, and a replacement component is provided |
|   | Load balancing | Netflix Ribbon | Compatible |
|   | Service invocation | Feign RestTemplate | Compatible |
| Configuration management |   | Config Server Consul Config | Compatible, and a replacement component is provided |
| Service gateway |   | Spring Cloud Gateway Netflix Zuul | Compatible |
| Distributed tracing |   | Spring Cloud Sleuth | Compatible, and a replacement component is provided |
| Message-driven: Spring Cloud Stream |   | RabbitMQ binder Kafka binder | Compatible, and a replacement component is provided |
| Message bus: Spring Cloud Bus |   | RabbitMQ Kafka | Compatible, and a replacement component is provided |

evelopment

| Security | Spring Cloud Security | Compatible |
|---|---|---|
| Distributed task scheduling | Spring Cloud Task | Compatible |
| Distributed coordination | Spring Cloud Cluster | Compatible |

#### Implement service registration and

**discovery**

Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS) provides a commercial version of the Nacos registry. You can deploy applications developed with Nacos as the registry to EDAS without code modification to use the shared registry that EDAS provides. This topic describes how to develop a pair of sample Spring Cloud microservice applications, a service provider and a service consumer, based on Nacos in a local environment.

**How to select a registry**

Microservice applications use registries to implement service registration and discovery. When you develop an application, you can select a registry as needed. The following figure shows your options. evelopment You can use Nacos as the registry to implement service registration and discovery for your application. You can also use other types of user-created registries, such as Eureka, ZooKeeper, and Consul. After you deploy your application to EDAS, you can use the application hosting, microservice governance, and cloud-native Platform as a Service (PaaS) capabilities of EDAS, regardless of the registry type. For more information about how to deploy an application to EDAS, see Application creation and deployment overview (ECS) and Application creation and deployment overview (K8s). You can follow the instructions in this topic to implement service registration and discovery for your application. You can also download the application demos: service-provider and service-consumer.

**Preparations**

Download Maven and set the environment variables. Download the latest version of Nacos Server. Start Nacos Server as follows: i. Decompress the downloaded Nacos Server package. ii. Go to the `nacos/bin` directory and start Nacos Server. On a Linux, Unix, or macOS system, run the `sudo sh startup.sh -m standalone` command. On a Windows system, double-click the `startup.cmd` file. iii. **Optional:** When you develop applications locally, you can use the Alibaba Cloud Toolkit plug-in to enable mutual calls between local applications and applications deployed in EDAS, which is called end-to-cloud interconnection. This way, you do not need to set up a VPN and can improve development efficiency. For more information, see Overview of end-to-cloud interconnection.

**Procedure**

#### Implement load balancing

Spring Cloud uses Ribbon components to balance loads. Ribbon provides load balancing algorithms for software at clients. In Spring Cloud, the underlying load balancing for RestTemplate and FeignClient is implemented by Ribbon.

**Background information**

Spring Cloud Alibaba Cloud Application Naming Service (ANS) integrates with Ribbon. The AnsServerList class implements the com.netflix.loadbalancer.ServerList interface provided by Ribbon. This interface is generic. Other service discovery components, such as Nacos, Eureka, Consul, and ZooKeeper, also implement corresponding ServerList interfaces, such as NacosServerList, DomainExtractingServerList, ConsulServerList, and ZookeeperServerList. By implementing this interface, your application adopts the Spring Cloud load balancing specification. When you switch from service discovery solutions such as Eureka, Consul, or ZooKeeper to the Spring Cloud Alibaba service discovery solution, you can implement load balancing without changing any code for RestTemplate, FeignClient, or the deprecated AsyncRestTemplate. The implementation methods for RestTemplate and Feign are different. The following sections describe how to use load balancing with RestTemplate and Feign in your application. This topic describes key information for local development. For a complete Spring Cloud program example, download service-provider and service-consumer.

**RestTemplate**

evelopment RestTemplate is a client that is provided by Spring Cloud to access RESTful services. It provides multiple convenient methods to access remote HTTP services. This makes code compiling at clients more efficient. To use load balancing of RestTemplate, modify the code in your application based on the following example:

```java
public class MyApp {
    // Inject the RestTemplate that was constructed with the @LoadBalanced annotation.
    // This annotation adds a LoadBalancerInterceptor to the RestTemplate.
    // The LoadBalancerInterceptor internally uses RibbonLoadBalancerClient, an
implementation class of the LoadBalancerClient interface, to perform load balancing.
    @Autowired
    private RestTemplate restTemplate;
    @LoadBalanced // Use the @LoadBalanced annotation to modify the constructed RestTem
plate to enable load balancing.
    @Bean
    public RestTemplate restTemplate() {
        return new RestTemplate();
```

`}`

```
    // Use RestTemplate to call a service. Load balancing is used internally for the ca
ll.
    public void doSomething() {
        Foo foo = restTemplate.getForObject("http://service-provider/query",
Foo.class);
        doWithFoo(foo);
```

`}`

```
    ...
```

`}`

Feign is an HTTP client that is implemented in Java to simplify RESTful API calls. To implement load balancing on Feign, perform the following steps:


2. Use the @EnableFeignClients and @FeignClient annotations to make load-balanced
requests. i. Use the @EnableFeignClients annotation to enable Feign.

```java
@SpringBootApplication @EnableFeignClients // Enable the Feign feature. public class MyApplication { ...
```

`}` evelopment ii. Use the @FeignClient annotation to define a Feign client.

```
@FeignClient(name = "service-provider") public interface EchoService { @RequestMapping(value = "/echo/{str}", method = RequestMethod.GET) String echo(@PathVariable("str") String str);
```

`}` iii. Inject EchoService and call the echo method. When you call the echo method, an HTTP request is initiated.

```java
public class MyService { @Autowired // Inject the EchoService that was constructed with the @FeignClient ann otation. private EchoService echoService; public void doSomething() { echoService.echo("test"); // This is equivalent to sending a request to http://service-provider/echo/test.
```

`}`

```

```

`}`

#### Implement configuration management

When developing Spring Cloud applications, you can use Nacos (https://nacos.io) to manage application configurations in on-premises environments. Nacos is an open-source implementation of Application Configuration Management (ACM). After deploying an application to Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS), you can manage and push application configurations using the integrated ACM service. You can follow the instructions in this topic to develop a sample application from scratch and use Spring Cloud Alibaba Nacos Config to manage configurations. You can also download the nacos-config-example demo.

**Note**

Spring Cloud Alibaba Nacos Config integrates the Nacos and Spring Cloud frameworks and supports the configuration injection specification of Spring Cloud.

**Preparations**

Before you start, make sure that you have completed the following tasks: evelopment Download Maven and set the environment variables. Download the latest version of Nacos Server. Start Nacos Server. i. Decompress the downloaded Nacos Server package. ii. Go to the `nacos/bin` directory to start Nacos Server. On Linux, Unix, or macOS, run the `sh startup.sh -m standalone` command. On Windows, double-click the `startup.cmd` file. Create a configuration in the on-premises Nacos Server console. i. Log on to the on-premises Nacos Server console. The default username and password are both nacos. ii. In the navigation pane on the left, click **Configurations**. On the **Configurations** page, click the Create Configuration icon in the upper-right corner. iii. On the **Create Configuration** page, set the following parameters and click **Publish**.

#### Build a service gateway

This topic describes how to use Nacos with Spring Cloud Gateway and Spring Cloud Netflix Zuul to build a service gateway for your application.

**Why use the EDAS service registry for a service gateway**

The Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS) service registry is the commercial version of the open source Nacos Server. Applications developed with the open source `Spring Cloud Alibaba Nacos Discovery` can directly use the commercial service registry provided by EDAS. Compared with the open source versions of Nacos, Eureka, and Consul, the commercial version of the EDAS service registry offers the following advantages: Shared components: Reduces the cost of deploying and maintaining Nacos, Eureka, or Consul. Link encryption: Encrypts traffic during service registration and discovery. This protects your services from being discovered by unauthorized applications. Tight integration: The EDAS service registry is tightly integrated with other EDAS components to provide a complete microservice solution that includes features such as environment isolation, graceful online and offline operations, and phased releases.

**Preparations**

Download Maven and set the environment variables. You can skip this step if Maven is already installed. Download the latest version of Nacos Server. ### Use Dubbo to develop

**applications**

#### Dubbo overview

EDAS supports the native Dubbo microservice framework. By adding dependencies and modifying configurations, you can enable enterprise-level EDAS capabilities for microservices developed in this framework without modifying your code. These capabilities include application hosting, microservice administration, monitoring and alerts, and application diagnostics.

**Dubbo architecture**

The following figure shows the Dubbo architecture. Figure 1. Dubbo architecture evelopment Initializatio Asynchron Sync Registry 3. 2. Subscribe Register 4. Notify 5. Invoke Consumer Provider Service running container 6. Statistics Monitoring center
1. The service running container starts, loads, and runs providers.
2. During startup, the provider registers with the registry.
3. During startup, the consumer subscribes to required services from the registry.
4. The registry returns a list of provider addresses to the consumer. If the list changes, the
registry pushes the updated data to the consumer over a persistent connection.
5. The consumer selects a provider from the list of provider addresses based on a software
load balancing algorithm. If the call fails, the consumer calls another provider.
6. The consumer and provider store the cumulative number of calls and call durations in
memory. Every minute, they send statistical data to the monitoring center.

#### Use Spring Boot to develop Dubbo

**microservice applications**

Spring Boot simplifies the configuration and deployment of microservice applications. This lets you choose your own registry and configuration management. This topic describes how to use Spring Boot annotations to develop a sample Dubbo microservice application that uses Nacos. If you have an existing Dubbo application developed with Spring Boot, you can skip this topic and deploy the application directly to EDAS.

### Use HSF to develop

**applications**

#### HSF overview

High-speed Service Framework (HSF) is a distributed remote procedure call (RPC) service framework that is widely used within Alibaba. HSF connects different business systems and decouples their implementation dependencies. HSF provides a unified method for publishing and invoking services for distributed applications. This simplifies the development of distributed applications and the process of providing or using shared functional modules. HSF also abstracts away complex technical details, such as remote communication, serialization, performance overhead, and the implementation of synchronous or asynchronous calls.

**HSF architecture**

HSF is a client-only RPC framework and has no server-side cluster. All HSF service invocations are point-to-point between service consumers (Consumers) and service providers (Providers). However, to implement a complete distributed service system, HSF depends on the following external systems. Figure 1. HSF architecture evelopment Address registry Persistent configuration center ConfigServer Diamond HSF console
2. Subscribe to address
1. Register address

| Subscribe to service governance rule |   | s |
|---|---|---|
|   | Service consumer |   |

3. RPC
invocation Report Service provider Metadata storage metadata HSF Provider center HSFC Rdi Address registry HSF depends on a registry for service discovery. Without a registry, service providers cannot publish their service information, and service consumers cannot discover the machines that provide the services. This limits HSF to simple point-to-point calls. The registry acts as an intermediary for service information to enable service discovery. ConfigServer is used as the address registry. Persistent configuration center The persistent configuration center stores various governance rules for HSF services. During startup, HSF clients subscribe to these service governance rules, such as routing rules, grouping rules, and weight rules. This allows clients to influence the address selection logic during the invocation process based on these rules. Diamond is used as the persistent configuration center. Metadata storage center Metadata refers to information about HSF services, such as method lists and parameter structures. The metadata storage center is not a mandatory dependency because metadata does not affect the HSF invocation process. However, to simplify service O&M, HSF clients report metadata to the metadata storage center during startup. The metadata can then be used for various O&M tasks. Redis is used as the metadata storage center.

**Features**

As a distributed RPC service framework, HSF supports several service invocation methods. Synchronous call By default, HSF clients use synchronous calls to consume services. In this mode, the client code waits for a result to be returned after making a call. Asynchronous call For service calls that do not require an immediate response, HSF provides asynchronous calls. This prevents the client from being blocked by an HSF call operation. HSF supports two types of asynchronous calls: Future call: The client actively retrieves the invocation result by calling `HSFResponseFuture.getResponse(int timeout)` when the result is needed. Callback: This call uses HSF's internal callback mechanism. After an HSF service call is completed and returns a result, the HSF framework invokes the user-implemented `HSFResponseCallback` interface. The client then receives the result through a callback notification. Generalized call evelopment In a typical HSF call, the client depends on the service's second-party package and uses the APIs in that package to make programmatic calls and obtain results. A generalized call, however, lets you initiate an HSF call and obtain results without depending on the service's second-party package. In some platform products, generalized calls can significantly reduce dependencies on second-party packages, which allows the system to run in a lightweight mode. Invocation filter extension HSF includes a built-in invocation filter. HSF can automatically discover user-defined filter extensions and integrate them into the HSF invocation chain. This allows developers to add custom processing logic to HSF requests.

**Application development methods**

You can develop applications with the HSF framework in two ways: with Ali-Tomcat or with Pandora Boot.
**Ali-Tomcat**: This method depends on Ali-Tomcat and Pandora and provides all HSF
features. These features include service registration and discovery, implicit parameter passing, asynchronous calls, generalized calls, and invocation filter extensions. The application must be deployed as a WAR package.
**Pandora Boot**: This method depends on Pandora and provides most HSF features,
including service registration and discovery and asynchronous calls. The application can be packaged into a standalone JAR file for deployment.

The lightweight configuration registry uses ports 8080, 8848, and 9600. We recommend that you install and start the registry on a dedicated machine. If you use the registry on your local machine, change the ports for your application to avoid conflicts.

#### Use Ali-Tomcat to develop applications

##### Ali-Tomcat overview

evelopment Ali-Tomcat and Pandora are required to develop High-speed Service Framework (HSF) applications. Ali-Tomcat is a runtime container required by services in Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS). It integrates core features such as service publishing, subscription, and call tracing. You can publish applications in this container in both development and runtime environments. Pandora is a lightweight isolation container, also known as taobao-hsf.sar. It isolates dependencies between applications and middleware, and between different middleware. Pandora for EDAS integrates various middleware plug-ins for features such as service discovery, configuration push, and call tracing. You can use these plug-ins to monitor, administer, track, and analyze EDAS applications for comprehensive operations and maintenance (O&M).

**Note**

In EDAS, only HSF applications in WAR package format require Ali-Tomcat.

###### Define service interfaces

HSF services are implemented based on interfaces. After an interface is defined, the provider can implement a specific service through this interface. The consumer also subscribes to the service over this interface.

**Background information**

**Important**

This topic only describes how to define a service interface. However, in actual application scenarios, you need to add routes in an interface and implement them through an instance because definition alone is inadequate.

**Procedure**

1. In the demo project, locate the itemcenter-api folder, and locate and open the
ItemService.java file. In the file, the service interface com.alibaba.edas.carshop.itemcenter.ItemService is defined and has the following content:

```
public interface ItemService {
 public Item getItemById( long id );
 public Item getItemByName( String name );
```

`}` evelopment The interface provides two methods: getItemById and getItemByName, indicating that the com.alibaba.edas.carshop.itemcenter.ItemService service provides the getItemById and getItemByName methods.
2. Define new service interfaces based on planning or actual implementation.

###### Implement services as a provider

The provider implements an interface to provide specific services. Besides code implementation, you must define the XML file used for service publishing because HSF is implemented based on the Spring framework.

```java
        Item car = new Item();
        car.setItemId( 1l );
        car.setItemName( "Mercedes Benz" );
        return car;
```

`}`

```java
    @Override
```

`}` `}`

This topic describes how to configure provider services.

**Background information**

Then, use the <hsf /> tag in the Spring profile to register and publish the service.

**Procedure**

1. Add the following Maven dependencies to the pom.xml file:

```xml
<dependencies> <dependency> <groupId>javax.servlet</groupId> <artifactId>servlet-api</artifactId> <version>2.5</version> <scope>provided</scope> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId>com.alibaba.edas.carshop</groupId> <artifactId>itemcenter-api</artifactId> <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId>org.springframework</groupId> <artifactId>spring-web</artifactId> <version>2.5.6 (or later)</version> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId>com.alibaba.edas</groupId> <artifactId>edas-sdk</artifactId> <version>1.5.0</version> </dependency> </dependencies>
```

2. Add the HSF-specific Spring configurations. The following content of the HSF profile

```
<? xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"? > <beans xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:hsf="http://www.taobao.com/hsf" xmlns="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans" xsi:schemaLocation="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans/spring-beans-2.5.xsd http://www.taobao.com/hsf http://www.taobao.com/hsf/hsf.xsd" default-autowire="byName"> <! -- Define the specific implementation of the service. --> <bean id="itemService" class="com.alibaba.edas.carshop.itemcenter.ItemServiceImpl" /> <! -- Use the hsf:provider tag to define a service provider. --> <hsf:provider id="itemServiceProvider" <! -- Use the interface property to indicate that the service is an implementation of the interface class. --> interface="com.alibaba.edas.carshop.itemcenter.ItemService" <! -- The Spring object that is implemented by the service --> ref="itemService" <! -- The version number of the published service. The version number is user-defined and the default value is 1.0.0. --> version="1.0.0" </hsf:provider> </beans>
```

###### Checklist of provider configuration

**properties**

This topic describes the configuration properties for a provider. The following properties are available for configuring a High-Speed Service Framework (HSF) provider:

| Property | Description |
|---|---|
| interface | Required. The interface that the service provides. The value must be a string. |
| version | Optional. The version of the service. The value must be a string. The default value is 1.0.0. |
| clientTimeout | This property applies to all methods in the interface. However, if a client specifies a timeout for a method using the methodSpecial property, the timeout configured on the client prevails for that method. Other methods are not affected and still use the timeout that is configured on the provider. |
| serializeType | Optional. The serialization type. The value must be a string. Valid values: hessian and java. Default value: hessian. |
| corePoolSize | Specifies the core thread pool for this service. This creates a dedicated thread pool partitioned from the common thread pool. |
| maxPoolSize | Specifies the maximum thread pool size for this service. This creates a dedicated thread pool partitioned from the common thread pool. |
| enableTXC | Enables distributed transactions with GTS. |
| ref | Required. The ID of the Spring Bean to publish as an HSF service. |
| methodSpecials | Optional. Configures a specific timeout for a method in milliseconds (ms). This allows methods in an interface to have different timeouts. This configuration has a higher priority than clientTimeout but a lower priority than the client-side methodSpecials configuration. |

Tag configuration example: evelopment

```xml
<bean id="impl" class="com.taobao.edas.service.impl.SimpleServiceImpl" />
    <hsf:provider id="simpleService" interface="com.taobao.edas.service.SimpleService"
        ref="impl" version="1.0.1"  clientTimeout="3000" enableTXC="true"
        serializeType="hessian">
        <hsf:methodSpecials>
            <hsf:methodSpecial name="sum" timeout="2000" />
        </hsf:methodSpecials>
    </hsf:provider>
```

###### Other JVM startup parameters

This topic describes additional JVM startup parameters. You can use the following startup parameters for the service provider to change the behavior of the High-Speed Service Framework (HSF).

| Property | Description |
|---|---|
| -Dhsf.server.port | Specifies the port that the HSF startup service binds to. The default value is 12200 . |
| -Dhsf.serializer | Specifies the serialization method for HSF. The default value is hessian . |
| -Dhsf.server.max.poolsize | Specifies the maximum size of the HSF provider thread pool. The default value is 600 . |
| -Dhsf.server.min.poolsize | Specifies the minimum size of the HSF provider thread pool. The default value is 50 . |

###### Subscribe to services as a consumer

evelopment Service subscription for consumers is coded in two steps. In the first step, use the <hsf:consumer/> tag in the Spring profile to define a bean. In the second step, the bean can be retrieved from the Spring context when you use the bean. In the demo project, detail shows a consumer-specific example.

###### Consumer configuration

This topic describes the service configuration for consumers. A consumer's configuration file includes Maven dependencies and Spring configurations, similar to a producer. The Maven dependencies are the same for both. For more information, see Service configuration. In addition to the required Spring configurations, you must add a consumer definition to the Spring configuration file. The High-Speed Service Framework (HSF) uses this definition to subscribe to required services from the service center. The following code shows the content of the /resource/hsf-consumer-beans.xml file and provides explanations:

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?> <beans xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
       xmlns:hsf="http://www.taobao.com/hsf"
       xmlns="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans"
       xsi:schemaLocation="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans
       http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans/spring-beans-2.5.xsd
       http://www.taobao.com/hsf
       http://www.taobao.com/hsf/hsf.xsd" default-autowire="byName">
    <!-- Example of consuming a service -->
    <hsf:consumer
        <!-- The bean ID. Use this ID to inject and use the object in your code. -->
            id="item"
        <!-- The service name. This must match the corresponding configuration of the s
ervice provider. HSF queries and subscribes to the required service based on the interf ace and version. -->
            interface="com.alibaba.edas.carshop.itemcenter.ItemService"
        <!-- The version number. This must match the corresponding configuration of the
service provider. HSF queries and subscribes to the required service based on the inter face and version. -->
            version="1.0.0"
    </hsf:consumer>
</beans>
```

###### Act as a consumer to use services

This topic provides sample code for consuming a service. The following sample code is from the demo: evelopment

```java
public class StartListener implements ServletContextListener{
    @Override
    public void contextInitialized( ServletContextEvent sce ) {
        ApplicationContext ctx = WebApplicationContextUtils.getWebApplicationContext( s
ce.getServletContext() );
        // Get the subscribed service based on the bean ID "item" in the Spring
configuration.
        final ItemService itemService = ( ItemService ) ctx.getBean( "item" );
        ...
        // Call the getItemById method of ItemService.
        System.out.println( itemService.getItemById( 1111 ) );
        // Call the getItemByName method of ItemService.
        System.out.println( itemService.getItemByName( "myname is le" ) );
        ...
```

`}` `}`

###### Consumer configuration properties

This topic describes the consumer configuration properties. In addition to the `Interface` and `Version` properties shown in the sample code, you can also use the properties listed in the following table.

| Property | Description |
|---|---|
| interface | Required. A string that specifies the interface of the service to call. |
| version | Optional. A string that specifies the version of the service to call. The default value is 1.0.0. |
| methodSpecials | Optional. Configures a specific timeout period in milliseconds (ms) for each method. This allows different methods in the same interface to have different timeout periods. This configuration has a higher priority than the timeout configuration on the service provider side. |
| target | This property is mainly used in unit testing environments and in development environments where `hsf.runmode` is set to `0`. In a runtime environment, this property is invalid. Instead, the target service address pushed from the configuration center is used. |
| connectionNum | Optional. Specifies the number of connections to the server. The default value is 1. For small data transfers that require low latency, you can increase this value to improve Transactions Per Second (TPS). |

evelopment

| clientTimeout | Sets a uniform timeout period in milliseconds (ms) for all methods in an interface. The priority of timeout settings, from highest to lowest, is: consumer `MethodSpecial`, consumer interface level, provider `MethodSpecial`, and provider interface level. |
|---|---|
| asyncallMethods | Optional. A list of method names that must be invoked asynchronously when calling this service. By default, this property is an empty collection, which means all methods are invoked synchronously. |
| maxWaitTimeForCsA ddress | Configures the time that a thread waits for a service address to be pushed when a service is subscribed. This blocking period prevents "address not found" errors that can occur if the service is called before its address is available. If the address is not pushed before the time expires, the thread stops waiting and proceeds with initialization. |

The following code provides an example of a tag configuration.

```xml
<hsf:consumer id="service" interface="com.taobao.edas.service.SimpleService"
        version="1.1.0" clientTimeout="3000"
        target="10.1.6.57:12200?_TIMEOUT=1000" maxWaitTimeForCsAddress="5000">
               <hsf:methodSpecials>
            <hsf:methodSpecial name="sum" timeout="2000" />
        </hsf:methodSpecials>
    </hsf:consumer>
```

This topic describes how to use the features of High-speed Service Framework (HSF). A Demo that covers all features is available for download.

###### Add the edas-sdk dependency to the

**pom.xml file**

This topic describes how to add the edas-sdk dependency to the pom.xml file. To use High-speed Service Framework (HSF) features, add the following edas-sdk dependency to the pom.xml file:

```xml
<dependency>
```

###### Implicit parameter passing

evelopment In most cases, implicit parameter passing is used to pass simple key-value (KV) data based on a method that does not call API operations. This method is similar to cookies. Only strings can be passed in parameters. You can pass a single parameter or multiple parameters.

**Pass a single parameter**

Service consumer:

```
RpcContext.getContext().setAttachment("key", "args test");
```

Service provider:

```
String keyVal=RpcContext.getContext().getAttachment("key");
```

**Pass multiple parameters**

Service consumer:

```
Map<String,String> map=new HashMap<String,String>(); map.put("param1", "param1 test"); map.put("param2", "param2 test"); map.put("param3", "param3 test"); map.put("param4", "param4 test"); map.put("param5", "param5 test"); RpcContext rpcContext = RpcContext.getContext(); rpcContext.setAttachments(map);
```

Service provider:

```java
Map<String,String> map=rpcContext.getAttachments(); Set<String> set=map.keySet(); for (String key : set) { System.out.println("map value:"+map.get(key));
```

`}`

###### Asynchronous calls

You can implement asynchronous calls using Callback or Future methods.

**Callback method**

When using the callback method, configure a listener on the client that implements the HSFResponseCallback interface. After the result is returned, High-speed Service Framework (HSF) calls the method in the HSFResponseCallback interface.

**Important**

The listener for the HSFResponseCallback interface cannot be an inner class. Otherwise, the Pandora classloader reports an error during loading. XML configuration: evelopment

```xml
<hsf:consumer id="demoApi" interface="com.alibaba.demo.api.DemoApi"
    version="1.1.2">
    <hsf:asyncallMethods>
    <hsf:method name="ayncTest" type="callback"
    listener="com.alibaba.ifree.hsf.consumer.AsynABTestCallbackHandler" />
    </hsf:asyncallMethods>
</hsf:consumer>
```

In the preceding configuration, the AsynABTestCallbackHandler class implements the HSFResponseCallback interface. The DemoApi interface contains an asyncTest method. Code example:

```java
public void onAppResponse(Object appResponse) { // Get the value after the asynchronous invocation. String msg = (String)appResponse; System.out.println("msg:"+msg);
```

`}`

**Note**

Methods are identified only by name. Therefore, the system does not distinguish between overloaded methods. Methods that have the same name are set to the same invocation type. Do not initiate another HSF call from within an existing call. This can cause the I/O thread to suspend and prevent it from resuming.

**Future method**

If you use the future method on the client, you can retrieve the result by calling public static Object getResponse(long timeout) in HSFResponseFuture after the invocation. XML configuration:

```xml
<hsf:consumer id="demoApi" interface="com.alibaba.demo.api.DemoApi" version="1.1.2"> <hsf:asyncallMethods>
        <hsf:method name="ayncTest" type="future"  />
</hsf:asyncallMethods> </hsf:consumer>
```

The following are code examples: Asynchronous processing for a single operation:

```
// Initiate the call. demoApi.ayncTest(); // Process the business logic. ... // Directly get the message. You can skip this step if you do not need the result. String msg=(String) HSFResponseFuture.getResponse(3000);
```

evelopment Concurrent processing for multiple operations: For concurrent processing of multiple operations, first obtain the futures, store them, and then use them after the calls are complete.

```
// Define a collection. List<HSFFuture> futures = new ArrayList<HSFFuture>();
```

Parallel invocation within a method:

```
// Initiate the call. demoApi.ayncTest(); // First, get the future object. HSFFuture future=HSFResponseFuture.getFuture(); futures.add(future); // Call other services asynchronously. HSFFuture future=HSFResponseFuture.getFuture(); futures.add(future); // Process the business logic. ... // Get the data and process it. for (HSFFuture hsfFuture : futures) { String msg=(String) hsfFuture.getResponse(3000); // Process the corresponding data. ...
```

`}`

###### Generic calls

Generic calls do not depend on service APIs and can combine interfaces, methods, and parameters for remote procedure calls (RPCs).

**Procedure**

1. Add the generic property to the service consumer configuration.

```
<hsf:consumer id="demoApi" interface="com.alibaba.demo.api.DemoApi" generic="true"/>
```

**Note**

The generic property indicates generic parameters. The value true indicates that generic parameters are supported, and the value false indicates that generic parameters are not supported. The default value is false. The following code describes the DemoApi method:

```
public String dealMsg(String msg); public GenericTestDO dealGenericTestDO(GenericTestDO testDO);
```

methodName: the name of the method that you want to call parameterTypes: the type of the parameters of the method that you want to call args: the parameter value that you want to pass.


###### Query services

Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS) supports service registration for Dubbo and High-speed Service Framework (HSF). However, you cannot view Dubbo services in the EDAS console if they are published to an external registry, such as ZooKeeper. This topic describes how to query HSF services.

###### Query HSF services in a development

**environment**

During development and debugging, if you use the lightweight configuration center for service registration and discovery, you can query the corresponding service providers and consumers in the administration console.

**Background information**

evelopment This topic describes how to query High-speed Service Framework (HSF) services in the Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS) configuration center. For this example, assume that you have started the configuration center on a machine with the IP address 192.168.1.100.

**Procedure**

1. Open your browser, enter http://192.168.1.100:8080/ in the address bar, and log on to the
EDAS configuration center.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, click **Service List**. Enter a **service name**, a **service**
**group name**, or an **IP address**, and then click **Search**.

**Important**

By default, after the configuration center starts, it uses the address of the first network interface card (NIC) for service discovery. If a developer's machine has multiple NICs, you can set the `SERVER_IP` variable in the startup script to explicitly bind an address.
3. View the corresponding service providers and service consumers.
Providers list page Enter an IP address in the search box and click **Search** to find the services that are provided by the machine with that IP address. Enter a service name or service group in the search box to find the IP addresses that provide this service. Consumers list page Enter an IP address in the search box and click **Search** to find the services that are invoked by the machine with that IP address. Enter a service name or service group in the search box to find the IP addresses that have invoked this service.

###### Query HSF services in an online

**environment**

After developed services are packaged and deployed in the Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS) console and the applications are confirmed to start properly, you can query the services in the EDAS console.

**Procedure**

1. Log in to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Application Management > Application List**.
3. On the **Applications** page, click the name of a specific application.
4. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Services**.
The Services page consists of the **Published services** and **Services consumed** tabs.
**Published services** display the service providers that you have configured for the
application. **Services consumed** display the service consumers that you have configured for the application. evelopment

**Important**

If you log on as a RAM user, confirm that you have the permissions to view the **Service**
**List** page. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **System Administration > All**
**Permissions**. On the Permission Management page, verify that you have permission to
view the service list under **Application List**.

**FAQ**

If the service that you want to query does not appear in the corresponding service list, perform the following steps to troubleshoot the issue: Confirm that the service is configured correctly in the code. Confirm that the Tomcat process for the service starts properly and that no errors are reported in the logs. Check the TOMCAT_HOME/logs/catalina.out and $TOMCAT_HOME/logs/localhost.log.$DATE_FORMAT files. Confirm that you are using the latest software version. To check the version, choose
**Software Version** in the navigation pane on the left of the service information page. If you
are not using the latest version, confirm that the corresponding HSF group is created. Confirm that the machine's host does not have special network bindings. Normally, online machines do not require any host bindings. Confirm that the network and Elastic Compute Service (ECS) security group configurations for the machine do not have obvious restrictions.

##### Migrate Dubbo applications to HSF (not

**recommended)**

###### Notes for developing Dubbo applications

This topic describes considerations for developing Dubbo applications.
1. Dubbo configuration files support multiple consumer groups. However, Enterprise
Distributed Application Service (EDAS) supports only a single group that is configured using the group property.
2. In Dubbo, you must specify the version information when you consume a service, for
example, version="1.0.0". In EDAS, you can omit this field because the version is 1.0.0 by default.
3. The remote procedure call (RPC) framework of Dubbo supports various protocols, such as
remote method invocation (RMI) and Hessian. However, EDAS supports only the Dubbo protocol. For example, you must specify <dubbo:protocol name="dubbo" port="20880">. Using other protocols causes an error similar to the following: "com.alibaba.dubbo.config.ServiceConfig service [xx.xx.xxx] contain xx protocal, HSF not supportted".
4. The method for retrieving RPC contextual information differs between Dubbo and EDAS.
Dubbo uses the RpcContext.getContext() method, while EDAS uses com.taobao.hsf.util.RequestCtxUtil through its internal High-speed Service Framework (HSF). After a service is transformed for EDAS, calling RpcContext.getContext() causes the following error: "Caused by: java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException: not support getInvocation method in HSF".

###### Modify Dubbo application configurations

evelopment You can migrate applications developed using Dubbo to HSF by steps such as modifying the application configuration, configuring multiple registries, and converting JAR to WAR. However, we recommend that new users do not use this method because EDAS supports applications in the native Dubbo framework. For more information about developing applications that use the native Dubbo framework, see Develop Dubbo microservice applications with Spring Boot. EDAS supports two methods for configuring Dubbo applications, which can be producers or consumers: XML file configuration and annotation configuration. This topic provides examples of both methods. XML configuration for a producer

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?> <beans xmlns="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans"
    xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
xmlns:dubbo="http://code.alibabatech.com/schema/dubbo"
    xsi:schemaLocation="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans
http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans/spring-beans.xsd
    http://code.alibabatech.com/schema/dubbo
http://code.alibabatech.com/schema/dubbo/dubbo.xsd">
    <dubbo:application name="edas-dubbo-demo-provider" ></dubbo:application>
    <bean id="demoProvider" class="com.alibaba.edas.dubbo.demo.provider.DemoProvider"
></bean>
    <dubbo:registry address="zookeeper://127.0.0.1:2181" ></dubbo:registry>
    <dubbo:protocol name="dubbo" port="20880" threadpool="cached"
        threads="100" ></dubbo:protocol>
    <dubbo:service delay="-1" interface="com.alibaba.edas.dubbo.demo.api.DemoApi"
        ref="demoProvider" version="1.0.0" group="dubbogroup" retries="3"
timeout="3000"></dubbo:service> </beans>
```

**Note**

The following parameters are optional: threadpool, threads, delay, version, retries, and timeout. All other options are required. You can change the order of the parameters in the XML file as needed. XML configuration for a consumer evelopment

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?> <beans xmlns="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans"
    xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
xmlns:dubbo="http://code.alibabatech.com/schema/dubbo"
    xsi:schemaLocation="http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans
http://www.springframework.org/schema/beans/spring-beans-2.5.xsd
    http://code.alibabatech.com/schema/dubbo
http://code.alibabatech.com/schema/dubbo/dubbo.xsd">
    <dubbo:application name="edas-dubbo-consumer" />
    <dubbo:registry address="zookeeper://127.0.0.1:2181" />
    <dubbo:reference id="demoProviderApi"
        interface="com.alibaba.edas.dubbo.demo.api.DemoApi" version="1.0.0"
group="dubbogroup" lazy="true" loadbalance="random">
        <!-- Specify a method that does not need to wait for a return value -->
        <dubbo:method name="sayMsg" async="true" return="false" />
    </dubbo:reference>
    <bean id="demoConsumer" class="com.alibaba.edas.dubbo.demo.consumer.DemoConsumer"
        init-method="reviceMsg">
        <property name="demoApi" ref="demoProviderApi"></property>
    </bean>
</beans>
```

**Note**

The following parameters are optional: version, group, lazy, loadbalance, async, and return. All other options are required. You can change the order of the parameters in the XML file as needed. Registry configurations do not take effect in EDAS. All Dubbo services are automatically registered with the EDAS configuration center. No manual configuration is required.

| Implicit parameter passing | None | None | None | Support |

#### Use Pandora Boot to develop

**applications**

##### Pandora Boot overview

Pandora Boot is a lightweight service built on Pandora. Pandora Boot is based on Pandora and Fat Jar technologies. You can start a Pandora environment directly in an Integrated Development Environment (IDE), which greatly improves your development and debugging efficiency. Pandora Boot is deeply integrated with Spring Boot AutoConfigure, allowing you to benefit from the convenience of the Spring Boot framework. Both Spring Boot users who need High-speed Service Framework (HSF) and existing Pandora Boot users can use Pandora Boot to develop Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS) applications.

##### Configure the local repository path and

**the lightweight configuration center of EDAS**

evelopment Before you use Pandora Boot to develop High-speed Service Framework (HSF) applications, you must configure the local repository path and the lightweight configuration center of Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS). Third-party packages of Spring Cloud for Aliware are released only in the local repository of EDAS. Therefore, you must configure the local repository path of EDAS in Maven. The lightweight configuration center must be started for on-premises development and debugging. The lightweight configuration center provides the lightweight version of EDAS service discovery and configuration management.

##### Use Pandora Boot to develop HSF

**applications**

evelopment Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS) fully supports Spring Cloud applications. Therefore, you can directly deploy Spring Cloud applications to EDAS. Spring Boot is based on the "Build Anything" concept. It simplifies complex XML configuration problems. Spring Cloud is based on the "Coordinate Anything" concept. It simplifies distributed microservice development by providing many spring-cloud-starter components for easy integration. EDAS also implements its own Spring Cloud Starter HSF. Therefore, you can use Spring Cloud to develop High-speed Service Framework (HSF) applications. This topic describes how to use Spring Cloud to develop HSF applications.

###### Example of HSF application development

This topic provides an example to demonstrate how to develop an HSF application based on Spring Cloud. To develop an HSF application, you must create a service provider and a service consumer.

###### Create a service provider

Learn how to create a service provider and publish services through an interface.

**Procedure**

1. Create a Spring Cloud project and name it sc-hsf-provider.
2. Add the required dependencies to the pom.xml file.
evelopment

```xml
 <parent>
     <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
     <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
     <version>1.5.8.RELEASE</version>
     <relativePath/>
 </parent>
 <dependencies>
     <dependency>
         <groupId>org.springframework.cloud</groupId>
         <artifactId>spring-cloud-starter-hsf</artifactId>
         <version>1.1</version>
     </dependency>
     <dependency>
         <groupId>org.springframework.cloud</groupId>
         <artifactId>spring-cloud-starter-pandora</artifactId>
         <version>1.2</version>
     </dependency>
     <dependency>
         <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
         <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
     </dependency>
 </dependencies>
 <dependencyManagement>
     <dependencies>
         <dependency>
             <groupId>org.springframework.cloud</groupId>
             <artifactId>spring-cloud-dependencies</artifactId>
             <version>Dalston.SR4</version>
             <type>pom</type>
             <scope>import</scope>
         </dependency>
     </dependencies>
 </dependencyManagement>
```

The High-speed Service Framework (HSF) does not depend on a web environment. However, EDAS requires web-related features to manage the application lifecycle. Therefore, you must add the spring-boot-starter-web dependency. If you do not want to set the project's parent to spring-boot-starter-parent, you can manage dependency versions by adding dependencyManagement and setting the scope to import.

```xml
 <dependencyManagement>
     <dependencies>
         <dependency>
             <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
             <artifactId>spring-boot-dependencies</artifactId>
             <version>1.5.8.RELEASE</version>
             <type>pom</type>
             <scope>import</scope>
         </dependency>
     </dependencies>
 </dependencyManagement>
```

3. Define a service interface by creating an interface class named
com.aliware.edas.EchoService. evelopment

```
 public interface EchoService {
     String echo(String string);
```

`}` The HSF service framework uses interfaces for service communication. After an interface is defined, producers use it to implement and publish services. Consumers use the same interface to subscribe to and consume these services. The `com.aliware.edas.EchoService` interface provides an `echo` method. This means the `com.aliware.edas.EchoService` service also provides an `echo` method.
4. Add the EchoServiceImpl implementation class for the service provider and publish the
service using an annotation.

```java
 @HSFProvider(serviceInterface = EchoService.class, serviceVersion = "1.0.0")
 public class EchoServiceImpl implements EchoService {
     @Override
     public String echo(String string) {
         return string;
```

`}` `}` In addition to the `serviceInterface`, HSF requires a `serviceVersion` to uniquely identify a service. In this example, set the `serviceVersion` property in the `@HSFProvider` annotation to "1.0.0". The service is then identified by the combination of the `interface`

```
name com.aliware.edas.EchoService and the service version 1.0.0 .
```

Properties configured in the @HSFProvider annotation have the highest priority. If a property is not configured in the annotation, HSF searches for a global configuration for that property in the resources/application.properties file when the service is published. If the property is not found in either location, HSF uses the default value from the @HSFProvider annotation.
5. In the resources folder, configure the application name and listener port in the
application.properties file.

```
 spring.application.name=hsf-provider
 server.port=18081
 spring.hsf.version=1.0.0
 spring.hsf.timeout=3000
```

**Best practice**: Configure both the **service version** and the **service timeout** in the
`application.properties` file.
6. Add the main function entry point to start the service.

```java
 @SpringBootApplication
 public class HSFProviderApplication {
     public static void main(String[] args) {
         // Start Pandora Boot to load the Pandora container.
         PandoraBootstrap.run(args);
         SpringApplication.run(ServerApplication.class, args);
         // Mark the service as started and set the thread to wait. This prevents the
container from exiting after the business code finishes running.
         PandoraBootstrap.markStartupAndWait();
```

`}` `}` evelopment

###### Create a service consumer

This example shows how to create a service consumer. The consumer calls the service provider using the API that HSFProvider provides.

**Procedure**

1. Create a Spring Cloud project named sc-hsf-consumer.
2. Add the required dependencies to the pom.xml file:
The Maven dependencies for HSFConsumer and HSFProvider are identical.

```xml
 <parent>
     <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
     <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
     <version>1.5.8.RELEASE</version>
     <relativePath/>
 </parent>
 <dependencies>
     <dependency>
         <groupId>org.springframework.cloud</groupId>
         <artifactId>spring-cloud-starter-hsf</artifactId>
         <version>1.1</version>
     </dependency>
     <dependency>
         <groupId>org.springframework.cloud</groupId>
         <artifactId>spring-cloud-starter-pandora</artifactId>
         <version>1.2</version>
     </dependency>
     <dependency>
         <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
         <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
     </dependency>
 </dependencies>
 <dependencyManagement>
     <dependencies>
         <dependency>
             <groupId>org.springframework.cloud</groupId>
             <artifactId>spring-cloud-dependencies</artifactId>
             <version>Dalston.SR4</version>
             <type>pom</type>
             <scope>import</scope>
         </dependency>
     </dependencies>
 </dependencyManagement>
```

3. Copy the `com.aliware.edas.EchoService` service interface, including the package name,
from the service provider to your local project.

```
 public interface EchoService {
     String echo(String string);
```

`}`
4. Inject the **service consumer** instance into the Spring context using an annotation.
evelopment

```java
 @Configuration
 public class HsfConfig {
     @HSFConsumer(clientTimeout = 3000, serviceVersion = "1.0.0")
     private EchoService echoService;
```

`}`
**Best practices**: Configure @HSFConsumer once in the Config class. Then, inject and use it
in multiple places using @Autowired. An HSF Consumer is typically used in multiple places. Do not mark each place with @HSFConsumer. Instead, write a single Config class and directly inject it where it is needed using @Autowired.
5. For testing, use a SimpleController to expose an `/hsf-echo/*` HTTP endpoint. The `/hsf-`
`echo/*` endpoint calls the HSF service provider.

```java
 @RestController
 public class SimpleController {
     @Autowired
     private EchoService echoService;
     @RequestMapping(value = "/hsf-echo/{str}", method = RequestMethod.GET)
     public String echo(@PathVariable String str) {
         return echoService.echo(str);
```

`}` `}`
6. Configure the application name and listener port in the `application.properties` file in the
`resources` folder.

```
 spring.application.name=hsf-consumer
 server.port=18082
 spring.hsf.version=1.0.0
 spring.hsf.timeout=1000
```

**Best practices**: Configure both the **service version** and **service timeout** in the
`application.properties` file.
7. Add the main function entry point to start the service.

```java
 @SpringBootApplication
 public class HSFConsumerApplication {
     public static void main(String[] args) {
         PandoraBootstrap.run(args);
         SpringApplication.run(HSFConsumerApplication.class, args);
         PandoraBootstrap.markStartupAndWait();
```

`}` `}`

###### Advanced HSF features

This topic describes how to use Pandora Boot to develop advanced High-speed Service Framework (HSF) features, such as unit testing and asynchronous calls.

**Background information**

You can download the demo source code from sc-hsf-provider and sc-hsf-consumer.

**Procedure**

evelopment

**Unit testing**

The spring-cloud-starter-hsf implementation relies on Pandora Boot. To run unit tests for Pandora Boot, you can use PandoraBootRunner. It integrates seamlessly with SpringJUnit4ClassRunner.
1. Add the spring-boot-starter-test dependency in Maven.


###### Local debugging

After you develop a High-Speed Service Framework (HSF) application, debug the application locally before you publish it.

**Procedure**

1. Start the lightweight configuration center.
Use the lightweight configuration center for local development and debugging. The lightweight configuration center includes a lightweight version of the EDAS service registry for service providers. For more information, see Start the lightweight configuration and registration center.
2. Start the application.
You can start the application locally in two ways. Start in an integrated development environment (IDE) Configure the startup parameter **-Djmenv.tbsite.net={$IP}** in VM options and start the application using the main method. **{$IP}** is the IP address of the machine where the lightweight configuration center service is started. For example, if you start the lightweight configuration center on your local machine, set **{$IP}** to 127.0.0.1. Alternatively, instead of configuring Java Virtual Machine (JVM) parameters, you can modify the hosts file to bind **jmenv.tbsite.net** to the IP address of the machine where the lightweight configuration center service is started. For more information, see Start the lightweight configuration and registration center. Start using a FatJAR Add the FatJAR packaging plug-in. To package the pandora-boot project into a FatJAR using Maven, add the following plug-in to the pom.xml file.

**Note**

To prevent conflicts with other packaging plug-ins, do not add other FatJAR plug-ins to the plugin element in the build configuration.

```xml
  <build>
       <plugin>
           <groupId>com.taobao.pandora</groupId>
           <artifactId>pandora-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
           <version>2.1.7.8</version>
           <executions>
               <execution>
                   <phase>package</phase>
                   <goals>
                       <goal>repackage</goal>
                   </goals>
               </execution>
           </executions>
       </plugin>
  </build>
```

3. After you add the plug-in, run the Maven command `mvn clean package` in the project's
home directory. The packaged FatJAR file is generated in the target directory. evelopment

```
 java -Djmenv.tbsite.net=127.0.0.1 -
Dpandora.location=/Users/{$username}/.m2/repository/com/taobao/pandora/taobao-hsf.sar /dev-SNAPSHOT/taobao-hsf.sar-dev-SNAPSHOT.jar -jar sc-hsf-provider-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.ja
```

##### Develop RESTful applications (not

**recommended)**

This topic describes how to develop RESTful applications based on Spring Cloud in Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS).

###### Terms

This document explains terms and concepts that you may encounter when you develop applications based on Spring Cloud.

**Pandora**

Pandora is a lightweight isolation container used within Alibaba. It is used by Aliware to isolate and load classes. Pandora is a **required** dependency for using Spring Cloud with Aliware.

**VIPServer**

VIPServer is the service discovery server for RESTful applications in Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS). Its corresponding client is VIPClient.

**Lightweight configuration center**

evelopment The EDAS lightweight configuration center can run in an on-premises environment. It provides both service discovery and configuration management.

**FatJar**

A FatJar, also known as an executable JAR, is an archive that contains compiled classes and all the dependencies needed to run an application. You can use the `java -jar` command to run the application.

**EagleEye**

EagleEye is a distributed tracing system that is developed by Alibaba. It traces information based on the distributed tracing system of Google Dapper. EagleEye processes trillions of distributed trace data each day. It implements automatic tracking of logs by collecting and analyzing the data in various network calls to obtain trace relationships between systems for one request. This helps sort out the application request portals, service call sources, and dependencies. This also helps analyze system call bottlenecks, estimate the link capacities, and locate exceptions.

**HSF**

High-speed Service Framework (HSF) is a distributed service framework used within Alibaba. HSF supports developers of distributed applications by providing unified methods for publishing and invoking services. This makes it easier to develop distributed applications and to provide or use shared functional modules. Developers do not need to handle the complex details of distributed systems, such as remote communication, performance overhead, call transparency, or the implementation of synchronous or asynchronous call methods.

###### Service registration and discovery

This topic describes how to implement service registration and discovery by using Spring Cloud.

###### Preparations

Before you develop service registration and discovery using Spring Cloud, you must complete the required preparations.

**Configure the EDAS private repository address in Maven**

Third-party packages for Spring Cloud for Aliware are published only to the Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS) private repository. Therefore, you must configure the private repository address. For more information about configuring Maven and a Maven private repository, see the official documentation. The EDAS private repository address is http://edas-public.oss-cnhangzhou.aliyuncs.com/repository.

**Note**

Maven 3.x or later is required. Add the EDAS private server address to your Maven Settings file. You can download a sample file.

**Lightweight configuration center**

evelopment For local development and debugging, you must start the lightweight configuration center. The lightweight configuration center provides a lightweight version of EDAS service discovery and configuration management. For more information and downloads, see the Start the lightweight configuration center section.

###### Implement service registration and

**discovery**

This topic uses a simple example to describe how to discover and call services.

**Background information**

The process involves two roles: Service provider: Provides a simple echo service and registers itself with the service discovery center. Service consumer: Calls services using three clients: RestTemplate, AsyncRestTemplate, and FeignClient.

**Procedure**

The service provider implements a service and registers it with the service discovery center.

```java
.class);
```

###### FAQ

This topic describes possible issues and solutions for scenarios where service registration and discovery are implemented based on Spring Cloud.

**FAQ**

1. **AsyncRestTemplate cannot access service discovery.**
AsyncRestTemplate supports service discovery only in Spring Cloud Dalston and later versions. evelopment
2. **FatJar packaging plug-in conflicts.**
To avoid conflicts with other packaging plug-ins, do not add other FatJar plug-ins to the plugin element in the build.
3. **Can taobao-hsf.sar be included during packaging?**
Yes, it can, but this is not recommended. You can modify the pandora-boot-maven-plugin plug-in and set excludeSar to false. This automatically includes taobao-hsf.sar during packaging.

```xml
   <plugin>
     <groupId>com.taobao.pandora</groupId>
     <artifactId>pandora-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
     <version>2.1.7.8</version>
     <configuration>
       <excludeSar>false</excludeSar>
     </configuration>
     <executions>
         <execution>
             <phase>package</phase>
             <goals>
                 <goal>repackage</goal>
             </goals>
         </execution>
     </executions>
   </plugin>
```

After packaging, you can start the application without configuring a Pandora address.

```
java -jar -Dvipserver.server.port=8080 sc-vip-server-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar
```

Before you deploy the application to Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS), restore the default configuration to exclude taobao-hsf.sar.

###### Distributed tracing

To reduce development costs and improve development efficiency, EDAS provides the EagleEye component for distributed tracing. After the EagleEye tracking point is configured in the code, you can use the distributed tracing function of EDAS without considering log collection, analysis, and storage. This topic describes how to enable the distributed tracing feature of EDAS.

###### Connect to EagleEye

Before you use the distributed tracing feature, you must connect to EagleEye.

**Prerequisites**

Before you connect to EagleEye, you must configure the private server address for Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS) in your Maven settings.xml file. This step is necessary because third-party packages for Spring Cloud for Aliware are published only to the EDAS private server. ###### FAQ

This topic describes issues that may occur during distributed tracing and their solutions.

**Automatic tracking**

EagleEye in EDAS automatically tracks requests made by RestTemplate, AsyncRestTemplate, and FeignClient.

**AsyncRestTemplate**

AsyncRestTemplate must modify the automatic tracking configuration during the class instantiation phase. Therefore, the eagleEyeAsyncRestTemplate object must be injected to enable the distributed tracing feature. This object supports service discovery by default.

```java
@Autowired private AsyncRestTemplate eagleEyeAsyncRestTemplate;
```

**FatJar packaging plug-ins**

To create the pandora-boot project as a FatJar package in Maven, you must add the packaging plug-in of pandora-boot-maven-plugin to pom.xml. To prevent conflicts with other packaging plug-ins, do not add other FatJar plug-ins to the plugin field in build.

#### The HSF call process

This topic describes the call process of High-speed Service Framework (HSF). An HSF call is initiated by a consumer and sent to a provider over the network. The provider then returns the result to the consumer over the network. This process involves multithreaded interactions and various domain objects within HSF. The following figure shows the HSF call process. evelopment

| Proce dure | Description |
|---|---|
| 1 | The client thread serializes the request object, which contains the user's request parameters. The serialized content is stored in a request communication object. Note The request communication object corresponds to the HSF protocol. It includes information unrelated to the request object, such as the request ID. |
| 2 | The system passes the request communication object to an I/O thread, where it is encoded. |
| 3 | The encoded content is sent to the HSF provider's I/O thread. The client thread waits for a response. |
| 4 | The HSF provider's I/O thread receives the binary content. It decodes the content to generate a request communication object and passes the object to an HSF server thread. |
| 5 | The HSF server thread deserializes the communication object to restore the request object. |
| 6 | The server thread makes a reflective call and obtains the result: a response object. |
| 7 | The HSF server thread serializes the response object and stores it in a communication response object. |

evelopment

| 8 | The HSF server thread passes the communication response object to an I/O thread, where it is encoded. |
|---|---|
| 9 | The HSF provider sends the encoded content back to the HSF consumer. |
| 10 | The HSF consumer's I/O thread receives the binary content. It decodes the content to generate a response communication object and then wakes up the client thread. |
| 11 | The client thread deserializes the communication response object. The user receives the final response object, and the remote call is complete. |

#### Asynchronous calls

This topic describes how to make asynchronous calls in High-speed Service Framework (HSF).

**Prerequisites**

Before you develop an application, complete the following tasks: Configure the private server address and lightweight configuration center for EDAS. For more information, see Configure the private server address and lightweight configuration center for EDAS. Start the lightweight configuration and registration center. For more information, see Start the lightweight configuration and registration center.

**Synchronous calls**

In HSF, I/O operations are asynchronous. A synchronous call from a client essentially

| ms the | future.get(timeout) |   |
|---|---|---|
| timeout |   |   |
|   |   | is the timeout perio |

performs the `future.get(timeout)` operation and waits for a response from the server. Here, `timeout` is the timeout period for the client. The default is 3000 ms. A client does not need to wait for a synchronous response for every HSF service. For services that do not require a synchronous wait, HSF provides asynchronous calls. This prevents the client from being blocked by HSF operations. When an asynchronous call is made, the HSF service immediately returns a default value. For example, it returns 0 for an int return type or null for an Object return type. The actual result is retrieved later from HSFResponseFuture or a callback function.

**Future asynchronous calls**

| retrieve the | HSFFuture | object as |
|---|---|---|
| HSFFuture.getResponse(timeout) |   |   |

server. Configure HSF services using APIs HSF provides method-level configuration for asynchronous calls. The format is name:${methodName};type:future . Because methods are identified only by name, overloaded methods are not distinguished. Methods with the same name are configured with the same call type. evelopment

```java
HSFApiConsumerBean hsfApiConsumerBean = new HSFApiConsumerBean(); hsfApiConsumerBean.setInterfaceName("com.alibaba.middleware.hsf.guide.api.service.Order rvice"); hsfApiConsumerBean.setVersion("1.0.0"); hsfApiConsumerBean.setGroup("HSF"); // Configure the asynchronous future call. List<String> asyncallMethods = new ArrayList<String>(); // Format: name:{methodName};type:future asyncallMethods.add("name:queryOrder;type:future"); hsfApiConsumerBean.setAsyncallMethods(asyncallMethods); hsfApiConsumerBean.init(true); // Get the HSF proxy. OrderService orderService = (OrderService) hsfApiConsumerBean.getObject(); // ---------------------- Call -----------------------// // Make an HSF asynchronous call. This call returns null. OrderModel orderModel = orderService.queryOrder(1L); // Get the future object from the current call context immediately. // This object is stored in ThreadLocal and will be overwritten by subsequent calls i n the same thread. Retrieve it promptly. HSFFuture hsfFuture = HSFResponseFuture.getFuture(); // do something else // Get the actual result here. If the call is not complete, the thread blocks and waits. 5000 ms is the maximum wait time. try {
    System.out.println(hsfFuture.getResponse(5000));
} catch (InterruptedException e) {
    e.printStackTrace();
```

`}` The default timeout in HSF is 3000 ms. If the business object is not returned before the timeout, calling HSFFuture.getResponse throws a timeout exception. For HSFFuture.getResponse(timeout), if the business result is not returned within the specified timeout period but the call has not timed out, you can call getResponse multiple times to retrieve the result. Use Spring to configure HSF services Spring is a widely used application framework. If you prefer not to use APIs, you can configure HSF services using Spring XML. The following XML configuration is equivalent to the API configuration in the previous example. evelopment

```xml
<bean id="orderService" class="com.taobao.hsf.app.spring.util.HSFSpringConsumerBean">
    <property name="interfaceName"
value="com.alibaba.middleware.hsf.guide.api.service.OrderService"/>
    <property name="version" value="1.0.0"/>
    <property name="group" value="HSF"/>
    <!-- Set the interface for service subscription -->
    <property name="asyncallMethods">
        <list>
            <value>name:queryOrder;type:future</value>
        </list>
     </property>
</bean>
```

Use annotations to configure HSF services With the wide adoption of Spring Boot, using annotations to assemble Spring beans is a common choice. HSF also supports configuration with annotations to subscribe to services. You can add the starter dependency to the project.

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.alibaba.boot</groupId>

```

An HSF Consumer is often used in multiple places. You do not need to mark each use with @HSFConsumer. Instead, you can write a single Config class and then inject it with @Autowired where needed. The following annotation configuration is equivalent to the API configuration in the previous example.

```java
@Configuration public class HsfConfig {
    @HSFConsumer(serviceVersion = "1.0.0", serviceGroup = "HSF", futureMethods = "say
HelloInFuture")
    OrderService orderService;
```

`}` You can inject it directly where it is used.

**Callback asynchronous calls**

When the client is configured for callback-style calls, you must configure a listener that implements the HSFResponseCallback interface. After the result is returned, HSF invokes the method in HSFResponseCallback. Configure HSF services using APIs

**Callback invocation context**

Before you make a call, use CallbackInvocationContext.setContext(Object obj) to set context information for the call. This information is stored in ThreadLocal. In the listener's callback function, you can retrieve the object using CallbackInvocationContext.getContext().

**Callback function example**

evelopment

```java
public class CallbackHandler implements HSFResponseCallback {
    // Triggered on application exceptions.
    @Override
    public void onAppException(Throwable t) {
        t.printStackTrace();
```

`}`

```java
    // Application return result.
    @Override
    public void onAppResponse(Object result) {
        // Get the context set during the callback call.
        Object context = CallbackInvocationContext.getContext();
        System.out.println(result.toString() + context);
```

`}`

```java
    // HSF exception.
    @Override
    public void onHSFException(HSFException e) {
        e.printStackTrace();
```

`}` `}`

OrderService orderService = (OrderService) hsfApiConsumerBean.getObject();

```
API.

// Make the call. orderService.queryOrder(1L); // This returns null. // Clear the context. CallbackInvocationContext.setContext(null); // do something else
```

You can set the context in the calling thread, then retrieve and use it in the listener. Compared to a Future asynchronous call, with a callback, you immediately know when the result is returned. Use Spring to configure HSF services evelopment
