**Important**

The callback function is invoked by a separate thread pool, which uses a LinkedBlockingQueue infinite queue. Do not perform time-consuming operations in the callback function because this can affect onAppResponse callbacks for other requests. By default, the corePoolSize and maxPoolSize of the callback thread pool are equal to the number of instance CPUs. You can use the following -D parameters to customize the configuration. Minimum size of the callback thread pool: `-Dhsf.callback.min.poolsize` Maximum size of the callback thread pool: `-Dhsf.callback.max.poolsize`

#### Generic calls

Unlike normal calls, which require client-side business JAR packages, generic calls do not depend on these packages. Generic calls use the GenericService interface to invoke a service by passing the method name, method signature, and parameter values. This approach is useful for components such as gateway applications that cannot depend on the client packages for all services. The service testing feature of hsf-ops also uses generic calls.

**Prerequisites**

Before you develop an application, complete the following tasks: Configure the private server address and lightweight configuration center for EDAS. For more information, see Configure the private server address and lightweight configuration center for EDAS. Start the lightweight configuration and registration center. For more information, see Start the lightweight configuration and registration center.

**Configure an HSF service using an API**

Set the HSFConsumerBean parameter `generic` to `true` . The High-speed Service Framework (HSF) client then ignores exceptions that occur when an interface fails to load.

```
HSFApiConsumerBean hsfApiConsumerBean = new HSFApiConsumerBean(); hsfApiConsumerBean.setInterfaceName("com.alibaba.middleware.hsf.guide.api.service.OrderSe ice"); hsfApiConsumerBean.setVersion("1.0.0"); hsfApiConsumerBean.setGroup("HSF"); // [Set] Generic configuration. hsfApiConsumerBean.setGeneric("true"); hsfApiConsumerBean.init(true); // Get the proxy using the generic interface. GenericService genericOrderService = (GenericService) hsfApiConsumerBean.getObject(); // ---------------------- Invoke -----------------------// // [Invoke] Initiate an HSF generic call. The call returns a result of the Map type. Map orderModelMap = (Map) genericOrderService.$invoke("queryOrder",
                            // An array of the input parameter types for the method (xxx
.getClass().getName()).
                            new String[] { Long.class.getName() },
                            // Parameters. If a parameter is a plain old Java object (PO
JO), convert it to a Map.
                            new Object[] { 1L});
```

evelopment The $invoke method provided by GenericService accepts the method name, input parameter types, and parameter values. This information allows the server to identify the correct method to invoke. Because the client does not depend on the server's API JAR package, you must convert any custom data transfer object (DTO) parameters to the `Map` type so that the client can serialize them.

**Method call and parameter description**

If a method has no input parameters, pass `null` for the parameter types and values. For example: service.$invoke("sayHello", null, null) . For generic types, such as `List<String>` , pass the raw type `java.util.List` . This corresponds to the value of List.class.getName(). Do not pass `java.util.List<String>` . If you do, the method cannot be found. If you are unsure about the method format, you can write a unit test that depends on the service's API package. In the test, use the generalize() method from the HSF utility class com.taobao.hsf.util.PojoUtils to generate a `Map` description for a POJO bean.

```
Map pojoMap = (Map) PojoUtils.generalize(new OrderModel());
```

The following code provides an example of how to pass POJO parameters.

```java
 class User {
    private String name;
    private int age;
    // The class must be in the standard POJO format. Getters and setters are omitted
here.
```

`}`

```
   // Directly use a map to construct the generic parameters for the POJO.
   Map param = new HashMap<String, Object>();
   param.put("age", 11);
   param.put("name","Miles");
   // If a passed parameter is a subclass of the declared parameter type, pass the 'c
lass' field to specify the actual type of the POJO. The provider must support this ty pe.
   param.put("class", "com.taobao.User");
```

**Configure an HSF service using Spring**

The Spring Framework is a widely used component. As an alternative to configuring HSF services using the API, you can use Spring XML. The following XML configuration is equivalent to the API configuration in the preceding example.

```
<bean id="CallHelloWorld" class="com.taobao.hsf.app.spring.util.HSFSpringConsumerBean">
    <!-- [Set] The interface of the service to subscribe to. -->
    <property name="interfaceName"
value="com.alibaba.middleware.hsf.guide.api.service.OrderService"/>
    <!-- [Set] The service version. -->
    <property name="version" value="1.0.0"/>
    <!-- [Set] The service group. -->
    <property name="group" value="HSF"/>
    <property name="generic" value="true"/>
</bean>
```

**Notes**

evelopment For generic calls, routing rules do not take effect by default if the client does not have the interface class. The performance of a generic call is lower than that of a normal call. Set `-Dhsf.generic.throw.exception=true` to throw business exceptions. The default value is `false`, which generalizes the exception and returns it as a `Map`. If the exception class exists locally but is not a RuntimeException or its subclass, UndeclaredThrowableException is thrown. This happens because the exception is not declared on com.taobao.hsf.remoting.service.GenericService. You can retrieve the actual exception using `getCause`. If the exception class does not exist locally, com.taobao.hsf.util.GenericInvocationException is thrown.

#### Call context

The call context includes call properties and transmitted custom data other than interfacespecific parameters. The call properties include the IP address, name of the application that initiates the call, and timeout period.

**Specify and retrieve the ongoing call context**

com.taobao.hsf.util.RequestCtxUtil provides a static method to specify and retrieve the call context. Based on ThreadLocal, getxxx removes the xxx property from the ThreadLocal variable. This method takes effect for only a single call of the current thread. The following table describes the methods that are used to specify and retrieve specific properties. Consumers

| Method | Description |
|---|---|
| setRequestTimeout() | Specifies the timeout period for a single call. |
| setUserId() | Specifies the user ID of the unit service in the current call. This method is required for generic calls. |
| getProviderIp() | Retrieves the IP address of the provider that was latest called. |
| setTargetServerIp(String ip) | Specifies the IP address of the required provider in the next call of the current thread. This IP address must be included in the IP address list for memory-provided services. |
| setDirectTargetServerIp(String targetIp) | Specifies the IP address of the provider in the next call of the current thread. This method bypasses the registry and ignores the IP address list in the memory. |

Providers

| Method | Description |
|---|---|
| getClientIp() | Retrieves the IP address of the caller. |
| getAppNameOfClient() | Retrieves the name of the application that is used by the caller. |

evelopment

| isHttpRequest() | Specifies whether the call is an HTTP call. |
|---|---|
| getHttpHeader(String key) | Retrieves the header property of the HTTP request. |

**Transmit the custom request context**

RpcContext provides a method to transmit additional data to the provider without interface modification. The parameter type can be the custom domain object (DO) type or a basic type. Make sure that the peer end can serialize parameters of the same type. Specify the context before the consumer initiates a call.

```
//setup context before rpc call RPCContext rpcContext = RPCContext.getClientContext(); rpcContext.putAttachment("tetantId", "123"); //This is an RPC call. The call context is also transmitted to the peer end.
 orderService.queryOrder(1L);
```

Retrieve the context by using the methods of the provider.

```
//get context data RPCContext rpcContext = RPCContext.getServerContext(); String myContext = (String)rpcContext.getAttachment("tetantId");
```

#### Select a serialization method

The serialization process converts a Java object into a byte array that can be transmitted over a network. The deserialization process converts a byte array into a Java object.

**Overview**

When you select a serialization method, you must consider factors including compatibility and performance. High-speed Service Framework (HSF) supports serialization in Java and serialization based on Hessian 2.0. By default, HSF uses the serialization method based on Hessian 2.0. |   |   |   |   |   |   | Good |   |
|   |   | hessian2</artifac tId> | ian2</artifac |   |   |   |   |
|   |   |   |   | ian2") |   |   |   |
| java |   | <artifactId>hsf- io-serialize- |   | setPreferSeri |   | Excellent | Average |
|   |   |   |   |   | setPreferSeri |   |   |

**Use Spring to configure HSF services**

Spring Framework is a component that is widely used in applications. If you do not want to configure HSF services using APIs, you can configure them using Spring XML. The following XML configuration has the same effect as the preceding API configuration:

```
<bean class="com.taobao.hsf.app.spring.util.HSFSpringProviderBean" init-method="init">
```

#### Configure a time-out period

This topic describes how to configure a timeout period when you develop High-Speed Service Framework (HSF) applications.

**Prerequisites**

Before you develop an application, complete the following tasks: Configure the private server address and lightweight configuration center for EDAS. For more information, see Configure the private server address and lightweight configuration center for EDAS. Start the lightweight configuration and registration center. For more information, see Start the lightweight configuration and registration center.

**Background information**

evelopment You must configure a timeout period for network call requests. The default HSF timeout period is 3000 ms. You can configure a timeout period for both the provider and the consumer. By default, the timeout period configured for the consumer takes precedence. If a timeout period is not configured for the consumer, the timeout period configured for the provider is used. When you configure a timeout period for the provider, consider the total duration of the service execution, serialization, and network communications. We recommend that you configure a default timeout period for each service on the provider. You can configure a timeout period for the consumer based on your business scenarios. For example, you can set the timeout period to a small value for frontend applications that need to return results to users as soon as possible. The following table describes the objects and scopes of related API operations. The operations are sorted by priority in descending order.

| Priority | API | Scope | Scope |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | com.taobao.hsf.util.Re questCtxUtil#setRequ estTimeout | Client | Single calls |
| 1 | HSFApiConsumerBean #setMethodSpecials | Client | Methods |
| 2 | HSFApiConsumerBean #setClientTimeout | client | Interface |
| 3 | - DdefaultHsfClientTime out | Client | All API operations |
| 4 | HSFApiProviderBean# setMethodSpecials | Server-side | Methods |
| 5 | HSFApiProviderBean# setClientTimeout | Server-Side | API operations |

**Note**

Consumer-specific configurations take precedence over provider-specific configurations. Method-specific configurations take precedence over API operation-specific configurations.

**Configure a time-out period for the consumer**

Use APIs to configure HSF services. Set the clientTimeout property of HSFApiConsumerBean. The unit is milliseconds (ms). The following code sets the timeout period to 1000 ms for the API operation and 100 ms for the queryOrder method: evelopment

```
HSFApiConsumerBean consumerBean = new HSFApiConsumerBean(); // Configure the time-out period at the API operation level. consumerBean.setClientTimeout(1000); //xxx MethodSpecial methodSpecial = new MethodSpecial(); methodSpecial.setMethodName("queryOrder"); // Configure the time-out period at the method level. This setting takes precedence o ver the time-out setting that is configured at the API operation level. methodSpecial.setClientTimeout(100); consumerBean.setMethodSpecials(new MethodSpecial[]{methodSpecial});
```

Use Spring to configure HSF services. The Spring Framework is a component that is widely used in applications. If you do not want to configure HSF services using APIs, you can configure them using Spring XML. The following XML configuration has the same effect as the preceding API configuration:

```xml
<bean id="CallHelloWorld" class="com.taobao.hsf.app.spring.util.HSFSpringConsumerBean">
    ...
    <property name="clientTimeout" value="1000" />
    <property name="methodSpecials">
      <list>
        <bean class="com.taobao.hsf.model.metadata.MethodSpecial">
          <property name="methodName" value="queryOrder" />
          <property name="clientTimeout" value="100" />
        </bean>
      </list>
    </property>
    ...
</bean>
```

Annotation configuration Spring Boot is widely used. You can use annotations to configure Spring beans, configure HSF services, and subscribe to HSF services. i. Add the starter dependency to the project.

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.alibaba.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>pandora-hsf-spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

ii. Add annotations in the code. In most cases, an HSF consumer is used in multiple places. However, you do not need to use @HSFConsumer to mark every place where the HSF consumer is used. You only need to write a unified Config class and use @Autowired to directly inject the class where the HSF consumer is needed. The following annotation configuration has the same effect as the preceding API configuration:

```
 @HSFConsumer(clientTimeout = 1000, methodSpecials =
@HSFConsumer.ConsumerMethodSpecial(methodName = "queryOrder", clientTimeout = "100"
```

**Configure a time-out period for the provider**

Use APIs to configure HSF services. Set the clientTimeout property of HSFApiProviderBean. The unit is milliseconds (ms). The following code shows an example:

```
HSFApiProviderBean providerBean = new HSFApiProviderBean(); // Configure the time-out period at the API operation level. providerBean.setClientTimeout(1000); //xxx MethodSpecial methodSpecial = new MethodSpecial(); methodSpecial.setMethodName("queryOrder"); // Configure the time-out period at the method level. This setting takes precedence o ver the time-out setting that is configured at the API operation level. methodSpecial.setClientTimeout(100); providerBean.setMethodSpecials(new MethodSpecial[]{methodSpecial});
```

Use Spring to configure HSF services. The Spring Framework is a component that is widely used in applications. If you do not want to configure HSF services using APIs, you can configure them using Spring XML. The following XML configuration has the same effect as the preceding API configuration:

```xml
<bean class="com.taobao.hsf.app.spring.util.HSFSpringProviderBean" initmethod="init">
```

```java
@HSFProvider(serviceInterface = OrderService.class, clientTimeout = 3000) public class OrderServiceImpl implements OrderService {
```

#### Configure a provider thread pool

This topic describes how to configure a provider thread pool when you develop High-Speed Service Framework (HSF) applications.

**Prerequisites**

Before you develop an application, complete the following tasks: Configure the private server address and lightweight configuration center for EDAS. For more information, see Configure the private server address and lightweight configuration center for EDAS. Start the lightweight configuration and registration center. For more information, see Start the lightweight configuration and registration center.

**Business thread pool diagram**

An HSF provider thread pool includes I/O threads and business threads. The I/O threads use the Netty reactor network model. This topic focuses on configuring the business thread pool, which can be a default business thread pool or a service-specific thread pool. A servicespecific thread pool is partitioned from the default thread pool.

| I/O Connector | Default biz thread1 Submit request Default biz thread2 Com Return mon Default biz response Busi thread3 ness Thread Default biz threadN Pool ServiceA biz thread1 Submit request ServiceA biz thread2 Cus Return tom response ServiceB biz Busi thread1 ness Thread ServiceB biz Pool thread2 | Default biz thread1 Default biz thread2 Com mon Default biz Busi thread3 ness Thread Default biz threadN Pool |
|---|---|---|
|   |   | ServiceA biz thread1 ServiceA biz thread2 Cus tom ServiceB biz Busi thread1 ness Thread ServiceB biz Pool thread2 |

**Configure the default thread pool**

The provider thread pool is responsible for running business logic. By default, the core size is 50, the maximum size is 720, and the keep-alive time is 500 s. The pool uses a `SynchronousQueue` and does not have a cache queue, which prevents user requests from accumulating. If all 720 threads in the provider thread pool are processing requests, new requests are immediately rejected and a `Thread pool is full` exception is returned. You can configure the pool using the following VM parameters (-D parameters). evelopment Minimum pool size: `-Dhsf.server.min.poolsize` Maximum pool size: `-Dhsf.server.max.poolsize` Keep-alive time for thread convergence: `-Dhsf.server.thread.keepalive`

**Configure a service-specific thread pool**

For slow or high-concurrency services, you can configure a dedicated thread pool. This prevents these services from using too many business threads, which can affect other services in the application. Configure HSF services using an API

```
HSFApiProviderBean hsfApiProviderBean = new HSFApiProviderBean(); hsfApiProviderBean.setCorePoolSize("50"); hsfApiProviderBean.setMaxPoolSize("200");
```

Configure HSF services using the Spring framework The Spring framework is a popular component in many applications. If you prefer not to use an API to configure HSF services, you can use Spring XML instead. The following XML configuration is equivalent to the API configuration shown above.

```
<bean class="com.taobao.hsf.app.spring.util.HSFSpringProviderBean" initmethod="init">
    <!-- Specifies the interface for the service to be published. -->
    <property name="serviceInterface"
value="com.alibaba.middleware.hsf.guide.api.service.OrderService"/>
    <property name="corePoolSize" value="50" />
    <property name="maxPoolSize" value="200" />
</bean>
```

Configure HSF services using annotations Because Spring Boot is widely used, configuring Spring beans with annotations is a common practice. HSF also supports using annotations to configure and publish services. i. Add the starter dependency to the project.

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.alibaba.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>pandora-hsf-spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

ii. Configure `@HSFProvider` for the implementation class. The following annotation configuration is equivalent to the API configuration shown above. evelopment

```java
@HSFProvider(serviceInterface = OrderService.class, corePoolSize = 50, maxPoolSize = 200) public class OrderServiceImpl implements OrderService {
    @Autowired
    private OrderDAO orderDAO;
    @Override
    public OrderModel queryOrder(Long id) {
        return orderDAO.queryOrder(id);
```

`}` `}`

#### API manual

Among the API operations of HSF applications, the key API operations are the operations that are related to creating provider beans and consumer beans.

**Background information**

Four key classes are available for different scenarios. com.taobao.hsf.app.api.util.HSFApiProviderBean: Creates provider beans programmatically. com.taobao.hsf.app.api.util.HSFApiConsumerBean: Creates consumer beans programmatically. com.taobao.hsf.app.spring.util.HSFSpringProviderBean: Creates provider beans using Spring configuration. com.taobao.hsf.app.spring.util.HSFSpringConsumerBean: Creates consumer beans using Spring configuration. The configuration properties of HSFSpringxxBean correspond to the setter methods of HSFApixxBean. This topic describes the APIs for these four classes from the perspective of provider and consumer beans.

**ProviderBean**

API programming method - HSFApiProviderBean You can publish HSF services by configuring and initializing com.taobao.hsf.app.api.util.HSFApiProviderBean. The com.taobao.hsf.app.api.util.HSFApiProviderBean configuration and initialization process is implemented only once for the same service. We recommend that you cache the HSFApiProviderBean object because the object is complex. Sample code

```
// Instantiate and configure a provider bean. HSFApiProviderBean hsfApiProviderBean = new HSFApiProviderBean(); hsfApiProviderBean.setServiceInterface("com.taobao.hsf.test.HelloWorldService"); hsfApiProviderBean.setTarget(target); // target indicates the implementation object of the operation that is specified by serviceInterface. hsfApiProviderBean.setServiceVersion("1.0.0"); hsfApiProviderBean.setServiceGroup("HSF"); // Initialize the provider bean for service publishing. hsfApiProviderBean.init();
```

**ConsumerBean**

API programming method - HSFApiConsumerBean You can subscribe to HSF services by configuring and initializing com.taobao.hsf.app.api.util.HSFApiConsumerBean. The com.taobao.hsf.app.api.util.HSFApiConsumerBean configuration and initialization process is implemented only once for the same service. We recommend that you cache the HSFApiConsumerBean object and the retrieved HSF agent because the object size is large.

**Note**

In the HSF, HSFApiConsumerBean caches service configuration. If a subscribed service is configured multiple times, only the first configuration takes effect. evelopment Sample code

```
// Instantiate and configure a consumer bean. HSFApiConsumerBean hsfApiConsumerBean = new HSFApiConsumerBean(); hsfApiConsumerBean.setInterfaceName("com.taobao.hsf.test.HelloWorldService"); hsfApiConsumerBean.setVersion("1.0.0"); hsfApiConsumerBean.setGroup("HSF"); // Initialize the consumer bean for service subscription. // true indicates waiting for address push (time-out period: 3000 ms). The default value is false and indicates an asynchronous call. hsfApiConsumerBean.init(true); // Retrieve the HSF agent. HelloWorldService helloWorldService = (HelloWorldService) hsfApiConsumerBean.getObject(); // Initiate an HSF call. String helloStr = helloWorldService.sayHello("Li Lei");
```

#### Set JVM -D startup parameters

This topic describes the configuration information about JVM -D startup parameters when you develop High-speed Service Framework (HSF) applications.

```
-D hsf.server.port
```

Specifies the bound port for starting HSF services. The default value is 12200. Change the port if you start multiple HSF providers in an on-premises environment.

```
-D hsf.server.max.poolsize
```

Specifies the maximum size of the thread pool of the HSF server. The default value is `720` .

```
-D hsf.server.min.poolsize
```

Specifies the minimum size of the thread pool of the HSF server. The default value is `50` .

```
-D hsf.client.localcall
```

Enables or disables the precedence of local calls. The default value is `true` .

```
-D pandora.qos.port
```

Specifies the Pandora monitoring port. The default value is `12201` . Change the port if you start multiple HSF providers in an on-premises environment.

```
-D hsf.http.enable
```

Specifies whether to enable the HTTP port. The default value is `true` .

```
-D hsf.http.port
```

Specifies the HTTP port that is open to HSF applications. The default value is `12220` . Change the port if you start multiple HSF providers in an on-premises environment.

```
-D hsf.run.mode
```

evelopment Specifies whether the HSF consumer can perform targeted calls that bypass Config Server. The value `1` indicates that targeted calls are not allowed and the value `0` indicates that targeted calls are allowed. The default value is `1` . We recommend that you do not set this parameter to `0` .

```
-D hsf.shuthook.wait
```

Specifies the waiting time for gracefully disconnecting an HSF application. The default value is `10000` . Unit: ms.

```
-D hsf.publish.delayed
```

Specifies whether to delay publishing all services. The default value is false. This indicates that a delay in service publishing is not required.

```
-D hsf.server.ip
```

Specifies the IP address to be bound. When multiple NICs exist, the IP address of the first network interface card (NIC) is bound by default. You can use this parameter to specify the IP address to which you want to bind.

**-D HsfBindHost**

Specifies the host to be bound. When multiple NICs exist, the HSF server binds the IP address of the first NIC and reports it to the address registry by default. You can use this parameter to specify a host to which you want to bind. For example, if you set this parameter to `-` `DHsfBindHost=0.0.0.0` , the HSF server port is bound to all NICs of the host.

```
-D hsf.publish.interval=400
```

Specifies the time interval between the publishing of two services. HSF services become accessible immediately when they are published. You can set this parameter to mitigate the burden on starting applications during service exposure. The default value is 400. Unit: ms.

```
-D hsf.client.low.water.mark=32 -D hsf.client.high.water.mark=64 -
```

| D | hsf.client.low.water.mark=32 |   |
|---|---|---|
| hsf.server.low.water.mark=32 |   | - |

| D | hsf.client.high.water.mark=64 |   |
|---|---|---|
| hsf.server.high.water.mark=64 |   |   |

Specifies the write buffer limit for each channel of the HSF consumer or provider. Specifies the write buffer limit for each channel of the HSF consumer. When the consumer exceeds the upper limit, the channel forbids writing new requests and returns an error. Unit: KB. Write operations are resumed when the write buffer drops below the lower limit. Specifies the write buffer limit for each channel of the HSF provider. When the provider exceeds the upper limit, the channel forbids writing new responses, and the consumer times out because no response is received. Unit: KB. Write operations are resumed when the write buffer drops below the lower limit. The upper and lower limits must be set as a pair, and the upper limit must be greater than the lower limit.

```
-D hsf.generic.remove.class=true
```

Retrieves the result of a generic call, but displays no information about the `class` field.

```
-D defaultHsfClientTimeout
```

Specifies the global timeout period of the HSF consumer.

```
-D hsf.invocation.timeout.sensitive
```

evelopment Determines whether the HSF call duration includes time-consuming logic, such as connection creation and address selection. The default value of `hsf.invocation.timeout.sensitive` is false. anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs

## Application management

**for Kubernetes clusters**

### Resource management

#### Overview of Kubernetes resource

**management**

EDAS enables you to manage containerized applications on Alibaba Cloud Kubernetes clusters and hybrid cloud clusters. Hybrid cloud clusters include self-managed clusters in other cloud environments or in your data centers. If your applications require isolated runtime environments, create and use microservices namespaces to isolate resources and services.

**Microservices namespace**

A microservices namespace provides an isolated runtime environment for applications, such as development, testing, and production environments. Use a microservices namespace to isolate resources and services. EDAS provides a default microservices namespace. You can also create your own microservices namespaces.

**Cluster management**

EDAS enables you to manage containerized applications on Alibaba Cloud Kubernetes clusters and hybrid cloud clusters. Hybrid cloud clusters can be self-managed clusters in other cloud environments or in your data centers. Simply import your Kubernetes cluster into the EDAS console to host applications on it. No other complex operations are required. EDAS does not provide a direct link to create Kubernetes clusters. Go to the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console to create an Alibaba Cloud cluster or register a hybrid cloud cluster. ACK deeply integrates Kubernetes networking with Alibaba Cloud Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) to provide a stable, high-performance container network. Different VPCs are logically isolated from each other.

**Alibaba Cloud Kubernetes clusters**

EDAS seamlessly integrates with Alibaba Cloud ACK. You can import dedicated Kubernetes clusters and dedicated edge Kubernetes clusters that you create in the ACK console. For more information about how to create a dedicated Kubernetes cluster, see the
**Create a Kubernetes cluster** topic in the **Container Service for Kubernetes User**
**Guide**.
For more information about how to create a dedicated edge Kubernetes cluster, see the
**Create an edge Kubernetes cluster** topic in the **Container Service for Kubernetes**
**User Guide**.

**Hybrid cloud clusters**

During daily operations and maintenance (O&M), you might manage multiple Kubernetes clusters on the cloud and in your data centers. You can register these clusters with the ACK console. This allows for unified security administration, application management, monitoring, and logging, which helps reduce O&M costs. When you import a hybrid cloud cluster into EDAS, it is managed as an ACK cluster. anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs

**Note**

The process for hosting an application is similar for both Alibaba Cloud Kubernetes clusters and hybrid cloud clusters. In both cases, the application is hosted on one or more pods.

#### Manage microservice namespaces

##### Manage microservices namespaces in the

**EDAS console**

Microservices namespaces provide isolated runtime environments for applications, such as development, testing, and production environments. You can use microservices namespaces to isolate services. You cannot create two microservices namespaces with the same name in the same region.

**Scenarios**

For example, if you have development, testing, and production environments in a single VPC, you can create a separate microservices namespace for each environment, such as Dev, Test, and Prod. Applications and services in different microservices namespaces are isolated from each other. You cannot call services or push configurations across microservices namespaces.

**Default microservices namespace**

When you create an application in EDAS, you can select the **Default** microservices namespace. The default microservices namespace is equivalent to having no microservices namespace, which means that the application does not use any microservices namespace to isolate services. If you select the default microservices namespace for a region in the application list, the applications that appear are not part of any microservices namespace.

**Create a microservices namespace**

#### Manage Kubernetes clusters

##### Use the console to manage Kubernetes

**clusters**

Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS) integrates Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK), allowing you to easily manage containerized applications on Alibaba Cloud using Kubernetes. You can create Kubernetes clusters in the ACK console. You can also register hybrid cloud clusters, such as Kubernetes clusters on third-party clouds or self-managed Kubernetes clusters in data centers, with the ACK console. After registration, you can import these clusters into EDAS to deploy applications. EDAS provides high-availability management and improves operations and maintenance (O&M) efficiency for containerized applications, allowing you to focus on application development and management.

**Features of Kubernetes clusters in EDAS**

EDAS lets you import dedicated and managed Kubernetes clusters that you create in the Container Service for Kubernetes console. In EDAS, imported dedicated and managed Kubernetes clusters are referred to as ACK clusters. Before importing hybrid cloud clusters, such as clusters on third-party clouds or self-managed clusters in data centers, you must first register them in the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console. In EDAS, these imported hybrid cloud clusters are also referred to as ACK clusters. Managing Kubernetes clusters in EDAS provides the following advantages over self-managed Kubernetes clusters: Built on cloud-native Kubernetes, EDAS provides application hosting capabilities. This allows for one-stop administration for open source microservices and lightweight O&M for Kubernetes applications from an application-centric perspective. anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs From an application-centric perspective, EDAS manages native Kubernetes workloads, such as deployments and pods. It also provides high-availability deployments by distributing instances across multiple zones. EDAS provides phased and canary releases based on traffic ratios and request parameters. EDAS monitors the entire change process to ensure that your change records are traceable. EDAS integrates with mainstream DevOps systems to help enterprises implement continuous integration (CI) and continuous delivery (CD), which helps enterprises reduce costs and improve efficiency. Built on open source microservice systems, EDAS lets you migrate microservice applications that use Spring Cloud and Dubbo frameworks without code modification. EDAS supports the following microservice administration capabilities for all application frameworks: Graceful shutdown and stress testing during application release. Service authentication, throttling, degradation, and outlier ejection during application runtime. Service search and testing during application O&M. Alibaba Cloud packages its principles of observability, canary release, and rollback for production security into its services. This allows your enterprise to immediately implement production security. Observability: Provides end-to-end monitoring across multiple dimensions based on application overviews, release change records, and automatically generated release reports. Canary release: Supports canary releases for applications based on traffic ratios or request content policies. Rollback: Supports one-click rollbacks during the release process. You can also roll back running applications to an earlier version.

**Workflow for Kubernetes clusters**

To deploy an application in a Container Service for Kubernetes cluster, you must create or register a cluster in the Container Service for Kubernetes console and then import the cluster into the EDAS console. After the cluster is imported, you can deploy the application using a deployment package or an image in the imported Container Service for Kubernetes cluster.

| Create a K8s cluster |   | Import a K8s cluster into EDAS |   | Deploy an application in a K8s cluster |
|---|---|---|---|---|

**Note**

After hybrid cloud clusters are imported into EDAS, the procedure for managing them is similar to the procedure for managing Alibaba Cloud Kubernetes clusters. This topic uses an ACK cluster as an example.

**Prerequisites**

EDAS is activated. ACK is activated and role authorization is complete. The Resource Access Management (RAM) user that you use to manage Kubernetes clusters has been granted the required permissions, such as logon permissions, by your Alibaba Cloud account. anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs

**Create a Kubernetes cluster in the ACK console**

To use Kubernetes clusters in EDAS, you must first create a managed or dedicated Kubernetes cluster in the Container Service for Kubernetes console.

**Import a Kubernetes cluster to the EDAS console**

**Important**

Importing a Kubernetes cluster involves some operational constraints. Please read them carefully. For more information, see Constraints on importing a Kubernetes cluster.
1. Log in to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Resource Management > Kubernetes**
**Clusters**.
3. In the top menu bar, select a region and a target **Microservices Namespace**, and then
click **Sync Container Service for Kubernetes Cluster**.
4. In the **Actions** column of the imported Kubernetes cluster, click **Import**.
5. In the **Import Dry Run** dialog box, click **Continue Import**.
6. In the **Import Kubernetes Cluster** dialog box, select a **Microservices Namespace**, and
click **Import**.

**Note**

If you have not created a microservices namespace, the default microservices namespace is used. The Kubernetes cluster is successfully imported into EDAS when the cluster status is
**Running** and the **Import Status** is **Import Successful**.

**View Kubernetes cluster details in the EDAS console**

1. Log in to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Resource Management > Kubernetes**
**Clusters**.
3. Click the cluster ID to go to the **Cluster Details** page.
On the **Cluster Details** page, you can view information about the cluster, such as **Cluster**
**Information**, **EDAS Components**, **ECS Instances**, **Application List**, **Configuration**
**Items**, and **Secrets**.
**Cluster Information**: This section displays basic information about the cluster, such as
**Cluster Ownership**, **Cluster ID**, **csClusterId**, **Cluster Name**, **Microservices**
**Namespace**, **Cluster Type**, **VPC ID**, **Network Type**, **Virtual Switch**, **Container CIDR**
**Block**, **Cluster Status**, and **Description**.
In the upper-right corner of the **Cluster Information** section, click **View Details** to view detailed information about the cluster. In the upper-right corner of the **Cluster Information** section, click **Edit** to modify the cluster description.
**EDAS Components**: This section displays information about the EDAS components, such
as **Type**, the associated **Microservices Namespace**, **Name**, and **Status**. In the EDAS component area, click **View YAML** in the Actions column to view the component's details. anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs In the EDAS component area, click **Restart** in the Actions column for the desired component.
**ECS Instances**: This section displays the list of ECS instances in the cluster and their
summary information, such as **Instance ID/Name**, **IP Address**, **Specifications**, **Health**
**Check**, **Deployed Applications**, and **Time Joined Cluster**. You can click an application
name in the **Deployed Applications** column to go to the application details page.
**Application List**: This section displays the applications in the cluster. You can view the
**Application Name**, **JDK Version**, **Application Runtime Environment**, **Total**
**Instances**, **Running Instances**, and **Application Owner**. You can click an application
name to go to the application details page.
**Configuration Items**: This section displays information about the configuration items,
such as **Configuration Item Name**, **K8s Namespace**, **Cluster Name/Cluster ID**, and
**Creation Time**.
In the **Configuration Items** section, click **Create Configuration Item**. In the **Create**
**Configuration Item** dialog box, enter the **Configuration Item Name** and **K8s**
**Namespace**, specify the **Configuration Mapping**, and then click **OK**.
In the **Configuration Item** area, click **Details** in the Actions column for a configuration item to view its **Basic Information** and **Configuration Mapping**. In the **Configuration Items** area, click **Edit** in the Actions column. Edit the
**Configuration Mapping** and click **OK**.
In the **Configuration Item** area, click **Delete** in the Actions column. In the Delete Configuration Item dialog box that appears, click **OK**. In the **Configuration Items** area, click **View Associated Applications** in the Actions column. In the **Associated Applications** dialog box, you can view the **Associated**
**Application** information.
**Secrets**: This section displays information about secrets, such as **Secret Name**, **Type**,
**K8s Namespace**, **Cluster Name/Cluster ID**, and **Creation Time**.
In the **Secrets** section, click **Create Secret**. In the **Create Secret** dialog box, enter the **Secret Name** and **K8s Namespace**, select the **Type**, and specify the **Base64**
**Encoded Data** and **ConfigMap**. Then, click **OK**.
In the **Secret** area, click **Details** in the Actions column to view the **Basic Information** and **Configuration Mapping Data** for the configuration item. In the **Secret** section, click **Edit** in the Actions column. Modify the **Self-signed**
**Certificate** and the **ConfigMap**, and then click **OK**.
In the **Secret** area, click **Delete** in the Actions column. In the dialog box, click
**Confirm**.
In the **Secrets** section, click **View Associated Applications** in the Actions column. The **Associated Applications** dialog box displays the **Associated Applications** and
**Associated Application Routing** information for the secret.

**Cancel the import of and clean up a Kubernetes cluster in the**

**EDAS console**

1. Log in to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Resource Management > Kubernetes**
**Clusters**.
3. In the top menu bar, select a region. At the top of the page, select the microservices
namespace where the cluster is located. Then, click **Cancel Import** in the **Actions** column of the target Kubernetes cluster, and click **OK** in the **Prompt** dialog box. anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs If a cluster whose import is canceled has a **Cluster Status** of **Running**, you can reimport it to EDAS to create applications. If a cluster whose import was canceled has a **Cluster Status** of **Deleted**, you can click
**Clean Up** in the **Actions** column to remove the cluster from the cluster list in EDAS.

**Note**

For information about the operations and frequently asked questions (FAQ) related to deleting a cluster, see the **Delete Cluster** section in the **Container Service for**
**Kubernetes User Guide**.

**Constraints on importing a Kubernetes cluster**

| Constraint | Description |
|---|---|
| Cluster security group configuration constraints | Ensure that all cluster nodes are in the cluster's security group or can communicate with it. Do not delete the default rules that ACK sets for the cluster security group. |
| Cluster node configuration constraints | Reserve allocatable CPU, memory, and pod resources for the cluster. This ensures that the EDAS control components run as expected. Do not delete the KubernetesWorkerRole-* RAM role that ACK configures for nodes. |
| Cluster API server SLB configuration constraints | Do not block access requests from the internal endpoint 100.104.0.0/16. Do not delete the built-in tags that ACK adds to the SLB. Do not reuse port 6443 of the SLB. |
| Cluster Helm chart operation constraints | Do not delete the ahas-sentinel-pilot, arms-eventer, arms-pilot, and arms- prom components that EDAS installs. This includes all resources installed by these Helm charts. Do not install the open source oam-runtime, kubevela, keda, or flagger. Do not delete or modify any Kubernetes resources in the edas-oam- system namespace. |
| ClusterRole operation constraints | Do not use the ACK console, kubectl, or any third-party interface to delete or modify edas-default-cluster-role. |
| ClusterRoleBinding operation constraints | Do not use the ACK console, kubectl, or any third-party interface to delete or modify edas-default-cluster-role-binding, edas-oam-cluster-role-binding, or keda-hpa-controller-external-metrics. |

**Prerequisites**

EDAS lets you import dedicated and managed Kubernetes clusters that are created in the Container Service for Kubernetes console. After you import dedicated or managed Kubernetes clusters into EDAS, they are managed as Container Service for Kubernetes clusters. Hybrid cloud clusters, which are self-managed clusters in other clouds or data centers, must first be registered with the Container Service for Kubernetes console before you can import them into EDAS. After they are imported, they are also managed as Container Service for Kubernetes clusters. #### Create and deploy applications

**overview (Kubernetes)**

EDAS supports hosting applications in ECS environments and Kubernetes environments. When you choose a Kubernetes environment, EDAS supports hosting Java applications and polyglot applications, such as Node.js, Go, and Python applications. This topic describes the deployment methods supported for each application type.

**Java applications**

After you develop Spring Cloud, Dubbo, HSF, or J2EE applications, you can deploy them to a Kubernetes cluster using WAR files, JAR files, or container images.

| Deployment method | Description | Runtime environmen t | Monitoring and administrati on solution | Example document |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Image deployment | Use this method to deploy applications using custom container images in a Kubernetes cluster. | Custom | EDAS automatically mounts the Java Agent by default for fine-grained monitoring. It also provides full microservice administratio n, including canary releases, service authenticatio n, rate limiting, and degradation. | See Deploy Java microservice applications using images in a Kubernetes cluster. |
| JAR file deployment | Use this method for Dubbo and Spring Boot applications. | Java |   | See Deploy Java microservice applications using JAR or WAR files in a Kubernetes cluster. |
| WAR file deployment | Use this method for Dubbo and Spring applications. | Java, Apache |   |   |
| WAR or FatJar file deployment | Use this method for HSF applications. | EDAS- Container |   |   |
| WAR, JAR (EJB), EAR, or ZIP file deployment | Supports J2EE application deployment | Alibaba Application Server |   |   |

anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs

**Note**

To create multiple Java applications in a Kubernetes environment at once, call the InsertK8sApplication API. For more information, see the **EDAS Developer Guide**, specifically the **InsertK8sApplication** section.

**Polyglot applications**

You can host polyglot applications on EDAS using custom container images. Istio (Service Mesh) provides full microservice administration, including canary releases, service authentication, rate limiting, and degradation. Example document: See Deploy polyglot microservice applications using images in a Kubernetes environment.

**Note**

To create multiple polyglot applications in a Kubernetes environment at once, call the InsertK8sApplication API. For more information, see the **EDAS Developer Guide**, specifically the **InsertK8sApplication** section.

#### Java applications

##### Use JAR packages or WAR packages to

**deploy applications**

###### Use a JAR or WAR package to deploy a

**Java microservices application in an ACK cluster**

Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS) fully integrates with Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) based on cloud-native Kubernetes. EDAS allows you to manage the full lifecycle of Kubernetes containerized applications. An ACK cluster is embedded with the capabilities of Alibaba Cloud in virtual machines, storage, networking, and security, and provides an excellent runtime environment for Kubernetes containerized applications. This topic describes how to use a JAR or WAR package provided by EDAS to deploy a Java application in an ACK cluster.

**Background information**

To deploy an application in an ACK cluster, create an ACK cluster in the ACK console first. Then, import the cluster in the EDAS console, and use a deployment package to deploy the application in the imported cluster.

| Create an ACK cluster |   | Import the ACK cluster to EDAS |   | Deploy an application in the ACK cluster |
|---|---|---|---|---|

anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs

**Note**

JAR or WAR packages can be used to create only Java applications. For more information about how to use an image to deploy a Java application or an application of different programming languages, see Use an image to deploy an application in an ACK cluster or Deploy multi-language microservices to K8s with images.

**Prerequisites**

EDAS and ACK are activated for your Apsara Stack tenant account.

The IP substring length specifies the number of digits to be truncated from the end of the node IP address. The IP substring length ranges from 5 to 12. **Step 2: Import the ACK cluster to EDAS in the EDAS console**

1. Log in to the EDAS console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Resource Management > Container Service**
**Kubernetes Clusters**.
3. In the top navigation bar, select the region in which you want to import the cluster, and
click **Synchronize Container Service Kubernetes Cluster**.
4. In the **Actions** column of the ACK cluster that you want to import, click **Import**.
5. In the **Precheck for Import** dialog box, click **Continue**.
6. In the **Import Kubernetes Cluster** dialog box, select the microservices namespace to
which you want to import the ACK cluster from the **Microservice Namespace** drop-down list, and click **Import**. If the value of the Cluster Status parameter is **Running** and the value of the **Import**
**Status** parameter is **Imported** for the ACK cluster, the ACK cluster is imported to EDAS.

the top navigation bar, select a region. In the upper part of the Applications page, select a microservices namespace from the **Microservice Namespace** drop-down list. Then, click

##### Use images to deploy applications

###### Create an application image

You can use local development tools to package an application into a WAR or JAR file. After you package the application, you can create an application image from the file and upload the image to an Alibaba Cloud image repository for application deployment. This topic describes how to build an Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS) application image using a Dockerfile and upload the image to an Alibaba Cloud image repository.

**Prerequisites**

Before you create an application image, read Appendix: Runtime environment variables and follow the instructions provided in this topic.

**Usage notes**

The Dockerfiles and images that are described in this topic are available in the GitHub repository.

**Specifications and limits**

When you create an EDAS application image using a Dockerfile, the following specifications and limits apply. Tenant and encryption information This includes user authentication and encryption credentials for EDAS applications. Table 1. Resources

|---|---|---|

| accessKey | String | The AccessKey ID for authentication. |
| secretKey | String | The AccessKey secret for authentication. |

anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs Table 3. Local files

| Path | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| /home/admin/.spas key/d _ efault | File | The authentication information of the EDAS tenant, which includes the preceding environment variable information. |

Service information This includes information such as the EDAS domain name and port required for runtime connections. Table 4. Resources

| Resource type | Resource name | Description |
|---|---|---|
| ConfigMap | edas-envs | EDAS service information. |

Table 5. Environment variables

| Environment variable Key | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| EDAS ADDRESS SERVER DOM _ _ _ AIN | String | The domain name or IP address of the configuration center service. |
| EDAS ADDRESS SERVER PORT _ _ _ | String | The service port of the configuration center. |

**Required:** Application runtime environment variables
When you deploy an application, EDAS provides its own environment variables to ensure that the application runs as expected. Do not overwrite these configurations. For more information, see Appendix: Runtime environment variables.

**Create a standard Dockerfile**

A Dockerfile is a text-based configuration file that you can use to quickly create images. You can create images for High-speed Service Framework (HSF), Spring Cloud, or Dubbo applications using framework-specific Dockerfiles. The following examples show how to create Dockerfiles for applications that use these frameworks. anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs A standard EDAS Dockerfile contains all the instructions for creating an application runtime environment in EDAS. These instructions include downloading, installing, and starting components such as OpenJDK, Tomcat, and WAR and JAR packages. You can also modify the Dockerfile to replace the OpenJDK version, modify Tomcat configurations, or change the runtime environment. For more information about how to use OpenJDK, see Custom image: Use a new version of OpenJDK. For more information about how to use Dockerfiles, see the following topics: Sample Dockerfile for an HSF application Sample Dockerfile for a Spring Cloud or Dubbo application

**Sample Dockerfile for an HSF application**

```bash
# Use centos7, openjdk8, ali-tomcat7, and pandora 3.5.9 for the base image.
FROM apaas-registry.cn-hangzhou.cr.aliyuncs.com/apaas/edas-centos-openjdk8-alitomcat7:l atest MAINTAINER Alibaba Cloud EDAS Team<edas***@list.alibaba-inc.com> ENV TZ="Asia/Shanghai"
# By default, put your application package into /home/admin/app/.
ENV APP_HOME /home/admin/app/
#####----> Case 1: Deploy a fat JAR file.
ARG APP_LOCATION=https://edas-hz.oss-cnhangzhou.aliyuncs.com/prod/demo/HSF_PROVIDER.jar
#####----> Case 2: Deploy a WAR file. Simply change the file name.
#ARG APP_LOCATION=https://edas-hz.oss-cn-
hangzhou.aliyuncs.com/prod/demo/HSF_PROVIDER.war
#####----> Case 3: Deploy a file from local storage.
#ARG APP_LOCATION=/Users/yanliang.lyl/workspace/java/demo/HSF_PROVIDER.war
# Download the package to /home/admin/app/.
ADD ${APP_LOCATION} ${APP_HOME}/
# The default working directory is /home/admin.
# WORKDIR /home/admin
# The entry point is /home/admin/bin/start.sh, which is included in the base image (apa
as/edas-centos-openjdk8-alitomcat8).
# CMD ["/home/admin/bin/start.sh"]
```

**Sample Dockerfile for a Spring Cloud or Dubbo application**

anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs

```bash
# Use centos7, openjdk8, and tomcat8 for the base image.
FROM apaas-registry.cn-hangzhou.cr.aliyuncs.com/apaas/edas:latest

ENV APP_HOME /home/admin/app/
##### SIMPLY REPLACE YOUR PACKAGE FILE
#####----> Case 1: Deploy a fat JAR file.

#####----> Case 2: Deploy a WAR file. Simply change the file name.
#ARG APP_LOCATION=https://edas-hz.oss-cn-
hangzhou.aliyuncs.com/prod/demo/DUBBO_PROVIDER.war
#####----> Case 3: Deploy a file from local storage.
#ARG APP_LOCATION=/Users/yanliang.lyl/workspace/java/demo/SPRINT_CLOUD_PROVIDER.war
# Download the package to /home/admin/app/.
ADD ${APP_LOCATION} ${APP_HOME}/
```

**Custom image: Use a new version of OpenJDK**

You can add custom settings to the standard Dockerfile as needed. Upgrade OpenJDK: In the Dockerfile, you can download and install a new version of OpenJDK. The following example shows how to download and install OpenJDK 9.

**Note**

When you use a custom image, EDAS supports JDK versions up to OpenJDK 21.

```bash
# Uninstall the previous JDK, and then download and install OpenJDK 9.
RUN yum erase -y java; yum -y install java-1.9.0-openjdk-devel
```

**Custom image: Upgrade the EDAS Container version (HSF**

**applications)**

For HSF applications that are deployed in Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) clusters, you can upgrade the application container version to use new features of the middleware or fix issues in the current version. To upgrade the version, perform the following steps:
1. Log in to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, click **Application Management > Applications**.
3. On the **Applications** page, click **Create Application**. On the **Basic Information** page, go
to the **Application Runtime Environment** section to find the **Pandora Version** and **Ali-**
**Tomcat Version**.
4. Replace the version number in the Dockerfile. For example, you can replace the version
number with 3.5.4.

```bash
# Set the version of the EDAS Container/Pandora application container.
ENV UPGRADED_CONTAINER_VERSION 3.5.4 RUN /home/admin/bin/upgradecontainer.sh
```

5. Create and publish the application image again.

**Custom image: Adjust JVM startup parameters in an image**

You can use the **JAVA_OPTS** environment variable to specify JVM startup parameters. The following example shows how to modify these parameters:

```bash
FROM apaas-registry.cn-hangzhou.cr.aliyuncs.com/apaas/edas:latest
# Set the JVM parameter ENV
    JAVA_OPTS="\
     -Xmx3550m \
     -Xms3550m \
     -Xmn2g \
     -Xss128k"
```

**Custom image: Modify application configurations for**

**SpringBoot applications**

To modify Tomcat startup configurations, such as the context path and startup port, for a FatJar application that uses an EDAS base image, you can use the **APP_ARGS** environment variable. The following example shows how to modify the configurations. anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs

```bash
FROM apaas-registry.cn-hangzhou.cr.aliyuncs.com/apaas/edas:latest
# The default configurations in the base image are as follows:
#    - The context path is "/".
#    - The URI encoding is ISO-8859-1.
#    - The application startup port is 8080.
#    - The number of threads in the Tomcat thread pool is 400.
# You can also overwrite the APP_ARGS environment variable to modify the default config
urations. Example:
              ENV APP_ARGS="--server.context-path=/  \
              --server.tomcat.uri-encoding=ISO-8859-1 \
              --server.port=8080 \
              --server.tomcat.max-threads=400"
```

**Build an image locally**

1. On your local command line, navigate to the directory that contains the Dockerfile and run
the **docker build** command to build an image.

```bash
docker build -t [tag_name, preferably the application name]:[version_number] . or docker build -t [tag_name, preferably the application name]:[version_number] -f /p ath/to/custom_dockerfile_name . # Use this command if your Dockerfile is in another directory or has a name other than Dockerfile.
```

Example:

```bash
docker build -t hsf-provider:1.0.0 .
```

2. Then, run the docker images | grep <image_tag_name> command to view the locally
packaged image.

**Upload an image to an image repository**

After you build the application image locally, you can upload it to an Alibaba Cloud Container Registry repository.

**Note**

Before you proceed, log on to the Container Registry (ACR) console. Switch to the region where your EDAS application is or will be deployed. In the console for that region, you can view the list of image repositories. Select an existing repository or create a new one to store the application image. For easy identification, we recommend that you name the repository after the application. On the **Basic Information** page of the image repository, run the commands in the **3. Push**
**the Image to the Registry** section to upload the local image to the repository.
anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs

```bash
docker login --username=[your_logon_account_name] registry.[region_id].aliyuncs.com
# The password is the fixed or temporary password that you set on the Access Credential
page for the default instance of Alibaba Cloud Container Registry. It is not your Aliba ba Cloud account password. docker tag [local_application_image_ID] registry. [region_id].aliyuncs.com/[namespace_name]/[image_repository_name]: [image_version_number] docker push registry.[region_id].aliyuncs.com/[namespace_name]/[image_repository_name]: [image_version_number]
```

Example:

```bash
docker login --username=td****@gmail.com registry.cn-hangzhou.aliyuncs.com docker tag 2b64f63601a7 registry.cn-hangzhou.aliyuncs.com/webapps/hsf-provider:1.0.0 docker push registry.cn-hangzhou.aliyuncs.com/webapps/hsf-provider:1.0.0
```

| EDAS CATALINA OPTS _ _ | String | The CATALINA OPTS _ parameters required by the middleware at runtime. |

###### Upload a local image

To deploy an application in a Kubernetes cluster using a local Nginx image, you must first upload the image.

**Prerequisites**

To upload locally built images to an Alibaba Cloud image repository, you need an ECS instance with an Elastic IP Address or a NAT configuration.

**Procedure**

1. Log on to the Container Registry (ACR) console.
2. Create a namespace.
i. In the navigation pane on the left, click **Instance List**. ii. On the **Instance List** page, click **Manage** for the target instance. This opens the **Image**
**Repository** page.
iii. On the **Image Repository** page, in the left navigation pane, choose **Namespaces**, and then click **Create Namespace**. anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs iv. On the **Create Namespace** page, select the organization, resource set, and region. Enter a name for the namespace in the **Namespace** text box, and then click **Submit**. The system automatically populates the organization, resource set, and region. You do not need to enter this information.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Organization | The organization to which the namespace belongs. |
| Resource Set | The resource set to which the namespace belongs. |
| Region | The region in which the namespace resides. |
| Sharing Scope | Valid values: Current Resource Set Current Organization and Subordinate Organizations Current Organization |
| Namespace | The value must be 2 to 30 characters in length, and can contain lowercase letters, digits, underscores ( ), and hyphens (-). It cannot _ start or end with an underscore ( ) or a hyphen _ (-). |

3. Create an image repository.
i. On the **Instance List** page, click **Manage** for the target instance to open the **Image**
**Repository** page.
ii. On the **Image Repository** page, click **Create Image Repository**.

**Note**

You set the region and namespace when you create the repository, so you do not need to select them on the **Image Repository** page. anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs iii. On the **Create Repository** page, set the image repository settings and click **Submit**. Image repository parameters:

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Organization | The organization to which the repository belongs. |
| Resource Set | The resource set to which the repository belongs. |
| Region | The region in which the repository resides. |
| Sharing scope | Valid values: Current Resource Set Current Organization and Subordinate Organizations Current Organization |
| Namespace | The namespace to which the image repository belongs. |
| Repository Name | The name of the image repository. The name must be 1 to 64 characters in length and can contain lowercase letters, digits, hyphens (-), and underscores ( ). It cannot start or end with _ a hyphen (-) or an underscore ( ). _ |
| Digest | The digest of the repository. |
| Details | The description of the repository. The description can be up to 2,000 characters in length. |
| Repository Type | The type of the image repository. Valid values: Public and Private. |

4. On the **Basic Information** page of the new repository, upload the image by following the
instructions on the **Operation Guide** tab.

###### Deploy a Java microservice to a K8s

**cluster**

anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs EDAS, built on cloud native K8s, integrates ACK to provide full lifecycle management for containerized applications. ACK integrates Alibaba Cloud capabilities such as virtual machines, storage, network, and security to provide a cloud runtime environment for K8s containerized applications. This topic explains how to deploy a Java microservices application to a K8s cluster using an image.

**Background**

To deploy an application to a K8s cluster, create a K8s cluster in the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console, import it into EDAS, and then deploy the application to the cluster by using a deployment package.

**Note**

JAR and WAR packages support only Java applications. To deploy Java or multi-language applications by using an image, see Deploy multi-language microservice applications in a K8s environment by using an image.

**Prerequisites**

You have access to both EDAS and Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK). You have built an application image and pushed it to an image repository. For detailed steps, see Build an application image and Push a local image.

**Step 1: Create an ACK cluster**

1. Log in to the ACK console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Clusters**. On the Clusters page, click **Create**
**Kubernetes Cluster** in the upper-right corner of the page.
3. On the **ACK Dedicated** tab of the **Create Kubernetes Cluster** page, configure the basic
settings of the cluster.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Cluster Name | The name of the cluster. The name must be 1 to 63 characters in length and can contain digits, letters, and hyphens (-). Note The cluster name must be unique among clusters that belong to the same Apsara Stack tenant account. |
| Resource Set | The resource set to which the cluster belongs. A resource set is a container used to store resources. Each resource must belong to a resource set. After you select a resource set, virtual private clouds (VPCs) and vSwitches are filtered based on the selected resource set. |
| Region | The region in which you want to deploy the cluster. |

anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs

| IPv4/IPv6 Dual- stack | Specifies whether to enable IPv4/IPv6 dual stack. Note You can enable IPv4/IPv6 dual stack only for clusters that run Kubernetes 1.20 or later. Master nodes and worker nodes still use IPv4 addresses to communicate with each other in a cluster. You must select Terway as the network plug-in. You must use a VPC and Elastic Compute Service (ECS) instances that support IPv4/IPv6 dual stack. |
|---|---|
| VPC | The VPC in which you want to deploy the cluster. |
| vSwitch | The vSwitches that you want to use. You can select up to three vSwitches that are deployed in differentz ones. |
| Kubernetes Version | The Kubernetes version of the cluster. |
| Container Runtime | Only containerd is supported. You must deploy ECS bare metal instances. We recommend that you select the latest version available in the ACK console. |
| Master Nodes | The number of master nodes that you want to use. You can create three or five master nodes. Note You can create a single master node. By default, this feature is unavailable. To use this feature, contact the technical support of Apsara Stack. |
| Instance Type | The instance type of master nodes. You can select multiple instance types. You can also select a dedicated host group for the master nodes. For more information, see Instance types in the ECS documentation. |

To encrypt disks, you need to configure the following parameters: Encryption method: You can select AES256 or SM4. Encryption key: You can select a key that is created in Key Management Service (KMS). Encryption is supported only when you select Premium Performance Disk or Standard Performance Disk as the system disk category. |

Number of Pods per Node: Specify the maximum number of pods on a node. Flannel Mode: If you select Enable Flannel VXLAN mode, you can enable cross-node container network communication through Virtual Extensible LAN (VXLAN) tunnels. Pod CIDR Block: Specify the CIDR block of pods. If you select Terway, the DataPath V2, Support for NetworkPolicy, and Support for ENI Trunking options are available. #### Multi-language applications

##### Use images to deploy multi-language

**microservices applications in Kubernetes clusters**

An increasing number of microservices applications use multiple programming languages such as Python, Go, and Node.js. Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS) allows you to deploy multi-language microservices applications in Kubernetes clusters by using a service mesh. EDAS provides the following service governance capabilities for microservices applications: application management, service discovery, tracing analysis, load balancing, and application monitoring. This topic provides an example on how to use images to deploy multi-language microservices applications in Kubernetes clusters in EDAS.

**Prerequisites**

An application image is created and uploaded to your Apsara Stack image repository. For more information, see Create an application image and Upload an on-premises image. To experience the deployment practice, you can use the sample application provided by EDAS. You can download the application from Bookinfo Sample. anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs

**Background information**

Applications have evolved from the original monolithic architecture to the current microservices architecture. The microservices architecture facilitates application development but increases complexity in service deployment and O&M. You can deploy applications that are developed in any programming languages as microservices. To provide service governance capabilities for these microservices, such as tracing analysis, service discovery, and load balancing, you can use either multi-language SDKs or service meshes. SDKs are intrusive to multi-language microservices applications. Service meshes can provide capabilities such as service discovery, load balancing, and tracing analysis while remaining non-intrusive to multi-language microservices applications. Therefore, EDAS offers the service mesh feature for multi-language microservices applications. A service mesh is a dedicated infrastructure layer that implements service-to-service communication. A service mesh provides a stable and reliable method to deliver requests. If you use a service mesh, you do not need to be concerned about the complex topology of services that compose a modern, cloud-native application. In most cases, a service mesh is implemented as an array of lightweight network proxies that are deployed in combination with an application code. This way, you do not need to be concerned about the status of the application.

**Sample scenario**

BookInfo is an application that displays the detailed information about a book. The application functions as a filter for an online bookstore. The application displays the description of a book, the book details such as the International Standard Book Number (ISBN) and the number of pages, and reviews on the book. BookInfo is a heterogeneous application that consists of several microservices applications. These microservices applications are developed in different programming languages. These microservices applications form a classic service mesh, which consists of multiple microservices that are written in different programming languages. Among these microservices, the Reviews microservice has multiple versions. Figure 1. Architecture for multi-language microservices anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs The BookInfo application consists of the following four independent microservices: Productpage: a Python microservice that calls the Details and Reviews microservices to generate a page. The Productpage microservice provides the login and logout features. Details: a Ruby microservice that contains book information. Reviews: a Java microservice that provides book reviews and calls the Ratings microservice. The Reviews microservice has the following three versions: Version 1, which does not call the Ratings microservice. Version 2, which calls the Ratings microservice and rates a book by using one to five black stars. Version 3, which calls the Ratings microservice and rates a book by using one to five red stars. Ratings: a Node.js microservice that provides ratings generated based on book reviews.

**Procedure**

Before you can deploy a multi-language microservices application in a Kubernetes cluster, you must create a Kubernetes cluster in the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console and import the cluster to EDAS in the EDAS console. Then, you can use a custom image to deploy an application in the cluster.
