#### Advanced settings

##### Configure microservices governance

Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS) enables Spring Cloud and Dubbo applications to connect to Microservices Engine (MSE) for non-intrusive microservices governance. You can configure features such as service registration and discovery, empty list protection, and graceful start when you create or deploy applications in EDAS. This topic describes how to configure microservices governance. anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs

**Note**

When you use an Apsara DevOps pipeline to deploy an EDAS application, the microservices governance parameters configured in the EDAS console take precedence. The Apsara DevOps pipeline cannot be used to configure these parameters.

**Background information**

**Service registration and discovery**

Eureka, ZooKeeper, and Nacos are popular service registries in the Java microservices model. Service registries implement service registration and discovery, which achieves service decoupling and eliminates the need for manual dependency management. This lets you dynamically manage microservices.

**Empty list protection**

This feature applies to scenarios where an exception occurs on a service provider. In this case, a client might request an instance list from a service registry and receive an empty list in return. If you enable empty list protection, the client ignores the empty list and retrieves the last successfully returned instance list from its local cache. This ensures that the client remains available even if its subscriptions are affected by unexpected events, such as a service registry configuration update, upgrade, downgrade, network disconnection, or power outage. Service consumers subscribe to the instance list of service providers from a service registry. When a service registry updates configurations, performs an upgrade or a downgrade, or encounters an exception such as a network disconnection or power outage, consumer subscriptions may be affected. This can degrade the availability of the consumers. To handle subscription errors caused by these exceptions, you can enable the empty list protection feature on the consumer side.

**Graceful start**

For any online application, operations such as release, scale-out, scale-in, and restart are inevitable. EDAS integrates a graceful start solution provided by MSE to protect applications during the startup phase. This solution provides features such as service prefetching, delayed service registration, and graceful rolling deployment. Service prefetching: This reduces the risk of process exceptions that can occur when a newly launched service is unable to handle a sudden traffic surge. You can configure the ramp-up period and prefetch curve. anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs Delayed service registration: This feature forces an application to wait for a specified period before it registers with the service registry. This provides the application with sufficient time to prepare asynchronous requests and initialize computing resources. This helps reduce request exceptions that can occur during an application release if resources are not yet initialized. For applications with a complex initialization process, registration might occur concurrently with initialization. This can cause the application to be registered with the service registry before it is fully initialized. If an external consumer invokes the application at this point, a request error may occur. By configuring a delayed registration, you can ensure that the application is fully initialized before it registers with the service registry and begins providing services. Graceful rolling deployment: A health check interface provides a method for clients outside the microservice system to check the readiness of an application. This interface can synchronize service status checks between microservice and non-microservice frameworks. It supports checking both the service registration status and the service prefetching status. A rolling deployment in Kubernetes divides the release process into multiple batches, which are released one at a time. After one batch is successfully deployed, the next batch is released, and this process continues until all batches are complete. For Kubernetes applications, EDAS connects the microservice lifecycle with the Kubernetes service lifecycle. EDAS provides graceful start capabilities, such as ensuring that service registration and prefetching are complete before the readiness probe succeeds. This helps maintain available service instances (replicas) during the application's rolling deployment, which in turn implements a graceful rolling deployment. Complete service registration before the readiness probe succeeds: After you enable the feature that associates the microservice lifecycle with the Kubernetes readiness probe, an agent non-intrusively provides a port that the application uses to report its registration status. If the application is registered, a status code of 200 is returned, which indicates to Kubernetes that the application is ready. If the application is not registered, a status code of 500 is returned, which indicates to Kubernetes that the application is not ready. Complete service prefetching before the readiness probe succeeds: In addition to using service prefetching alone, you can associate it with the Kubernetes readiness probe mechanism. Kubernetes sets the application to a ready state only after the application's service prefetching is complete.

**Zone affinity**

Zone affinity means that when an application invokes a service, it prioritizes invoking a service provider in the same zone. Spring Cloud, Dubbo, and HSF protocol applications all support zone affinity for service invocation. anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs When an application is deployed across multiple zones, cross-zone invocations may occur. The following figure shows the invocation path. In the figure, if Application A in Zone 1 invokes Application B in Zone 2 (for example, the application on Node A1 invokes the application on Node B2), the cross-zone invocation increases network latency and HTTP response time. After you enable zone affinity for an application service, the consumer application prioritizes invoking service providers in the same zone. The following figure shows the invocation path. This avoids the network latency caused by cross-zone invocations and reduces HTTP response time. If no service provider is available in the current zone, the service consumer invokes a service provider in another zone.

**Limits**

You can non-intrusively enable the empty list protection and graceful start features only for Spring Cloud and Dubbo applications. The following table describes the supported versions.

| Limits | Empty Push Protection | Graceful start |
|---|---|---|
| Spring Cloud | Spring Cloud Edgware and later | Spring Cloud Edgware and later |
| Dubbo | Dubbo 2.5.3 to 2.7.8 | Dubbo 2.7.3 to 2.7.8 |

Only the Nacos service registry is supported. anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs In most cases, gateway applications are not invoked through service registries but by directly exposing APIs. Therefore, the service prefetching feature provided by MSE is ineffective for such applications. In addition, gateway applications rarely change and have minimal business logic, so they typically do not require the service prefetching feature. For applications that use a canary release, you cannot enable the service prefetching feature for the first batch. However, subsequent batches support service prefetching.

| Empty List Protection | Specifies whether to enable empty list protection. Enable empty list protection: If a consumer subscribes to an empty list, empty list protection takes effect and discards the change. This ensures service availability. Disable empty list protection: If a consumer subscribes to an empty list, the business is interrupted and an error is reported. |

anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs

| Graceful Start | Specifies whether to enable graceful start. If you enable this feature, set the following parameters: Ramp-up Period (Seconds): The ramp-up period for the next startup of an application instance. The default value is 120. You can set this parameter to a value from 0 to 86400. The value 86400 is equal to 24 hours. Prefetch Curve: Based on the configured ramp-up period, the traffic weight of the prefetched application increases exponentially according to the configured prefetch curve. Within a specified ramp-up period, a larger prefetch curve value means a smaller traffic weight is allocated to the prefetched application at startup. This meets the prefetching needs of complex applications that require a longer time to prefetch. The default value is 2, which is suitable for common prefetching scenarios. This value indicates that the traffic received by the service provider during the ramp-up period follows a quadratic curve. You can set this parameter to a value from 0 to 20. For the same ramp-up period, a larger value indicates that the service provider receives less traffic at the beginning of prefetching, and the traffic increases more sharply as the ramp-up period ends. Registration Delay (Seconds): The application waits for x seconds after startup before registering with the service registry, where x is the value you set. You can set this parameter to a value from 0 to 86400. The value 86400 is equal to 24 hours. The default value is 0. Graceful Rolling Deployment: Configure graceful rolling deployment for the application. Complete Service Registration Before Readiness Probe Succeeds: Non-intrusively provides port 55199 for the application. The default path is /health. This is used to check whether the microservice has completed registration. If registration is complete, the port returns 200. Otherwise, it returns 500. Complete Service Prefetching Before Readiness Probe Succeeds: Non-intrusively provides port 55199 for the application. The default path is /health. This is used to check whether the microservice has completed prefetching. If prefetching is complete, the port returns 200. Otherwise, it returns 500. Note If you enable both Complete service registration before readiness probe succeeds and Complete service prefetching before readiness probe succeeds, port 55199 checks whether the service has completed prefetching. |

Enable empty list protection: If a consumer subscribes to an empty list, empty list protection takes effect and discards the change. This ensures service availability. Disable empty list protection: If a consumer subscribes to an empty list, the business is interrupted and an error is reported. |

anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs

| Graceful Start | Specifies whether to enable graceful start. If you enable this feature, set the following parameters: Ramp-up Period (Seconds): The ramp-up period for the next startup of an application instance. The default value is 120. You can set this parameter to a value from 0 to 86400. The value 86400 is equal to 24 hours. Prefetch Curve: The traffic weight for a prefetched application increases exponentially over the specified prefetch duration according to this curve. A larger curve value results in a smaller initial traffic weight, which is ideal for complex applications that require a longer prefetch period. The default value is 2, which is suitable for common prefetching scenarios. This value indicates that the traffic received by the service provider during the ramp-up period follows a quadratic curve. You can set this parameter to a value from 0 to 20. For the same ramp-up period, a larger value indicates that the service provider receives less traffic at the beginning of prefetching, and the traffic increases more sharply as the ramp-up period ends. Registration Delay (Seconds): The application waits for x seconds after startup before registering with the service registry, where x is the value you set. You can set this parameter to a value from 0 to 86400. The value 86400 is equal to 24 hours. The default value is 0. |
|---|---|
| Zone Affinity | If you enable zone affinity, the application prioritizes invoking service providers in the same zone. This avoids network latency from cross-zone invocations and reduces HTTP response time. Spring Cloud, Dubbo, and HSF protocol applications all support zone affinity for service invocation. Note The zone affinity policy takes effect only when the ratio of the number of instances in the current zone to the total number of instances is greater than the specified threshold. You can set the threshold to a value from 0 to 100. |

##### Configure a startup command

In the Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS) console, you can use an image, a JAR package, or a WAR package to deploy an application in a Kubernetes cluster. If you are proficient in Docker and Java Virtual Machine (JVM) and want to customize startup parameters, you can configure the startup and runtime commands for your container.

**Background information**

When you create an image, the container startup configurations that you specify in your Dockerfile using the ENTRYPOINT or CMD command are used first.

**Important**

If you are not familiar with the CMD or ENTRYPOINT content in the Dockerfile of the original image, do not customize the startup command and parameters. Using invalid custom commands causes the application creation to fail. The Docker runtime supports only one ENTRYPOINT command. The startup command that you set in the EDAS console overwrites the ENTRYPOINT and CMD commands that were set when you created the Docker container image. For example, if you configure the ENTRYPOINT: [nginx, '-g', 'daemon off;'] command in your Dockerfile, this command is the first to run when the container starts.

```
FROM ubuntu ENTRYPOINT [nginx, '-g', 'daemon off;']
```

You can configure a startup command when you create or deploy an application, or after an application is deployed. This topic describes how to configure a startup command in different scenarios. To configure a startup command when you create an application, see Configure a startup command when you create an application. If you configure a startup command after an application is deployed, the application restarts. Perform this operation during off-peak hours. For more information, see Configure a startup command when you update an application.

##### Configure environment variables

Applications require specific environment variables to run. For example, before a Java application can run its commands, you must configure the JAVA_HOME and PATH environment variables. This topic describes how to configure environment variables for applications in the Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS) console.

**Background information**

You can configure four types of environment variables: Custom: Custom environment variables that you can define when you create an application. Configuration Items: Predefined configurations that are not confidential. An application can use a configuration item only if the application is in the same region, cluster, and Kubernetes namespace as the configuration item. anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs For more information about how to create a configuration item, see Create a configuration item. Secrets: Predefined configurations, such as passwords and certificates, that are confidential. An application can use a secret only if the application is in the same region, cluster, and Kubernetes namespace as the secret. For more information, see Create a secret. Variables/Variable References: Environment variables that are set to Downward API values.

**Configure environment variables when you create an**

**application**

1. Log in to the EDAS console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Application Management > Applications**. In
the top navigation bar, select a region. In the upper part of the Applications page, select a microservices namespace from the **Microservice Namespace** drop-down list. Then, click
**Create Application** in the upper-left corner of the **Applications** page.
3. On the **Basic Information** tab, select a **Cluster Type** and an **Application Runtime**
**Environment**. Enter an **Application Name** and click **Next**.

| Configuration Item | Description |

##### Configure persistent storage

anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs By default, data stored in a container is not persistent and is lost when the container is destroyed. Because data loss can be disastrous in a production environment, EDAS Kubernetes clusters support mounting Persistent Volume Claims (PVCs). **Prerequisites**

**for Kubernetes User Guide > Create a Persistent Volume Claim** section.

##### Configure application lifecycle hooks and

**probes**

In the Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS) console, you can configure PostStart and PreStop lifecycle hooks to run custom operations immediately after an application starts or before it stops. You can also configure Liveness, Readiness, and Startup probes to check the health and readiness of containers. This topic describes how to configure these hooks and probes.

**Background information**

Some operations are performed immediately after an application starts or before it stops. For example, you might need to deploy resources before you launch an application, gracefully shut down an application, or notify other services before an application shuts down. EDAS integrates the lifecycle hook feature based on Kubernetes. This feature lets you configure PostStart and PreStop hooks for containers. anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs When you deploy an application to a Kubernetes cluster, you need to check whether the pods are alive and ready to provide services. EDAS integrates the pod probe feature based on Kubernetes. This feature lets you configure a Liveness probe to determine when to restart containers and a Readiness probe to determine whether containers are ready to accept traffic.

**Configure application lifecycle hooks and probes when you**

**create an application**

1. Log in to the EDAS console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Application Management > Applications**. In
the top navigation bar, select a region. In the upper part of the Applications page, select a microservices namespace from the **Microservice Namespace** drop-down list. Then, click
**Create Application** in the upper-left corner of the **Applications** page.
3. On the **Basic Information** tab, select a **Cluster Type** and an **Application Runtime**
**Environment**. Enter an **Application Name** and click **Next**.

|---|---|

| Application Runtime Environment | Select the application runtime environment. Java: Custom: Use a custom image to deploy the application in a Kubernetes cluster. Tomcat: Supports deployment from generic WAR packages. This option is suitable for Dubbo and Spring applications. You can change the Java environment and container version after you select this option. EDAS-Container (HSF): Deploy HSF applications from WAR or FatJar packages. You can change the Java environment, Pandora version, and Ali-Tomcat version after you select this option. Alibaba Cloud Application Server: Deploy J2EE applications. Supports WAR, JAR (EJB), EAR, and ZIP formats. Multi-language (Node.js, C++, Go, and more): Custom: Use a custom image to deploy the application in a Kubernetes cluster. |
| Monitoring and Governance Solution | Java: By default, a Java Agent is automatically mounted in the Kubernetes cluster for fine-grained monitoring. A complete microservice administration solution is also provided, which includes features such as canary releases, service authentication, and throttling and degradation. Multi-language: A complete microservice administration solution is provided through Istio (Service Mesh). This solution includes features such as canary releases, service authentication, and throttling and degradation. |

anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs
4. On the **Application Configurations** tab, set the environment context, basic information,
deployment mode, and resource parameters for the application. Then, click **Next**.
5. On the **Advanced Settings** tab, you can expand **Application Lifecycle Management**
and set the following parameters.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| PostStart | A container hook. This hook is triggered immediately after a container is created to notify the container that it has been created. The hook does not pass any parameters to its handler. If the hook handler fails, the container is terminated and restarted based on its restart policy. For more information, see Container Lifecycle Hooks. |
| PreStop | A container hook. This hook is triggered before a container is terminated. Its handler must complete before the request to terminate the container is sent to the Docker daemon. After the handler completes, the Docker daemon sends a SIGTERM signal to the container to terminate it, regardless of the handler's result. For more information, see Container Lifecycle Hooks |
| TerminationGracePeriod | Set the timeout period for graceful pod termination. Ensure that the time required for the PreStop operation and for the application to handle the SIGTERM signal is less than this period. You can also adjust this configuration to control the pod deletion duration. |
| Liveness | A probe that detects if an application is healthy. If the application is unhealthy, its container is deleted and recreated. For more information, see Pod Lifecycle. |
| Readiness | A probe that detects if an application has started and is running as expected. If the application is not running as expected, the container status is updated. For more information, see Pod Lifecycle. |
| Startup | A probe that detects the liveness of slow-starting containers. This startup probe prevents slow-starting containers from being killed before they are up and running. For more information, see Pod Lifecycle. |

6. After you complete the settings, click **Create Application**.

**Configure application lifecycle management**

**Configure PostStart and PreStop Hooks**

The configuration for PostStart and PreStop hooks is the same. Both support the following modes:
**Exec** mode: Runs a specific command inside a container. The command is considered
successful if it exits with a return code of 0.
**HttpGet** mode: Sends an HTTP GET request to a specific endpoint on the container. The
request is considered successful if the response has a status code greater than or equal to 200 and less than 400. The following examples show how to configure PostStart and PreStop container lifecycle hooks in EDAS. The examples use the PostStart hook for demonstration.

**Exec Mode**

For example, you want to run the following command after a container is created:

```
echo "container started"
```

EDAS supports the following two configuration methods: Method 1: Split the command into different parameters. Use this method if the command is short and has few parameters. anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs Method 2: Start a shell and run the command in the shell. Use this method if the command is long and has many parameters.

**HttpGet Mode**

The **HttpGet Mode** includes the following parameters:
**Host**: The host address for the HTTP request. If you leave this parameter empty, the
pod's IP address is used by default.
**Path**: The URI for the HTTP request. The default value is /.
**Port**: The port number for the HTTP request.
**Scheme**: The protocol. HTTP and HTTPS are supported. The default is HTTP.
**HttpHeaders**: Custom HTTP request headers.
The following figure shows an example of a PostStart hook that uses the **HttpGet** method. After the container starts, an HTTP GET request is sent to the `http://example.com:8080/healthz` endpoint.

**Note**

If a PostStart or PreStop hook fails, the container is automatically restarted. You can find information about the failure in the application's change records.

**Configure Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes**

EDAS supports the following three types of Kubernetes container probes: LivenessProbe: Detects whether a container is alive. If the probe fails, Kubernetes automatically terminates the container and then restarts it based on the restart policy. ReadinessProbe: Detects whether a container is ready to accept traffic. If the probe is successful, Kubernetes adds the pod to the list of service endpoints. anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs
**StartupProbe**: Detects whether a slow-starting container has started. If the probe is
successful, it prevents the container from being terminated before it has finished starting. The Liveness, Readiness, and Startup probes support the following three modes:
**Exec**: Runs a specific command inside a container. The probe is considered successful if
the command exits with a return code of 0.
**HttpGet**: Sends an HTTP GET request to a specific endpoint on the container. The probe is
considered successful if the response has a status code greater than or equal to 200 and less than 400.
**TcpSocket**: Checks whether a specified TCP port on the container's IP address is open. The
probe is considered successful if the port is open. All modes for Liveness, Readiness, and Startup probes support the following parameters: InitialDelaySeconds: The number of seconds to wait before the first probe is initiated after the container starts. The value must be between 1 and 1000. PeriodSeconds: The interval in seconds at which probes are performed. The value must be between 1 and 1000. SuccessThreshold: The number of consecutive successes required for the probe to be considered successful after a failure. The value must be between 1 and 1000. For Liveness probes, this value must be 1. TimeoutSeconds: The timeout in seconds for a probe. The value must be between 1 and 1000. FailureThreshold: The number of consecutive failures required for the probe to be considered failed after a success. The value must be between 1 and 1000. The following figure shows a sample configuration of a Liveness probe in TcpSocket mode. In this example, the Host parameter is empty, so the pod's IP address is used as the host address. The probe checks port 18081. The first probe runs 60 seconds after the container starts. Probes are performed every 10 seconds. A single successful probe is sufficient to consider the pod alive. The timeout for each probe is 5 seconds. If three consecutive probes fail, Kubernetes terminates the container and then restarts it based on the restart policy.

**Verify the result**

After you configure an application lifecycle hook, verify the result. For example, you configure a PostStart hook to write `Hello from the postStart handler` to a file. anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs After the application is deployed, use a web shell to check whether the file contains `Hello` `from the postStart handler` . If the text exists, the configuration is successful.

##### Configuration management

You can mount existing configuration items or secrets as files to a specified directory in a container. This injects configuration information into the container. This topic describes how to configure mounts for an application in the EDAS console.

**Background information**

The EDAS console supports two types of mount configurations: Configuration item: A type of configuration information that does not require encryption and is configured in advance. The application must be in the same region, cluster, and Kubernetes namespace as the configuration item to use it. For more information about how to create a configuration item, see Create a configuration item. Secret: A type of pre-configured information that requires encryption, such as passwords and certificates. The application must be in the same region, cluster, and Kubernetes namespace as the secret to use it. For more information about how to create a secret, see Create a secret.

**Configure a mount when you create an application**

1. Log in to the EDAS console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Application Management > Applications**. In
the top navigation bar, select a region. In the upper part of the Applications page, select a microservices namespace from the **Microservice Namespace** drop-down list. Then, click
**Create Application** in the upper-left corner of the **Applications** page.
3. On the **Basic Information** tab, select a **Cluster Type** and an **Application Runtime**
**Environment**. Enter an **Application Name** and click **Next**.

| Configuration Item | Description |
|---|---|
| Cluster Type | Select Kubernetes Cluster. |

anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs

| Application Runtime Environment | Select the application runtime environment. Java: Custom: Use a custom image to deploy the application in a Kubernetes cluster. Java: Supports deployment from generic JAR packages. This option is suitable for Dubbo and Spring Boot applications. You can change the Java environment after you select this option. Tomcat: Supports deployment from generic WAR packages. This option is suitable for Dubbo and Spring applications. You can change the Java environment and container version after you select this option. EDAS-Container (HSF): Deploy HSF applications from WAR or FatJar packages. You can change the Java environment, Pandora version, and Ali-Tomcat version after you select this option. Alibaba Cloud Application Server: Deploy J2EE applications. Supports WAR, JAR (EJB), EAR, and ZIP formats. Multi-language (Node.js, C++, Go, and more): Custom: Use a custom image to deploy the application in a Kubernetes cluster. |
|---|---|
| Monitoring and Governance Solution | Java: By default, a Java Agent is automatically mounted in the Kubernetes cluster for fine-grained monitoring. A complete microservice administration solution is also provided, which includes features such as canary releases, service authentication, and throttling and degradation. Multi-language: A complete microservice administration solution is provided through Istio (Service Mesh). This solution includes features such as canary releases, service authentication, and throttling and degradation. |

4. On the **Application Configurations** tab, set the environment context, basic information,
deployment mode, and resource parameters for the application. Then, click **Next**.

This is suitable for Dubbo and Spring Boot applications. After you select this option, you can change the Java Environment. Tomcat: Supports deployment of general WAR packages. This is suitable for Dubbo and Spring applications. After you select this option, you can change the Java Environment and Container Version. EDAS-Container (HSF): Suitable for deploying HSF applications using WAR or Fat JAR packages. **Implement pod affinity based on labels**

When you deploy applications in a Kubernetes cluster, you often need to consider the dependencies between different components. For example, you might need to schedule some pods to the same topology domain or prevent some pods from being scheduled to the same topology domain. In this case, configuring labels for applications can help you set up custom pod affinity and anti-affinity. The following section describes how to implement pod affinity using labels.

**Prerequisites**

An application with the label `demo-app-name=sc-server-demo` is deployed.

**Procedure**

Configure pod affinity in another application to schedule the pods of both applications to the same node.
1. Log on to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, click **Application Management > Application List**. In
the top menu bar, select a region. Then, select a **Microservices Namespace**. From the
**Cluster Type** drop-down list, select **K8s Cluster**. Then, click the name of your application.
3. In the upper-right corner of the **Basic Information** page, click **Deploy Application**.
anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs
4. On the **Select Deployment Mode** page, select a deployment mode, and then click **Start**
**Deployment** in the upper-right corner of that mode's section.

**Note**

This topic uses **One-Batch Release** as an example.
5. On the **One-Batch Release** page, modify the application's environment and deployment
package information. Then, expand **Scheduling Rules**. Set **Select Mode** to **Custom Configuration**. On the **Pod Affinity** tab, add a rule with the following parameter settings: Set **Topology Domain** to `kubernetes.io/hostname` . Set **Application Label Name** to `demo-app-name` . Set **Operator** to `In` . Set **Application Label Value** to `sc-server-demo` .

`name=sc-client-demo` . After you complete the configuration, click **OK**. After the application is deployed, you can use the `kubectl` command to check the nodes where the pods of the two applications are located.

```bash
kubectl get pod -l demo-app-name=sc-client-demo -o wide kubectl get pod -l demo-app-name=sc-server-demo -o wide
```

```

The output shows that the pods of the two applications are on the same node.

In Kubernetes, you can configure the DNS policy for an application's pods. This policy controls how pods access DNS services and handle domain name resolution, ensuring that they can find and communicate with other services. This topic describes how to set the DNS policy, DNS configuration, and host aliases for an application when you create it.

environment. Then, at the bottom of the page, click **Next**.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Cluster Type | Select Kubernetes Cluster. |

anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs

| Application Runtime Environment | Select the Java application type. DNS configuration is available for the following application types. Custom: Supports image deployment. This option uses the application's built-in Tomcat configuration. No Tomcat parameter configuration is required. Java: Supports deployment of general-purpose JAR packages. This option is suitable for Dubbo and Spring Boot applications. After you select this option, you can change the Java Environment. Tomcat: Supports deployment of general-purpose WAR packages. This option is suitable for Dubbo and Spring applications. After you select this option, you can change the Java Environment and Container Version. EDAS-Container (HSF): Suitable for deploying HSF applications using WAR or FatJar packages. After you select this option, you can change the Java Environment, Pandora Version, and Ali- Tomcat Version. Alibaba Application Server: Suitable for deploying J2EE applications. This option supports WAR, JAR (EJB), EAR, and ZIP packages. After you select this option, you can set the Java Environment and Alibaba Application Server Version. |
|---|---|

4. On the **Application Configurations** tab, set the environment context, basic information,
deployment mode, and resource parameters for the application. Then, click **Next**.
5. On the **Advanced Settings** tab, expand **DNS Configuration**. Then, configure the DNS
settings as needed.

| Configuration item | Description |
|---|---|
| DNS Policy (dnsPolicy) | The DNS Policy (dnsPolicy) field lets you configure a different DNS policy for each pod. ClusterFirst: Domain names are resolved by CoreDNS. The DNS server address configured in the pod's /etc/resolv.conf file is the kube-dns address of the cluster's DNS service. This is the default policy for workloads in the cluster. ClusterFirstWithHostNet: Used with the hostNetwork mode. This allows the pod to resolve both internal Kubernetes service domain names and external domain names. Default: The pod inherits the domain name resolution configuration from the cluster node. This means the pod directly uses the /etc/resolv.conf file of the ECS instance in the cluster. This file is configured with Alibaba Cloud DNS services. None: Ignores the cluster's DNS policy. You must provide the DNS Configuration (dnsConfig) field to specify DNS settings. |

anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs

| DNS Configuration (dnsConfig) | The parameters for DNS Configuration (dnsConfig) are as follows: nameserver: A list of IP addresses to be used as DNS servers for the pod. You can specify up to three IP addresses. Note When the pod's DNS Policy (dnsPolicy) is set to None, this list must contain at least one IP address. Otherwise, this property is optional. The listed DNS IP addresses are merged into the nameserver field of the domain name resolution file generated based on the DNS Policy (dnsPolicy). Duplicate addresses are removed. searches: A list of DNS search domains for hostname lookups in the pod. This property is optional. If specified, the provided list is merged into the base search domains generated from the selected DNS Policy (dnsPolicy). Duplicate domain names are removed. Kubernetes allows a maximum of six search domains. options: An optional list of objects. Each object can have aN ame property (required) and a Value property (optional). The content of this property is merged into the options generated from the specified DNS Policy (dnsPolicy). Duplicate entries are removed. |
|---|---|
| Host Aliases (hostAliases) | hostAliases lets you add local domain name resolution entries to the /etc/hosts file in a pod. IP Address: The destination IP address to which the hostnames are resolved. Hostnames: The hostnames to be resolved to the IP address. Separate multiple hostnames with commas (,). |

##### Configure throttling and degradation

anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs You can redeploy applications in Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) clusters to connect them to the trial version of Application High Availability Service (AHAS). After an application is connected, you can monitor its traffic in real time on the embedded monitoring page in Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS). This feature provides comprehensive visualization to help ensure your application's availability. This topic describes how to configure throttling and degradation rules for microservices using a Dubbo application as an example.

**Background information**

The trial version of AHAS is enabled by default in EDAS and provides basic protection. For each application class, you can set a maximum of two protection rules of the same type. To set more rules, navigate to the AHAS console and activate the Professional Edition. To delete or modify an existing rule, navigate to the application details page. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Throttling And Degradation > Rule Management**. Select the tab for the rule type that you want to manage. Then, select the rule from the list and delete or modify it.

##### Configure sidecar containers and init

**containers**

Configuring sidecar containers for an application can help you run auxiliary services, such as log collection, configuration updates, and network proxies. You can also configure init containers for an application to help you perform specific preparations before the application container starts. The preparations include setting up configuration files, downloading application dependencies, waiting for other services to get ready, and migrating databases. This topic describes how to configure sidecar and init containers when you create an application.

**Usage notes**

This feature is immediately available for Kubernetes (K8s) clusters that you import after an EDAS upgrade. You must upgrade existing clusters after the EDAS upgrade to use this feature.

**Terms**

**Sidecar Containers**

Works with an application container and provides the log collection and traffic hijacking capabilities for the application container. A sidecar container shares storage and network resources with an application container. This way, the sidecar container can directly communicate with the application container.

**Init Container**

Prepare resources and executes special scripts for an application container. Init containers are a set of special containers. Multiple init containers are executed in sequence. Application containers start only if all init containers are executed. For more information, see Init Containers.

**Procedure**

1. Log in to the EDAS console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Application Management > Applications**. In
the top navigation bar, select a region. In the upper part of the Applications page, select a microservices namespace from the **Microservice Namespace** drop-down list. Then, click
**Create Application** in the upper-left corner of the **Applications** page.
anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs
3. In the **Basic Information** step, configure the relevant parameters as required and click
**Next**.
4. In the **Configurations** step, configure the environment information, basic information, and
deployment method for the application, set the related resource parameters, and then click
**Next**.
5. In the **Advanced Settings** step, click **Configure sidecars and InitContainers**, configure
the parameters as needed, and then click **Next**. The following table describes the parameters.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Sidecar Container | You can configure only one sidecar container in a single editor. If you want to configure multiple sidecar containers, click + Add Sidecar Containers. Example 1: Mount a Sidecar container to an application container to provide the busybox toolbox. name: busybox image: busybox:latest command: ["tail","-f" ,"/dev/null"] Example 2: Mount a Sidecar container to an application container to collect logs using Logtail. For more information, see the Data Collection of Simple Log Service > Collect container text logs using Sidecar CRDs document. |
| Init Container | You can configure only one init container in a single editor. If you want to configure multiple init containers, click + Add Init Container. The following sample code provides an example on how to configure an init container that sleeps for 60 seconds before the application container starts. name: busybox image: busybox:latest command: ["sleep", "60"] |

6. After you configure the advanced settings, click **Create Application**. In the **Creation**
**Completed** step, click **Create Application**.
7. In the **Confirm Application Change Precheck** dialog box, click **Start Precheck**.
i. After the data in the dialog box is refreshed, confirm the precheck items and results and click **Continue**. ii. **(Optional)** If you modify the preceding precheck items, click **Check Again**. The application requires several minutes to be deployed. During the process, you can view the change records to track the deployment progress of the application on the **Change List** page. After you deploy the application, go to the **Application Overview** page to view the running status of pods. If the pods are in the **running** state, the application is deployed. You can click the running status of pods to view the **Deployments**, **pods**, and advanced configurations of the application instances.

**References**

anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs For more information about other configuration items for creating or deploying an application, see the Advanced Configuration documentation.

```

##### Configure a pod SecurityContext

A pod SecurityContext is a Kubernetes object that defines security settings at the pod level. You can set `runAsUser`, `runAsGroup`, and `fsGroup` to control the behavior of a pod and its containers. This improves security and resource control. This topic describes how to configure these settings.

**Configure a pod SecurityContext when you create an**

**application**

1. Log in to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, click **Application Management > Applications**.
3. In the top menu bar, select a **Microservices Namespace** and click **Create Application**.
4. On the **Basic Information** tab, select a **Cluster Type** and an **Application Runtime**
**Environment**. Enter an **Application Name** and click **Next**.

| Configuration Item | Description |
|---|---|
| Cluster Type | Select Kubernetes Cluster. |
| Application Runtime Environment | Select the application runtime environment. Java: Custom: Use a custom image to deploy the application in a Kubernetes cluster. Java: Supports deployment from generic JAR packages. This option is suitable for Dubbo and Spring Boot applications. You can change the Java environment after you select this option. Tomcat: Supports deployment from generic WAR packages. This option is suitable for Dubbo and Spring applications. You can change the Java environment and container version after you select this option. EDAS-Container (HSF): Deploy HSF applications from WAR or FatJar packages. You can change the Java environment, Pandora version, and Ali-Tomcat version after you select this option. Alibaba Cloud Application Server: Deploy J2EE applications. Supports WAR, JAR (EJB), EAR, and ZIP formats. Multi-language (Node.js, C++, Go, and more): Custom: Use a custom image to deploy the application in a Kubernetes cluster. |
| Monitoring and Governance Solution | Java: By default, a Java Agent is automatically mounted in the Kubernetes cluster for fine-grained monitoring. A complete microservice administration solution is also provided, which includes features such as canary releases, service authentication, and throttling and degradation. Multi-language: A complete microservice administration solution is provided through Istio (Service Mesh). This solution includes features such as canary releases, service authentication, and throttling and degradation. |

anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs
5. On the **Application Configurations** tab, set the environment context, basic information,
deployment mode, and resource parameters for the application. Then, click **Next**.
6. On the **Advanced Settings** tab, expand **Pod SecurityContext Settings** and configure
the parameters as needed. For more information, see Configure a Security Context for a Pod or Container.

| Configuration Item | Description |
|---|---|
| runAsUser | Sets the user ID (UID) for the entrypoint of the container process. For example, if you specify runAsUser: 65534 , all processes in the container run with the UID 65534 (the nobody user). |
| runAsGroup | Sets the group ID (GID) for the entrypoint of the container process. For example, if you specify runAsGroup: 65534 , all processes in the container run with the primary GID 65534 (the nobody user). |
| fsGroup | You can set a file system group ID for the volume to ensure that all files and folders in the mounted volume are assigned the specified group ID. For example, if you specify fsGroup: 65534, the UID and GID for created files and directories will be 65534 (the nobody user). |

**Start Dry Run**: Checks the preset items and generates a dry run result, analysis, and
suggestions. Click **Continue** to apply the application changes.

##### Configure Intra-zone provider first

**routing**

Intra-zone Provider Firstmeans that when an application invokes a service, it prioritizes providers in the same zone. Applications that use the Spring Cloud, Dubbo, and HSF protocols support this feature. This topic describes how to enable zone affinity for Kubernetes applications.

**Background information**

anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs When you deploy applications across multiple zones, service invocations may cross zones. The following figure shows an example call chain. In the figure, Application A is in Zone 1 and Application B is in Zone 2. If Application A calls Application B, the application on Node A1 calls the application on Node B2. This cross-zone call increases network latency and results in a longer HTTP response time. After you enable Intra-zone Provider First, the consumer application prioritizes providers in the same zone. The following figure shows the call chain. This approach avoids network latency from cross-zone calls and reduces HTTP response time. If no service providers are available in the current zone, the service consumer calls providers in other zones.

**Enable Intra-zone Provider First**

To use the Intra-zone Provider First feature, enable Intra-zone Provider First for the service provider.
1. Log in to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, click **Application Management > Applications**.
3. On the **Basic Information** page of the application, go to the **Application Settings**
section, turn on Locality Priority, and set the **Threshold**. anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs

#### Use a StatefulSet to create a stateful

**application**

This topic describes how to use a StatefulSet to create a stateful application in the Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS) console.

**Prerequisites**

EDAS and Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) are activated for your Apsara Stack tenant account. A microservices namespace is created. For more information, see Manage microservices namespaces in the EDAS console. Role authorization is complete in ACK.

**Background Information**

StatefulSets provide the following features.

| Feature | Description |
|---|---|
| Pod consistency | Pod consistency ensures that pods are started and terminated in the specified order and ensures network consistency. Pod consistency is determined by pod configurations, regardless of the node to which a pod is scheduled. |
| Stable and persistent storage | VolumeClaimTemplate allows you to mount a persistent volume (PV) to each pod. The mounted PVs are not deleted after you delete replicated pods or scale in the number of replicated pods. |
| Stable network identifiers | Each pod in a StatefulSet derives its hostname from the name of the StatefulSet and the ordinal of the pod. The pattern of the hostname is StatefulSet name-pod ordinal . |
| Stable orders | For a StatefulSet with N replicated pods, each pod is assigned an integer ordinal from 0 to N-1. The ordinals assigned to pods within the StatefulSet are unique. |

anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs

**Step 1: Create an ACK cluster**

Log in to the ACK console. Create an ACK cluster. For more information, see Step 1: Create a Kubernetes cluster.

**Step 2: Import the ACK cluster to EDAS in the EDAS console**

By default, the ack-ahas-sentinel-pilot, ack-arms-pilot, and ack-arms-prometheus components are installed when you import an ACK cluster to EDAS in the EDAS console. The ack-ahassentinel-pilot component is an application protection component for throttling and degradation. The ack-arms-pilot component is an Application Real-Time Monitoring Service (ARMS) monitoring component. The ack-arms-prometheus component is a Prometheus monitoring component.
1. Log in to the EDAS console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Resource Management > Container Service**
**Kubernetes Clusters**.
3. In the top navigation bar, select the region in which you want to import the cluster, and
click **Synchronize Container Service Kubernetes Cluster**.
4. Find the ACK cluster that you want to import, and click **Import** in the **Actions** column.
5. In the **Import Kubernetes Cluster** dialog box, select the destination microservices
namespace from the Microservice Namespaces drop-down list, turn on or off **Service Mesh** based on your business requirements, and click **Import**. If the value of the Cluster Status parameter is **Running** and the value of the **Import**
**Status** parameter is **Imported** for the ACK cluster, the ACK cluster is imported to EDAS.

**Step 3: Deploy an application in the ACK cluster**

1. Log in to the EDAS console.
2. In the left-side navigation pane, choose **Application Management > Applications**. In
the top navigation bar, select a region. In the upper part of the Applications page, select a microservices namespace from the **Microservices Namespace** drop-down list. Then, click
**Create Application** in the upper-left corner of the **Applications** page.
3. In the **Application Information** step, configure the parameters in the Cluster Type and
Application Runtime Environment sections, and click **Next**. The following table describes the parameters.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Cluster Type | The type of the cluster in which you want to deploy the application. Select Kubernetes Cluster. Note Kubernetes clusters can be integrated with Apsara Stack Service Mesh (ASM). |
| Deployment Type | The type of the application deployment. Select Stateful (StatefulSet). |
| Application Runtime Environment |   |

anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs

| Hosted Applications | The programming language based on which the application is developed. This topic describes how to deploy a Java application. In this example, Java is selected. For more information about how to deploy an application of different programming languages, see Use images to deploy multi-language microservices applications in Kubernetes clusters. |
|---|---|
| Select Application | The runtime environment of the application. This topic describes how to use a JAR or WAR package to deploy a Java application. Select Java, Tomcat, EDAS-Container (HSF), or Ali application server based on the type of your application and deployment package. Java: Select this option if you want to use a universal JAR package to deploy a Dubbo or Spring Boot application. You can configure the Java Environment parameter after you select this option. Tomcat: Select this option if you want to use a universal WAR package to deploy a Dubbo or Spring application. You can configure the Java Environment and Container Version parameters after you select this option. EDAS-Container (HSF): Select this option if you want to use a WAR or FatJar package to deploy the application as a High-speed Service Framework (HSF) application. You can configure the Java Environment, Pandora Version, and Ali-Tomcat Version parameters after you select this option. Ali application server: Select this option if you want to deploy applications on the Java 2 Platform, Enterprise Edition (J2EE). Applications in WAR, JAR (EJB), Enterprise Application Archive (EAR), and ZIP formats are supported. You can configure the Java Environment and Ali application server version parameters after you select this option. |

### Upgrade and roll back

**applications (Kubernetes)**

#### Overview of application upgrades and

**rollbacks (Kubernetes clusters)**

After you create and deploy an application in Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS), you will need to upgrade it through multiple iterations. If you find issues in an upgraded version, you can roll the application back to a previous version. This topic describes the application upgrade policies and methods that EDAS provides, and how to roll back an application when necessary.

**Upgrade an application**

Different application versions and scenarios require different upgrade policies and methods.

| Upgrad e policy | Scenario | Upgrade method | References |
|---|---|---|---|
| Release to all at once (direct upgrade ) | If an application has a small number of instances or a simple service architecture, you can directly upgrade the application by deploying the new version after development and testing. | Console API Plug-in or tool | For more information, see Use the console to release an application to all instances in a Kubernetes cluster at once. For more information, see the EDAS Developer Guide > DeployK8sApplication API Operation section. Use Cloud Toolkit to release an application to all instances in a Kubernetes cluster at once |

anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs

| Phased release | If an application has many instances or a complex service architecture, you can release it in multiple phases. In each phase, you upgrade only some of the instances. The release is complete when all instances are upgraded. If an error occurs during the release, you can stop the process and roll back the application. After the error is fixed, you can release the application again. | Console API Plug-in or tool | For more information, see Perform a phased release for an application in a Kubernetes cluster. For more information, see the EDAS Developer Guide > DeployK8sApplication section. Use toolkit-maven-plugin to perform a phased release for an application in a Kubernetes cluster |
|---|---|---|---|
| Canary release | A new application version needs to be verified on a small number of instances. If the verification is successful, you can upgrade the application on all instances. | Console | For more information, see Use the console to perform a canary release for an application in a Kubernetes cluster. |

**Roll back an application**

During an application upgrade, exceptions such as an unavailable deployment package or a failed health check can cause the upgrade to fail. In this case, the upgrade process is automatically stopped and the application is rolled back. If issues or exceptions occur in the new version of an application, you can manually roll back the application. The following two scenarios are available: Rollback during the upgrade: You can terminate the application upgrade process and roll back the application. Rollback after the upgrade: You can roll back the application by deploying a previous version of the application. EDAS provides two methods to roll back an application: using the console or calling API operations. For more information, see the following topics: Roll back an application using the console (K8s): For more information, see Roll back an application using the console (K8s). Terminate the upgrade process and roll back the application: For more information, see the
**EDAS Developer Guide > AbortAndRollbackChangeOrder** section.
Roll back to a previous version: For more information, see the **EDAS Developer Guide >**
**RollbackApplication** section.
anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs

After you create and deploy an application in Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS), you may frequently update the application. If the application is a small-scale application or uses a simple architecture, you can deploy a new version to update the application after you develop and test the new version. This topic describes how to use the EDAS console to release an application to all instances in a Kubernetes cluster at a time.

of the desired application.

5. In the **Single-batch Release** section of the **Select Deployment Mode** page, click **Start**
**Deployment**.
6. On the **Single-batch Release** page, upload the deployment package for the new
application version.

| Java Environment | Select a Java environment. |

Always: Forcibly pull the latest image from the remote image repository each time the container is started. IfNotPresent: Pull the image from the remote image repository only when the image does not exist on the on- premises machine. Never: Only local images are used. No image is pulled from the remote image repository. |
|---|---|

Note The file upload method that you specify must be the same as the file upload method that you use to deploy the application. JAR packages, WAR packages, and images are supported. In this example, a JAR package is used. |

Note If you enter the URL of an Object Storage Service (OSS) object that has a signature, EDAS caches the file for subsequent operations, such as rollbacks and scale-outs, when you release the application. |
| Version | The version number of the JAR deployment package. Specify a version number or click Use Timestamp as Version Number to generate a version number. |
| Time Zone | The time zone for the application. Specify the time zone of the specified region in UTC. |

##### Use Cloud Toolkit to deploy a Kubernetes

**application in a single batch**

After you develop, debug, and test an application locally, you can install the Cloud Toolkit plugin in IntelliJ IDEA to quickly deploy the application to Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS). This topic describes how to install Cloud Toolkit in IntelliJ IDEA and deploy an application to a Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) cluster.

**Prerequisites**

You have downloaded and installed Java Development Kit (JDK) 1.8 or later. You have downloaded and installed IntelliJ IDEA 2018.3 or later.

**Note**

The official server of the JetBrains plugin marketplace is located outside China. If you cannot download and install the plugin because of a slow network connection, join the DingTalk group mentioned at the end of this topic. You can obtain the offline installation package from Cloud Toolkit technical support. You have created an application and deployed it to a Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) cluster for the first time. For more information, see Deploy a Java microservice application in a Kubernetes cluster using an image.

**Procedure**

**Step 1: Install Cloud Toolkit**

1. Start IntelliJ IDEA.
2. Install the latest version of the plugin in IntelliJ IDEA.
If you have an earlier version of the plugin installed, upgrade it to the latest version. anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs
**MacOS**: Go to the **Preferences** page. In the navigation pane on the left, select **Plugins**.
In the search box on the right, enter **Alibaba Cloud Toolkit** and click **Install**.
**Windows**: In the navigation pane on the left, select **Plugins**. In the search box on the
right, enter **Alibaba Cloud Toolkit** and click **Install**. anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs
3. After the plugin is installed, restart IntelliJ IDEA. The Alibaba Cloud Toolkit icon (
) appears in the toolbar.

**Step 2: Configure a Cloud Toolkit account**

After you install Alibaba Cloud Toolkit, you must configure your account using an AccessKey ID and an AccessKey secret.
1. Start IntelliJ IDEA.
2. In the IntelliJ IDEA menu bar, select **Tools > Alibaba Cloud > Preferences…**.
3. In the navigation pane on the left, select **Alibaba Cloud Toolkit** > **Accounts**.
4. In the **Accounts** page, set the **AccessKey ID** and **AccessKey Secret** parameters, and
then click **OK**. If you use the AccessKey ID and AccessKey secret of a **RAM user**, make sure that the RAM user has at least the **Deploy Applications** permission. If you are an **EDAS on Apsara Stack Enterprise Edition** user, you must also configure an Endpoint to use the features of Cloud Toolkit. If you already have an Alibaba Cloud account, click **Get existing AK/SK** on the
**Accounts** page to navigate to the Alibaba Cloud logon page. After you log on with your
existing account, you are redirected to the security information management page to obtain the **AccessKey ID** and **AccessKey Secret**. If you do not have an Alibaba Cloud account, click **Sign up** on the **Accounts** page to navigate to the Alibaba Cloud account registration page and create an account. After the registration is complete, obtain the **AccessKey ID** and **AccessKey Secret** as described in the preceding step. anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs

**Step 3: Deploy the application to a Container Service for**

**Kubernetes cluster**

1. In the IntelliJ IDEA menu bar, select **Tools > Alibaba Cloud > Deploy to EDAS > EDAS**
**for Kubernetes Application**.
You can also select **Run > Edit Configurations** in the IntelliJ IDEA menu bar. In the
**Run/Debug Configurations** dialog box, select **Templates > EDAS on Alibaba Cloud >**
**EDAS for Kubernetes Application** in the navigation pane on the left.
2. In the **Deploy to EDAS** dialog box, configure the application deployment parameters.
anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs i. On the configuration page, select the **Region**, **Namespace**, and **Application** for the application based on your requirements.

**Important**

If you cannot find the application in the application list, see the FAQ section for troubleshooting steps.
**Region**: The region where the application is located.
**Namespace**: The microservices namespace where the application is located.
**Application**: The name of the application.
ii. Set the deployment method. The available options are determined by the method that you used for the initial deployment in the console.
**Maven Build**: When you select the Maven Build method to build an application, the
system adds a Maven task by default to build a deployment package.

**Note**

To deploy a multi-module project, see Deploy a multi-module project.
**Upload File**: Upload your WAR or JAR package for deployment.
**Build Image**: If you select the Build Image method to build the application, you must
enter the working directory in the **Content Directory** field, the path to the Dockerfile in the **Dockerfile** field, and the image tag in the **Version** field.
**Select Image**: If you select this deployment method, you can select the image to
deploy from the **Select Image** drop-down list. iii. Click **Advanced** to open the advanced deployment settings tab. On this tab, you can configure parameters such as **Application Environment**, **Startup Command**,
**Environments**, **Persistence**, **Storage**, and **Application Management**.
3. Click **Apply**, and then click **Run**.
The deployment logs are displayed in the Console tab of IntelliJ IDEA. You can check the deployment result based on the log information.

**Deploy a multi-module project**

Most Maven projects are multi-module projects. In a multi-module project, each module can be developed independently, and some modules may use features from other modules. anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs For example, if your project is a Maven multi-module project and you want to deploy a submodule, make sure that the last Maven job in the **Before launch** section on the **EDAS**
**Deployment Configurations** page is the build job for that submodule. For more information
about how to manage Maven build jobs, see Manage Maven build jobs. For example, a CarShop project has the following submodules.

```
carshop ├── itemcenter-api ├── itemcenter ├── detail
```

In this example, itemcenter and detail are submodules that both depend on the itemcenterapi module. To deploy the itemcenter module, you must add the following two Maven tasks in the **Before launch** section on the configuration page: Add a Maven task to run the `mvn clean install` command in the parent project `carshop`. Add a Maven task to run the `mvn clean package` command in the `itemcenter` submodule.

**Manage Maven build jobs**

#### Phased release (applicable to

**Kubernetes clusters)**

##### Phased release (applicable to Kubernetes

**clusters)**

During application release and product iteration, phased release is usually used to control release risks. This topic describes how to use phased release to release an application.

**Overview**

During a phased release, an application is updated only on a few instances in each phase. If an error occurs during a phased release, you can terminate the process and roll back the application. You can release the application in phases again after the error is fixed. When an application in a Kubernetes cluster is released in multiple phases, the instances of the application are evenly allocated to each phase. If the instances cannot be evenly allocated, the number of instances allocated to an earlier phase is smaller than the number of instances allocated to a later phase.

**Scenario**

anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs For example, an application is deployed on 10 instances, and the application needs to be updated from V1 to V2 on all instances. The following figure shows how the application is released to the instances based on a specific policy in three phases.

**Usage notes**

If you release an application in a Kubernetes cluster in multiple phases, a Deployment is created for the application release.

**Procedure**

The following example shows how to deploy an application in multiple phases by using a JAR package and a WAR package.
1. Log in to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, click **Application Management > Applications**.
3. On the **Applications** page, select the region and microservices namespace from the
**Microservice NamespaceMicroservice Namespaces** drop-down list, and click the name
of the desired application.
4. In the upper-right corner of the **Basic Information** page, click **Deploy Application**.
5. In the **Batch Release** section of the **Select Deployment Mode** page, click **Start**
**Deployment**.
6. On the **Batch Release** page, upload the deployment package for the new application
version.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Enable application monitoring | If application monitoring is disabled, the monitoring and alerting, trace query, microservices query, service authentication, outliner removal, graceful undeployment, and canary release features are unavailable. |
| Application Runtime Environment | Specify a runtime environment for the application. Default value: Standard Java Application Runtime Environment. |
| Java Environment | Select a Java environment. |

anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs

| Configure Image | This parameter is displayed if you use a custom image to deploy the application. Manually modify the image URL. Click Select an option. On the Select Image page, you can select Image Repository Namespace and Image Repository Name. |
|---|---|
| Mirror pull strategy | Select an image pulling policy based on your business requirements. Always: Forcibly pull the latest image from the remote image repository each time the container is started. IfNotPresent: Pull the image from the remote image repository only when the image does not exist on the on-premises machine. Never: Only local images are used. No image is pulled from the remote image repository. |
| File Uploading Method | Specify a file upload method. Valid values: Upload JAR Package and JAR Package Address. Note The file upload method that you specify must be the same as the file upload method that you use to deploy the application. JAR packages, WAR packages, and images are supported. In this example, a JAR package is used. |
| Upload JAR Package | If you set the File Uploading Method parameter to Upload JAR Package, click Select File to select a JAR package. |
| JARPackage Address | If you set the File Uploading Method parameter to JAR Package Address, enter the URL of a JAR package. Note If you enter the URL of an Object Storage Service (OSS) object that has a signature, EDAS caches the file for subsequent operations, such as rollbacks and scale-outs, when you release the application. |
| Version | The version number of the JAR deployment package. Specify a version number or click Use Timestamp as Version Number to generate a version number. |
| Time Zone | See the UTC time zone that corresponds to the specified region. |
| Application Description | The description of the application. The description can be up to 128 characters in length. |

anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs

| Single Pod Resource Quota | The amount of CPU and memory resources that you want to reserve for a pod. To set a limit, enter a numeric value. The default value 0 indicates that no limit is set on the CPU and memory quotas. Note For more information about how to configure ACK resource quotas, see Container Service for Kubernetes User Guide > Configure resource quotas and limits. On the Resource Quotas tab, if you have specified CPU Limit, make sure that the value of CPU CPU Limit is not 0. On the Resource Quotas tab, if you have specified Memory Limit, make sure that the value of Memory CPU Limit is not 0. |
|---|---|

7. Configure the parameters in the **Release Policy** section.
The following table describes the parameters in the **Release Policy** section.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Release Batch | The number of phases in which the application is released to the instances. |
| Batch Mode | Valid values: Automatic and Manual. Automatic: The system automatically releases the application in phases at an interval that is specified by the Interval parameter. The Interval parameter indicates the time interval between two phases. Unit: minutes. Manual: You must manually trigger the release of the next phase. |
| Intra-Batch Deployment Interval | If the number of instances is greater than 1, the application is deployed to the application instances at the specified interval. Unit: seconds. |

8. Optional. Configure advanced settings, such as startup commands, environment variables,
and application lifecycle management. For more information, see Advanced settings.
9. After you configure the parameters, click **OK**.

**Verify the results**

Go to the application details page. In the left-side navigation pane, click **Change Records** to view the status of the phased release. If the application is released in all phases, the phased release is complete. anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs On the application details page, view the instance deployment information. If the instance version is V2 and all instances are in the **Running** state, the release is succeeds.

**Roll back the application**

During a phased release, if the application is not updated to the new version on one or more instances, the phased release is in the **Executing** state. When you monitor an upgrade, if you notice that an application instance in the first batch stops responding, you can go to the Change Details page of the instance and click **Roll Back** to roll back the released instance to the previous service package and configuration. If an exception occurs during batch release, see How do I resolve problems in a change process? for troubleshooting. Exceptions such as deployment package unavailability and health check failures may lead to failures of application updates. The current application update is automatically terminated, and the application is rolled back. During an update, the maximum timeout period for a single phase is 30 minutes. If the update process is suspended due to a timeout error, you must go to the **Change Details** page to terminate the release and roll back the application.

##### Phased release of a K8s application by API

This topic describes how to use the EDAS Java SDK to perform a phased release of an application. The application can be deployed from a JAR package, a WAR package, or an image.

**Prerequisites**

Complete the following preparations before you perform a phased release of an application by using an API: An application exists in the EDAS K8s environment. You can choose from multiple methods to create an application based on your requirements. If an application already exists, you can call the **EDAS Developer Guide > ListApplication** API operation to query the application list and obtain the **AppId** of the target application. For example, the AppId is 6b bc57a2-a017-4bec-b521-49a15bd3****. The application deployment package (JAR package, WAR package, or image) is in the target location. JAR or WAR package: This example uses an OSS storage path, such as https:doc***.oss-c n-hangzhou.aliyuncs.com/sc-****-D-0.0.2-SNAPSHOT.jar. For an image, assume the image repository is image-demo-project and the image address is registry-vpc.cn-hangzhou.aliyuncs.com/image-demo-project/provider:2.0.

**Background information**

For phased releases via an API, we recommend using automatic batching. If you use manual batching, you must also call the **EDAS Developer Guide > ContinuePipeline** API operation to manually confirm each subsequent batch. For more information, see Manually confirm the next release batch. The following are two example phased release strategies. Select and modify a strategy based on your business requirements. Two-batch release with manual batching.

```json
{"type":"BatchUpdate","batchUpdate":{"batch":2,"releaseType":"manual"}}
```

Two-batch release with automatic batching and a 2-minute interval between batches. anagement for Kubernetes cluste rs

```json
{"type":"BatchUpdate","batchUpdate": {"batch":2,"releaseType":"auto","batchWaitTime":2}}
```

##### Use the EDAS console to implement canary

**releases of applications in Kubernetes clusters**

For Spring Cloud or Dubbo microservice applications that are deployed in a Kubernetes cluster, you can implement a canary release. A canary release, also known as a phased release, lets you verify a new application version on a small number of instances. If the verification is successful, you can update the application on all of your instances to the new version. This ensures a secure update process.

**Limits**

High-Speed Service Framework (HSF) applications: Canary releases are not supported. Dubbo applications are unlimited. Spring Cloud applications: If your application uses features or configurations that depend on Deployment.Metadata.Name or Deployment.Metadata.Uid, do not implement a canary release. Otherwise, the native features of the application may malfunction after the release.

**Procedure**

1. Log in to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, click **Application Management > Applications**.
3. In the top menu bar, select a region. Then, in the upper part of the page, select a
**Microservice Namespace**.
4. On the **Applications** page, select **Container Service Kubernetes Cluster** from the
**Cluster Type** drop-down list. Then, click the name of the target application.
5. In the upper-right corner of the **Application Overview** page, click **Deploy Application**.
6. In the **Canary Release (Phased)** section of the **Select Deployment Mode** page, click
**Start Deployment** in the upper-right corner.
7. On the **Canary Release (Phased)** page, set the deployment parameters, release policy,
and canary release rules for the new application version. Then, click **OK**. i. Set the deployment parameters. Table 1. Deployment parameter description

| Java Environment | Select a Java environment. |
