#### Ensure the availability of Dubbo

**applications using outlier ejection**

In a microservices model, if an application instance of a service provider becomes abnormal and service consumers cannot detect the issue, normal service calls are affected. This degrades consumer service performance and may even impact service availability. The outlier ejection feature detects the availability of application instances and performs dynamic adjustments to ensure successful service calls, thereby improving business stability and service quality. This topic describes how to create an outlier ejection policy.

**Background information**

In the example scenario shown in the following figure, a system contains four applications: A, B, C, and D. Application A invokes applications B, C, and D separately. If some instances of applications B, C, or D become abnormal—as indicated by the red circles in the figure— application B has one abnormal instance, and applications C and D each have two abnormal instances—and application A cannot detect this, some calls will fail. If many instances of B, C, or D are abnormal, application A’s performance or even service availability may be affected. To protect application A’s service performance and availability, configure outlier ejection for application A. After configuration, monitor the instance status of applications B, C, and D and perform dynamic adjustments—such as ejecting or adding instances—to ensure successful service calls. The outlier ejection process is as follows:
1. When an instance of application B, C, or D becomes abnormal, the system detects it and,
based on the configured **Maximum Ejection Ratio**, determines whether to eject the instance from the application.
2. After ejecting the instance, call requests from application A are no longer distributed to the
abnormal instances of applications B, C, or D.
3. Based on the configured **Recovery Detection Unit Time**, the system starts detecting
whether the abnormal instance has recovered.
4. The detection interval increases linearly with the number of detections, based on the
**Recovery Detection Unit Time** (default: 0.5 minutes). When the configured **Maximum**
**Unrecovered Cumulative Count** is reached, the system continues to detect whether the
abnormal instance has recovered at the maximum time interval. governance
5. When the instance recovers, the system adds it back to the application’s instance list to
process call requests. At the same time, it resets the detection interval to the **Recovery**
**Detection Unit Time**, such as 0.5 minutes.

**Note**

When the number of abnormal instances in a provider application is too high— exceeding the Maximum Ejection Ratio—the system ejects only the number of instances specified by the configured ratio. When only one available instance remains in a provider application, that instance is not ejected, even if its error rate exceeds the configured threshold.

**Create Outlier Ejection Policy**

1. Log on to the EDAS console.
2. In the left navigation pane, choose **Microservices Governance > Dubbo**.
3. In the navigation pane on the left, click **Outlier Ejection**. On the **Outlier Ejection** page,
click **Create Outlier Ejection Policy**.
4. In the **Create Outlier Ejection Policy** panel, complete the configurations, then click **OK**.

| Configuration Item | Description |
|---|---|
| Microservices Namespace | Select a region and microservices namespace from the list on the right. |
| Policy Name | The name of the outlier ejection policy. It supports uppercase and lowercase letters, digits, underscores ( ), and hyphens (-). The _ name can be up to 64 characters long. |
| Framework Used by Called Service | Select Spring Cloud, Dubbo, or Service Mesh as needed. |
| Select Effective Applications | After selecting the effective applications, click the > icon to add the applications to the Selected Applications list. After selecting the effective applications, all abnormal instances of the applications called by this application will be ejected. During ejection, call requests from the effective applications will no longer be distributed to abnormal instances. |
| Minimum Error Rate | If the error rate of an application instance in a called application exceeds the configured minimum, the instance will be ejected. The default value is 50%. For example, if the instance is called 10 times within the statistical time window and 6 calls fail, the error rate is 60%. If this exceeds the configured minimum error rate (50%), the instance is removed from the application. |

governance

| Advan ced Config uratio n | Click the icon to expand the Advanced Configuration options. |   |
|---|---|---|
|   | Exception Type | Includes Network Exception and Network Exception + Business Exception (Dubbo Exception). Select as needed. Note Network exceptions generally refer to Dubbo's RpcException, such as network timeouts, server-side Full GC slow responses leading to full server-side thread pools, and similar scenarios. Business exceptions generally refer to Dubbo's BizException, such as server-side thrown RuntimeExceptions and similar issues. |
|   | Minimum QPS | QPS is calculated based on the statistical time window. For Dubbo 2.7 applications, the statistical time window is 15 seconds. For other Dubbo versions and Spring Cloud applications, the statistical time window is 10 seconds. Error rate statistical analysis begins when the application's QPS reaches the configured minimum within the statistical time window (for example, 15 seconds). |
|   | Maximum Ejection Ratio | The maximum ratio of abnormal instances to eject. Once this threshold is reached, no more abnormal instances are ejected. The number of ejected abnormal instances is rounded down. For example, if the total number of application instances is 6 and the ejection ratio is set to 60%, the number of instances to eject is 6 × 60% = 3.6. The policy will eject a maximum of 3 instances. If the calculated result is less than 1, no instances are ejected. |
|   | Recovery Detection Unit Time | After an abnormal instance is ejected, the detection interval linearly accumulates based on this unit time to check if the abnormal instance has recovered. The unit is ms. The default is 30,000 ms, or 0.5 minutes. |

governance

|   | Maximum Unrecovered Cumulative Count | Continuously detect abnormal instances. The detection interval increases linearly with the number of detections based on the Recovery Detection Unit Time. When the configured maximum number of detections is reached, it continues to detect whether the abnormal instance has recovered at the maximum time interval. For example, if the Recovery Detection Unit Time is set to 30,000 ms and the Maximum Unrecovered Cumulative Count is set to 20, after the 20th detection, if the abnormal instance has not yet recovered, subsequent detections are performed at an interval of 10 minutes (20 × 30,000 ms). If the instance is detected to have recovered, the detection interval is reset to the initial interval, which is one Recovery Detection Unit Time. Note Do not set the Maximum Unrecovered Cumulative Count too high. Setting it too high results in a longer maximum detection interval. If an instance recovers early in the detection interval, the system still waits until the end of the interval to detect it. This wastes instance resources during that period and prevents timely processing of business call requests. |
|---|---|---|

**Result Validation**

After you configure and create an outlier ejection policy, outlier ejection is enabled. You can navigate to the **Advanced Monitoring** page where outlier ejection is configured to view monitoring information for the application. For example, use the **Topology Graph** to verify whether call requests are still forwarded to abnormal instances, or check whether the application’s **Error Rate/Minute** exceeds the configured **Error Rate Lower Limit**, to determine whether the outlier ejection policy is effective. For detailed steps, see the

**Application Real-Time Monitoring Service ARMS User Guide > Application Overview**

#### Implement Access Control for Dubbo

**Applications Using Service Authentication**

governance If a microservice application has security requirements, you can implement interface or method-level access control. This lets you authenticate callers, permitting only those that match authentication rules to initiate calls, thereby enhancing application security. This topic describes how to implement access control for Dubbo applications using service authentication.

**Background information**

This section uses an example to describe Dubbo service authentication scenarios. Consumers 1, 2, and 3, along with the Provider, are in the same namespace. By default, Consumers 1, 2, and 3 can call all services and interfaces of the Provider. You can set authentication methods for all services and interfaces of the Provider. For example, if you set the authentication method for Consumer 1 to blacklist (deny calls) for all services and interfaces of the Provider, then the authentication method for Consumers 2 and 3 is whitelist (allow calls). Additionally, you can set authentication methods for specific services and interfaces for Consumers. For example, while Consumers 2 and 3 can access all services and interfaces of the Provider based on the authentication method for all interfaces, if Service and Interface 2 of the Provider involve core business or data, and you do not want Consumer 2 to call it, you can set the authentication method for Service and Interface 2 for Consumer 2 to blacklist (deny calls). In this case, Consumer 2 can only access Service and Interface 1 or Service and Interface 3 of the Provider. The following figure shows the call diagram after authentication rules are set: governance

#### End-to-end traffic adjustment

##### Introduction to end-to-end traffic shaping

Canary release helps developers smoothly update applications to a later version. Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS) supports canary traffic adjustment on a single application and end-to-end traffic adjustment on multiple applications.

**Scenarios**

You can implement traffic adjustment on a single application and multiple applications based on the following two methods: HTTP and High-Speed Service Framework (HSF). Single-application upgrades New versions are continuously released in the application iteration process. Before a new version is officially released, you can use canary traffic adjustment to verify the new version on a small number of instances by collecting the user experience data. This way, you can check the metrics, such as features, performance, and stability, of the new application version before you perform a full update. Multi-application troubleshooting When your HSF microservice-oriented applications that are deployed in EDAS fail to work, you can perform end-to-end traffic adjustment to route specific traffic to an application for troubleshooting problems in the application. This ensures that all microservice-oriented applications can run as expected.

**Ingress application and traffic adjustment rules**

To implement end-to-end traffic shaping, you must first specify an ingress application. Then, you can set traffic shaping rules for HTTP and HSF. The following figure illustrates how the ingress application and grayscale traffic shaping rules work. governance HTTP HSF

| tra | ffic |
|---|---|
| Grayscale traffic detection and HSF rgoruatyinscgale rule |   |
| Normal Grayscale traffic traffic Application Application group group A0(Non- A1(Grayscale) Agprapylisccaatiloen) Application instance instance Application Application instance instance Ingress application Normal Grayscale traffic traffic |   |

traffic Grayscale traffic detection HTTP grayscale rule Ingress application Normal Grayscale traffic traffic For HTTP traffic, a grayscale evaluation is performed only after the traffic enters the ingress application. If the traffic meets the rule conditions, it is marked as grayscale traffic.

**Important**

Only the received HTTP traffic is evaluated for grayscale. End-to-end traffic shaping does not currently support grayscale routing for HTTP traffic. In practice, a grayscale evaluation is performed on HTTP traffic at the ingress application. Then, all HSF traffic generated in subsequent stages is routed based on the grayscale tag. Unlike with end-to-end traffic shaping, the HTTP traffic shaping rule for a single application applies to application groups. It performs both grayscale evaluation and grayscale routing. For HSF traffic, both a grayscale evaluation and standard grayscale routing are performed before the traffic enters the ingress application. If the ingress application has an application instance group that belongs to the current grayscale environment, the grayscale traffic is routed directly to that grayscale group. Otherwise, the grayscale traffic is downgraded and routed to the non-grayscale default group of the ingress application. You can specify a canary traffic adjustment rule for multiple applications in a similar way as the traffic adjustment rule for a single application. The difference is that you can specify multiple rules for canary traffic adjustment on multiple applications. You must specify a Protocol Type for each rule. The available types are HTTP and HSF. Each rule can contain multiple conditions, which are combined using AND or OR logic.

**Traffic adjustment environment**

governance EDAS manages canary releases by defining a traffic adjustment environment. A traffic adjustment environment consists of the ingress application and identification rules. It is also a logical space that contains application instance groups that are deployed in the traffic adjustment environment. Therefore, you can add or remove an instance group that is a nondefault group of an application to or from a traffic adjustment environment.

**Flexible features**

The end-to-end traffic adjustment solution of EDAS implements canary release and traffic adjustment using the EDAS console. The solution provides the following flexible features: You only need to prepare instance resources for the applications that require a phased release. You do not need to build an entirely new business system. Multiple grayscale environments are supported. This allows different applications to have their own grayscale controls, and an application can participate in multiple grayscale environments at the same time. Call chain grayscale is supported. This allows multiple applications to be in the same traffic shaping environment. Grayscale traffic detected in an upstream stage can pass through intermediate, non-grayscale application stages and still be routed to the corresponding grayscale application instance in a downstream stage.

##### How to upgrade a single application using

#### end-to-end traffic adjustment

During application iteration, use end-to-end traffic adjustment to validate the new version with a small canary release. After validation succeeds, upgrade the entire application to the new version.

**Scenario Overview**

Web application A has two application instances. Version V1 is deployed on an ECS cluster using a WAR package. After you finish developing version V2, first validate it on one instance. Then upgrade the other instance from V1 to V2 to complete the upgrade of application A.

**Canary Release Flow**

1. Create a canary group.
2. Configure and enable traffic shaping rules for the canary group.
3. Deploy the new version (V2) to the canary group. Verify that the specified traffic reaches
the instances in the canary group.
4. Validate the new version using traffic routed to the canary group.
5. After successful validation, upgrade the application version in the default group to V2.
If issues occur during validation, disable the traffic shaping rules for the canary group. Move the instances from the canary group back to the default group. After you fix V2, re-enable the traffic shaping rules for the canary group and redeploy and revalidate. governance
6. Disable the traffic shaping rules for the canary group. Delete the canary group.

##### Use end-to-end traffic adjustment to

**troubleshoot application issues**

When an HSF microservice application deployed in EDAS encounters issues, use end-to-end traffic adjustment to identify the specific application causing the problem in the call chain. This improves troubleshooting efficiency and ensures the entire microservice application runs normally. This topic uses an example to demonstrate how to troubleshoot application issues in a call chain using end-to-end traffic adjustment.

**Limits**

Using canary release to troubleshoot multi-application issues has the following limits: The cluster type must be an ECS cluster. The application runtime environment must be EDAS Container, which primarily supports HSF applications. Applications deployed using images are not supported.

**Example scenario**

governance A call chain for an HSF microservice application includes four applications: A, B, C, and D, running versions A1, B1, C1, and D1 respectively. The service provided by the entire call chain fails. Initial analysis indicates that applications B and D are problematic. Use end-to-end canary traffic adjustment to route specific traffic to the canary groups of applications B and D for troubleshooting.

**Troubleshooting flow**

The troubleshooting process has two phases: Phase 1 troubleshoots application D, and Phase 2 troubleshoots application B.

Done

**Procedure**

The following steps describe the actual operations based on the troubleshooting flow.
1. Create an instance group for application D to handle traffic adjustment traffic. For details,
see Manage application instance groups in ECS clusters using the console.
2. Create a traffic adjustment environment, set web application A as the ingress application,
configure throttling rules, add application D’s traffic adjustment group, and enable the canary environment. Splitting test and troubleshooting traffic at the HTTP ingress is convenient and common. In this example, the HTTP ingress application is A, and the target application to troubleshoot is D. Because traffic identification and handling occur on different applications, end-to-end traffic adjustment is required.

**Note**

If no instances are deployed in the canary group, it cannot handle canary traffic. The system triggers the “canary fallback” mechanism, routing canary traffic to instances in the default group. After adding instances to the canary group, the “canary fallback” mechanism is disabled, and canary traffic flows to the instances in the canary group.
3. Add instances to the canary group of application D. For details, see Manage application
instance groups in ECS clusters using the console. During instance addition, deploy using the version from the default group.
4. Verify that traffic distribution generally meets expectations and troubleshoot issues in
application D’s canary group. governance i. Use **traffic monitoring** in the canary group to check traffic distribution, confirm whether canary rules take effect, and verify if traffic distribution matches expectations. For details, see Monitor canary traffic. ii. Troubleshoot issues in application D’s canary group using canary traffic. If troubleshooting succeeds, prepare to troubleshoot target application B and create a canary group for it. The canary group for application D was created after setting up the traffic adjustment environment and configuring traffic adjustment rules. In practice, the order of activating throttling rules and deploying canary instances is flexible, allowing multiple strategies. For details, see End-to-end traffic adjustment policies. If configuration errors are found or a version update is needed during troubleshooting, disable the canary environment and remove instances from application D’s canary group. After preparing the new version or correcting the configuration, re-enable the canary environment and redeploy the application for validation.
5. Create an instance group for application B to handle canary traffic.
6. Add application B’s canary group to the traffic adjustment environment.
7. Add instances to application B’s canary group.
8. Check whether traffic distribution generally meets expectations and troubleshoot issues in
the canary groups of applications B and D. i. Use **traffic monitoring** in the canary group to check traffic distribution, confirm whether canary rules take effect, and verify if traffic distribution matches expectations. For details, see Monitor canary traffic. ii. Troubleshoot issues in the canary groups of applications B and D using canary traffic. If troubleshooting completes successfully, disable the canary environment and delete the canary groups for applications B and D (and delete the traffic adjustment environment). If configuration errors are found or a version update is needed during troubleshooting, update the application or configuration, redeploy, and validate again. Because application D is still under active troubleshooting, the traffic adjustment environment remains enabled. Only the canary instances for application B are removed.

##### Create an end-to-end traffic

**adjustmentenvironment**

The end-to-end traffic adjustmentfeature lets you create a traffic control environment quickly and flexibly. This environment enables a group of application instances to handle a specific range or volume of service traffic. Common use cases include testing new application versions online in a controlled manner and directing specific service traffic to a dedicated application instance group. In a traffic control environment, you can use rules to control which traffic enters the application instances, which effectively tags the traffic with a traffic control mark. You can also control which application instances belong to the environment, which effectively tags the instances with a traffic control mark.

**Application limitations**

The application must be deployed in an EDAS cluster, such as an ECS or Swarm cluster. Image-based deployment is not supported for Swarm clusters. The application must be an HSF application. The EDAS Container version for the application must support end-to-end traffic control. governance

click **Create Environment** in the upper-right corner.

required information, and then click **Next**.

The identifier can be up to 64 characters in length and can contain only letters, underscores ( ), _ and digits. It cannot start with a digit. |
| Canary EnvironmentDescription | Enter a description. |

information, and then click **Next**.

##### Monitor Phased Release Traffic

After a phased release, monitor traffic to verify success and assess the traffic status of applications and instances.

**Background information**

Monitoring phased release traffic includes monitoring traffic for a single application and monitoring end-to-end traffic shaping across multiple applications.

**Monitor Phased Release Traffic for a Single Application**

A single application undergoes a phased release based on application instance groups. After the release, you can monitor application and instance traffic by application instance group as follows:
1. Log on to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, click **Application Management > Application List**.
3. On the **Application List** page, click the name of the application that has undergone a
phased release.
4. On the application details page, click the **Instance Deployment Information** tab. In the
application instance group area, click **Traffic Monitoring** on the right.
5. In the **Traffic Monitoring** dialog box, on the right, select a monitoring perspective
(**Instance Perspective** or **Service Perspective**). Then, in the time window, select a monitoring period.
6. Monitor the application’s traffic data.
governance Instance Perspective: On the **Overview** tab, monitor upstream and downstream traffic, response time, number of requests, and number of errors for the application and its instances. Select an application or specific instance from the list on the left to monitor it. Additional routine monitoring includes JVM monitoring, host monitoring, and interface snapshots. Service Perspective: On the **Overview** tab, monitor upstream and downstream traffic, response time, number of requests, and number of errors for the services provided by the application. Select a service from the list on the left to monitor it. Additional routine monitoring includes interface snapshots.

**Monitor End-to-End Phased Release Traffic**

When multiple applications are involved, a phased release occurs based on the traffic shaping environment. After the release, you can monitor traffic for each application in the phased release environment as follows:

environment. The phased release traffic data for a specific application is consistent with the traffic monitoring for a single application. For more information, see Monitor Phased Release Traffic for a Single Application.

##### Limits on end-to-end throttling

End-to-end throttling enables flexible canary release methods. It also poses some limits and leads to specific conventions. If an application instance group belongs to multiple throttling environments, throttling conflicts may occur. Therefore, during end-to-end throttling, one application instance group can belong to only one throttling environment.

**Note**

If a High-speed Service Framework (HSF) rule is enabled for the application instance group during single application throttling, a throttling environment is created for this group.

**Uniqueness of the throttling property**

After a request is marked by a throttling rule, the request is never marked by another throttling rule even if this request matches another throttling rule.

**Priorities of throttling rules**

An application may be used as the ingress application for multiple throttling environments, and a request may match multiple throttling rules at the same time. You must set priorities for multiple throttling rules because a request can be marked by only one throttling rule. The throttling rules that are created or modified later preferentially take effect. governance

**Limits on the joint use of single application throttling and end-**

**to-end throttling**

An application may use both single application throttling and end-to-end throttling at the same time. An HSF rule created for single application throttling is equivalent to a throttling rule. An application instance group cannot belong to different throttling environments. If an application instance group has been added to a throttling environment, you can no longer create an HSF rule for throttling of the single application. Similarly, if an application instance group has an HSF rule, it cannot be added to another throttling environment.

**Unique rule for the same ingress endpoint of an ingress**

**application in single application throttling mode**

In single application throttling mode, the HTTP or HSF rules of an application are subject to the uniqueness limit. One ingress endpoint of an application can be defined by only one HTTP or HSF rule. The following list defines an ingress endpoint: For the HTTP protocol, an endpoint refers to an application, and only one group can be set for an application. For the HSF protocol, an endpoint refers to an interface method of an application. During single application throttling, only one HTTP rule can be defined for one application. Furthermore, an interface method of an application can be used only in one HSF rule.

##### End-to-end traffic adjustment policy

In canary release, you can specify a traffic adjustment rule and deploy a new version by using multiple policies. This is because the order of these two operations is not limited. The following table describes several available combination methods for canary release. You can evaluate the methods and choose an appropriate method based on your requirements.

| Method | Benefit | Problem |
|---|---|---|
| Deploy the new version > Specify a traffic adjustment rule | You can verify the maximum traffic for a canary group. Application deployment and canary rule configuration need to be joined only once. | Before the canary release rule takes effect, the inbound traffic of the instances for the application of the new version may not be canary traffic. |
| Deploy the earlier version > Specify a traffic adjustment rule > Upgrade to the new version | You can verify the maximum traffic for a canary group. | The smooth upgrade is also important. You need to check whether the upgrade of an application on relevant instances affects the requests that are being processed during the upgrade. Two application deployments are performed. |
| Specify a traffic adjustment rule > Deploy the new version | Application deployment and canary rule configuration need to be joined only once. | Before the application is deployed, canary traffic is downgraded and routed to the non-canary release environment. However, after the first batch of application instances of the new version is released, the instances may be affected by all the canary traffic. |

governance

| Specify an invalid traffic adjustment rule > Deploy the new version > Specify a traffic adjustment rule | This method has the optimal controllability. The application instances that are newly deployed receive canary traffic only after the new valid canary release rule takes effect. | Two canary rule configurations are performed. |
|---|---|---|

**Note**

We recommend that you use the third method. This method is simple and can ensure that only canary traffic enters the canary release environment. However, only a few canary application instances exist in the early phase of the deployment, and application instances may be affected by heavy canary traffic after the canary release. Therefore, make sure that the traffic received by instances is in the expected range. End-to-end traffic adjustment is similar to single-application traffic adjustment. The difference is that specifying a traffic adjustment rule is changed to creating a canary release environment in end-to-end traffic adjustment.

##### Traffic adjustment rule parameters

A canary release allows you to create traffic adjustment rules by HTTP and HSF, whose parameter settings are different. You can configure parameters for HTTP traffic adjustment rules based on the cookie, HTTP header, and URL parameter values. You can determine traffic based on the remainder range or list after the mod operation (mod 100). This type of rule is easy to configure and is not described in detail in this topic. If a parameter value contains a non-digit character, this character is converted to a digit by using the hash algorithm. If you use complex parameters, we recommend that you use lists to determine the traffic. This topic describes the parameters of HSF traffic adjustment rules. The end-to-end canary release allows you to obtain a property of a parameter by using a parameter expression. The following table describes supported parameter expressions.

| Expression | Description | Remarks |
|---|---|---|
| args0 | The value of the current parameter. | N/A |
| args0.name | The name property of the parameter. | It can be translated into the arg.getName() Java statement. |
| args0.isEnabled() | The enabled property of the parameter, which is of the BOOLEAN type. | In Java specifications, getter for the BOOLEAN type must be isXXX() . |
| args0[0] | The first value of the arg array. | N/A |

governance

| args0.get(0) | The first value of the arg list. | N/A |
|---|---|---|
| args0.get("key") | The value of the key in the arg map. | N/A |

If you select the first parameter, Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS) automatically generates an args0 prefix on the page. The preceding expressions can be combined. Example: `args0.persons[0].meta.get("name")` : retrieves the first parameter in the persons array and obtains the meta property of persons, which is a map. Then, the value of name in this map is retrieved.

**Supported conditions**

`=` : supports comparison between STRING, NUMBER, BOOLEAN, and CHAR values. != : supports comparison between STRING, NUMBER, BOOLEAN, and CHAR values. `>` : supports comparison between NUMBER values. `>=` : supports comparison between NUMBER values. `<` : supports comparison between NUMBER values. `<=` : supports comparison between NUMBER values.

**Supported value expressions**

A value expression for an HSF parameter matching condition represents a Java value. Only the basic data types of Java are supported, including STRING, NUMBER, BOOLEAN, and CHAR. Complex and custom data types are not supported. EDAS supports the following types of value expressions:

**Standard Java STRING type**

A standard Java STRING expression represents a string that is enclosed in double quotation marks ( `""` ). Example: `"tom"` : the tom string `"10"` : the 10 string `"abc "` : the abc string followed by a space `"a"` : the a string "\n" : the line feed "\"abc\"" : the `"abc"` string "a\bc" : the a\bc string This type of expression can represent arbitrary strings.

**NUMBER type**

If you want to express a NUMBER value, just enter the number. Example: 1.23 -3.14 governance 1.23f

**Note**

In Java, 1.23 is a DOUBLE value by default. The FLOAT value for 1.23 is 1.23f. This is determined by the precision in Java specifications.

**BOOLEAN type**

The BOOLEAN type has only two valid values: true and false.

**CHAR type**

A CHAR value represents a character that is enclosed in single quotation marks (''). Example: 'a'.

**NULL type**

The NULL type indicates the null value in Java. You can directly enter null.

**String literals**

A string literal exactly represents a string so that no characters in this string need to be escaped. Example:

| String literal | Java String |
|---|---|
| tom | "tom" |
| " | "\"" |
| \ | "\\" |
| a\b | "a\b" |

The following table lists the value expressions for all types of values.

| java.lang.String | Line wrapping | "\n" |
| java.lang.String | ' | "\'" |

| byte | 10 | 10 |

| java.lang.Boolea n | true | true |

**Parameters of the ARRAY type**

Assume that the parameter is a string array. You can enter `[0]` in the field to retrieve the first element of the array.

**Parameters of the LIST type**

### End-to-end traffic adjustment

#### Introduction to end-to-end traffic

**adjustment**

In Kubernetes (K8s) environments, Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS) supports end-to-end traffic adjustment for Spring Cloud microservice applications. This feature enables you to quickly and flexibly create a traffic shaping environment to route traffic with specific characteristics to a target application version.

**Background information**

When you deploy a new version of a Spring Cloud application in an EDAS K8s environment, calls between applications are random. This prevents you from routing traffic with specific characteristics to the target application version. The end-to-end traffic adjustment feature isolates the relevant application versions into independent runtime environments called lanes. By setting traffic shaping and routing rules, you can route request traffic that matches the rules to the target application version. This topic uses an order placement scenario in an e-commerce architecture to explain the end-to-end traffic adjustment feature. After a customer places an order, traffic enters through an ingress application or a microservice gateway. The ingress application calls the transaction center. The transaction center then calls the product hub, which in turn calls the downstream inventory center. The transaction center and the product hub each have two new versions (1 and 2) that require grayscale validation. You want to route request traffic that matches specific traffic shaping rules from the ingress application or microservice gateway to the new versions. All other traffic is routed to the online (official) version. governance Transaction Inventory Product Hub (Online version) Center Center (Online version) Other traffic Ingress header = red application Transaction Product Hub red lane (Isolated version Center Microservice (Isolated version 1) gateway header = 1) blue Ingress traffic rule Ingress traffic rule for red lane: for blue lane: Transaction blue lane Product Hub (Isolated version Center param=red in HTTP param=blue in HTTP (Isolatedversion 2) In the diagram, the transaction center and the product hub each have two new versions (1 and 2). Access requests are randomly forwarded to each version, which prevents traffic from being shaped. Using the end-to-end traffic adjustment feature, you can set version 1 as the red lane and version 2 as the blue lane. You can then set traffic shaping rules at the ingress application. When request traffic that enters the ingress application matches a rule, the traffic is routed to the target lane.

**Terms**

Ingress application The traffic entry point for a microservice system. An ingress application can be a Spring Cloud Gateway, a Netflix Zuul Gateway, or a Spring Boot, Spring MVC, or Dubbo application. Lane An isolated environment defined for applications of the same version. Only request traffic that matches the traffic shaping and routing rules is routed to the tagged applications in the corresponding lane. An application can belong to multiple lanes, and a lane can contain multiple applications. The relationship between applications and lanes is many-to-many. Lane group A collection of lanes. Lane groups are used to distinguish between different teams or scenarios.

**Limits**

Applications that use end-to-end traffic adjustment do not support canary releases. If you use Spring Cloud Gateway as an ingress gateway, the Spring Cloud Gateway version must be 2.1.x or later. The quotas for lane groups and lanes vary based on the EDAS edition: Standard Edition: You can create a maximum of one lane group across all regions. Within this lane group, you can create a maximum of five lanes. All editions except for Professional and Platinum are considered Standard Edition. Professional Edition: You can create a maximum of 10 lane groups across all regions. Within each lane group, you can create a maximum of 50 lanes. Platinum Edition: You can create a maximum of 10 lane groups across all regions. Within each lane group, you can create a maximum of 50 lanes. The quotas for lane groups and lanes are fixed. governance To request a quota increase, contact technical support for assistance.

#### Use end-to-end traffic shaping to route

**traffic to target applications**

You can configure end-to-end traffic shaping for Spring Cloud and Dubbo microservice applications that are deployed in an Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS) Kubernetes environment. This feature lets you route traffic with specific characteristics to a target version of an application.

**Prerequisites**

Before you configure end-to-end traffic shaping for applications, complete the following tasks: Deploy a new version of an application or upgrade an application. For more information, see Overview of application upgrades and rollbacks (Kubernetes). If the ingress application is a Spring Cloud Gateway or Netflix Zuul microservice gateway, create the microservice gateway and associate it with an EDAS microservices namespace. If you use Spring Cloud Gateway as the ingress gateway, the version of Spring Cloud Gateway must be 2.1.x or later. Bind a Server Load Balancer (SLB) instance to the ingress application. For more information, see Add Server Load Balancer (SLB) or Reuse an SLB instance.

**Background information**

This topic uses an order placement scenario in an e-commerce architecture to explain the end-to-end traffic adjustment feature. After a customer places an order, traffic enters through an ingress application or a microservice gateway. The ingress application calls the transaction center. The transaction center then calls the product hub, which in turn calls the downstream inventory center. The transaction center and the product hub each have two new versions (1 and 2) that require grayscale validation. You want to route request traffic that matches specific traffic shaping rules from the ingress application or microservice gateway to the new versions. All other traffic is routed to the online (official) version. Transaction Inventory Product Hub (Online version) Center Center (Online version) Other traffic Ingress header = red application Transaction Product Hub red lane (Isolated version Center Microservice (Isolated version 1) gateway header = 1) blue Ingress traffic rule Ingress traffic rule for red lane: for blue lane: Transaction blue lane Product Hub (Isolated version Center param=red in HTTP param=blue in HTTP (Isolatedversion 2)

## Configuration management

### Configuration Management

#### Configuration Management Overview

This integration lets you centrally manage application configurations in EDAS.

**Features**

EDAS provides application configuration management . You can select the configuration management features that you need.

| Feature | Description |
|---|---|
| Create a configuration | You can extract variables and parameters from your application code and save them in a configuration file. This way, you only need to change the configuration file to change the application's configuration. |
| Synchronize configuration s | You may need to synchronize configurations for multiple application environments, such as development and test environments. If your application is deployed in different Alibaba Cloud regions, you also need to synchronize configurations across regions. You can create multiple microservices namespaces, create a configuration in one namespace, and then synchronize it to the other namespaces. |
| Manage configuration s | After you create a configuration, you can search for, view, edit, or delete it in the EDAS console. |
| View historical versions and roll back configuration s | If a configuration has an issue, you can query its historical versions and roll it back to a specific historical version. |
| Query listener information | After you modify a configuration, check if the updated configuration was pushed to the instances that are listening for it. |

#### Configuration management terms

This topic describes the terms related to configuration management.

**Configuration**

A configuration is a set of parameters extracted from application code and stored in a separate file. Externalizing parameters from static build artifacts, such as WAR and JAR packages, allows the same artifact to run in different environments without code changes. management System administrators and operations engineers typically manage configurations as part of deployment. Modifying a configuration is one of the most efficient ways to adjust the behavior of a running system.

**Configuration management**

Configuration management covers all activities related to configurations throughout their lifecycle: Editing and storing configurations Distributing configuration updates to applications Controlling versions Auditing changes

**Static and dynamic configurations**

Configurations are either static or dynamic, depending on whether they change independently of the software version.
**Static configuration** -- Bound to a specific software version. The value stays fixed while
that version is deployed. Example: `build-version: 1.0.0`
**Dynamic configuration** -- Modifiable at any time while the software is running, regardless
of the deployed version. Example: Thread pool size, which can be modified as many times as needed when the software is running.

**Configuration item**

A configuration item is a single configurable parameter with its value range, expressed in `param-key=param-value` format. Example: logLevel=INFO|WARN|ERROR defines the log level parameter with three allowed values.

**Configuration set**

A configuration set is a collection of related or unrelated configuration items grouped into a single unit. A typical system configuration file is a configuration set that contains items such as data sources, thread pool sizes, and log levels.

**How configurations are organized**

EDAS uses three dimensions to uniquely identify each configuration set:

```
Namespace > Group > Data ID
```

Together, these three values form the unique address of a configuration set.

**Data ID**

A Data ID identifies a configuration set. Use Data IDs to distinguish between different configuration sets within the same application or system. A single application can have multiple configuration sets, each identified by a descriptive Data ID. The recommended naming convention follows the Java package format to help ensure global uniqueness:

```
com.taobao.tc.refund.log.level
```

This naming convention is not mandatory. management

**Group**

A group classifies configuration sets that share the same Data ID but serve different applications or components. Typical group names are descriptive strings such as `Buy` or `Trade` . Use groups when multiple applications share the same type of configuration -- for example, `database_url` or `MQ_topic` -- but each application needs its own values. Assign each application's configuration to a different group. If you do not specify a group when creating a configuration, EDAS assigns it to

```
 DEFAULT_GROUP .
```

**Namespace**

A namespace isolates configurations by tenant or environment. Different namespaces can contain configuration sets with identical Group and Data ID values without conflict. Use namespaces to separate environment-specific configurations. For example, place staging and production configurations in distinct namespaces to prevent accidental crossenvironment changes.

**Configuration push**

Configuration push is the end-to-end process of distributing a configuration update from the configuration management system to target applications and applying the changes.

**Push tracking**

Push tracking records the full lifecycle of a configuration update: when it was submitted, which applications and machines received it, when each target applied the change, and what impact the update had.

**Configuration monitoring**

Applications register listeners with the configuration management system through SDKs or other interfaces. When a configuration changes, the system notifies all registered listeners so that the applications can apply the update automatically.

**Configuration snapshot**

The configuration management client SDK automatically saves configuration snapshots to the local machine. If the client loses connectivity to the configuration management server, it falls back to the latest snapshot to keep the application running. Snapshots work similarly to local commits in Git or cache. Cache is updated at an appropriate time. Unlike a cache, snapshots do not expire.

#### Create a configuration

You can extract variables and parameters from code and manage them in a configuration file. The configuration is retrieved from the file when the code is executed. This lets you change parameters quickly and reduces code maintenance costs. This topic describes how to create a configuration.

**Procedure**

1. Log in to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Configuration Management > Microservice**
**Configurations**.
The **Configurations** page appears. management
3. On the **Configuration List** page, select a region and a **Microservices Namespace** at the
top of the page, and then click **Create Configuration**.
4. In the **Create Configuration** panel, set the parameters and click **Create**.
The following table describes the parameters.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Region | The region where the configuration belongs. You select the region on the Configuration List page. This parameter cannot be changed in this panel. |
| Microservices Namespace | The microservices namespace to which the configuration belongs. You select the namespace on the Configuration List page. This parameter cannot be changed in this panel. |

management

| Data ID | The ID of the configuration. We recommend that you use the package.class format. In this format, class is a business-specific name for the configuration, such as com.foo.bar.log.level . Note A Data ID must be unique within a group. |
|---|---|
| Group | The group for the configuration. Enter a product or module name. The group must be globally unique. |
| Data Encryption | Data encryption uses Advanced Encryption Standard (AES), a symmetric encryption algorithm. Two built-in encryption methods are available. AES 128: Suitable for scenarios that require high performance and _ moderate security. AES 256: Suitable for applications that require the highest level of _ security. |
| Configuration Format | The data format of the configuration content. |
| Configuration Content | Enter the content for the configuration. For example: threadPoolSize=5 logLevel=WARN |
| Configuration Description | The description of the configuration. |
| More Configuration | Application: Enter the name of the application to which the configuration belongs. Label: Enter label information in the text box and click the label selector. |

If the data ID and group of a configuration are the same as those of another configuration, the two configurations are considered duplicate. ## Resource management

This topic describes the resources used by Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS) and explains how to manage them. The EDAS console lets you view and use resources, such as Elastic Compute Service (ECS) and Server Load Balancer (SLB) instances. EDAS manages these resources at the application layer. EDAS also provides a resource group management feature. This feature lets you manage resource permissions for Alibaba Cloud accounts and Resource Access Management (RAM) users, which is useful when multiple users or departments use EDAS.

### Sync a VPC

A virtual private cloud (VPC) is a custom private network built on Alibaba Cloud. VPCs are logically isolated from each other. This service is ideal for users who require high network security and have some network management experience. A VPC that you create in the VPC console automatically syncs to the EDAS console, but with a short delay. You can manually sync a VPC to avoid delays that may affect your operations.

**Prerequisites**

Before you sync a VPC in EDAS, make sure you have created a VPC in the VPC console. For details, see the **VPC User Guide > Create and manage a VPC** topic.

**Procedure**

1. Log on to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Resource Management > VPC**.
3. On the **VPC** page, select a region from the top menu bar. Then, in the upper-right corner,
click **Synchronize VPC**.
4. After the VPC is synced, you can view its details in the EDAS console.
Table 1. VPC parameter descriptions

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| VPC ID | It is automatically generated upon VPC creation. |
| Name | You define this name when you create the VPC. |
| IPv4 CIDR block | The IPv4 CIDR block that you set when you create the VPC. |
| IPv6 CIDR block | The IPv6 CIDR block that you set when you create the VPC. |
| Status | A VPC has one of two statuses: active or configuring. |

nagement

### Manage microservices

**namespaces in the console**

Microservices namespaces provide applications with isolated runtime environments, such as development, testing, and production environments. You can use microservices namespaces to isolate resources and services. You cannot create two microservices namespaces that have the same name in the same region.

**Scenarios**

For example, you have three environments in a virtual private cloud (VPC) for application development, testing, and production. You can create a microservices namespace for each environment, such as Dev, Test, and Prod. The resources, applications, and services in different microservices namespaces are isolated from each other. Service invocations and configuration pushes are not allowed across microservices namespaces.

**Default microservices namespace**

When you create an application in Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS), you can select the **Default** microservices namespace. The default microservices namespace indicates that no specific microservices namespace is used. This means the application does not use a microservices namespace to isolate resources and services. On the application list page, if you select the default microservices namespace for a region, the resulting list shows applications that do not belong to any microservices namespace.

4. In the **Create Microservice Namespace** dialog box, configure the microservices
namespace parameters and click **Create**.

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| Microservice Namespace | Enter a name for the microservices namespace. |
| Microservice Namespace ID | Enter a custom ID for the microservices namespace. The ID can contain only letters and digits. |

nagement

EDAS Registry and Configuration Center: A free service registry and configuration center provided by EDAS. ### Manage ECS resources

#### Import ECS instances

Before you deploy applications in EDAS, you must import ECS instances to a specified cluster and install EDAS Agent.

**Background information**

EDAS deploys applications only to ECS instances that have the EDAS Agent installed. Application deployment includes initial installation and scale-out. In EDAS, an application instance is an ECS instance that has the EDAS Agent installed and an application deployed. If you want to use an existing ECS instance in EDAS, you must first install the EDAS Agent on it. The EDAS Agent provides the following features: Application lifecycle management: Deploys, starts, and stops applications. nagement Status reporting: Reports the application liveness status, health check status, and Ali- Tomcat container status. Information retrieval: Retrieves monitoring information from ECS instances and containers. The EDAS Agent facilitates communication between the EDAS console and your application. The agent helps ensure that your application is deployed correctly and promptly to an ECS instance. The EDAS Agent supports 64-bit CentOS 6.5 and later.

**Note**

You do not need to manage these features. You only need to install the EDAS Agent. EDAS provides two methods to install the EDAS Agent: Automatically install the EDAS Agent by importing an ECS instance Manually install the EDAS Agent using a command script

**Important**

By default, the EDAS Agent is installed with Java Development Kit (JDK) 8. If you want to use JDK 7 or another version, you must install the EDAS Agent using a command script. To use the script, you must log on to your ECS instance as the **root** user. You can run the script multiple times. Each time you run the script, it overwrites the existing EDAS Agent installation. The EDAS Agent does not have a separate update script. To update the EDAS Agent, run the installation script again. The installation script is region-specific. Switch to the region of your ECS instance, and then click **Install Agent**. The agent status varies based on the image and cluster type that you select. The agent status determines the application types that you can deploy on the ECS instance. Follow the instructions for your chosen installation method.

**Automatically install EDAS Agent by importing an ECS instance**

If you did not select the **EDAS JAVA Environment (Common ECS)** base image when you purchased your ECS instance, you can install the EDAS Agent using the **Import ECS** feature in the EDAS console. This feature lets you import an ECS instance either directly or after a conversion. nagement An ECS instance cannot be imported directly if it meets any of the following conditions: The instance was created before December 1, 2017. The instance is in a classic network and is being imported to a cluster that uses a classic network. The instance is stopped, starting, or stopping. The instance is a Windows-based instance or does not support simple Shell commands. The instance is not imported from another ECS cluster.

**Important**

If image conversion is required, the ECS instance is formatted. If you do not want to format the disks, install the EDAS Agent using a command script.
1. Log in to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Resource Management > ECS**.
3. On the **ECS** page, select a region from the top menu bar and a microservices namespace
(optional), and then click **Import ECS** in the upper-right corner.
4. On the **Select Cluster And Existing ECS Instances** tab in the **Import ECS** wizard, select
a **Microservices Namespace** and a **Select Destination Cluster**. From the instance list, select the ECS instance to import and click **Next**.

**Note**

If you do not have a destination cluster, click **Create Cluster** next to the **Select**
**Destination Cluster** drop-down list.
To perform a manual installation, click **Switch To Manual Installation** in the upper-right corner of the page. You are then redirected to the **Manually Install**
**EDAS Agent On Single Instance** page, where you can use a command script
to install the EDAS Agent.
5. On the **Ready To Import** tab, review the instance information.
For instances listed under **The Following Instances Can Be Imported Directly**
**Without Conversion**, click **Confirm And Import**.
nagement For instances in the **The Following Instances Need To Be Imported After**
**Conversion** section, select **I Agree To Convert The Preceding Instances That Need**

**To Be Imported, And I Understand That The Data In The Original System Will Be**

**Lost After The Conversion**. Enter a new logon password for the root user and click
**Confirm And Import**.
6. On the **Import** tab, you can view the import status of the instance.
For instances that can be imported directly: The **Import** page displays the import status. If the **The Instance Is Transferred** message is displayed, the instance has been imported. Click **Back To Cluster Details**. The instance is successfully imported into the cluster when its status changes to **Running**. For an instance that requires conversion, the **Import** page shows the import status as
**Converting. It Might Take 5 Minutes**. If you click **Back To Cluster Details** before the
import is complete, the health check status is **Converting** and a progress percentage is displayed. When the import is complete, the health check status changes to **Running**.

**Manually install EDAS Agent using a command script**

You can use this method only for ECS instances that are in an ECS cluster.
1. Log in to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Resource Management > ECS**.
3. On the **ECS** page, select a region from the top menu bar, select a microservices
namespace, and then click **Import ECS** in the upper-right corner.
4. On the **Import ECS** page, click **Switch To Manual Installation** in the upper-right corner.
The **Manually Install EDAS Agent On Single Instance** page appears. Click **Copy**. nagement

**Note**

To install using an image, click **Back** in the upper-right corner to return to the configuration page, where you can complete the import. For more information, see Automatically install EDAS Agent by importing an ECS instance.
5. Log on to the ECS instance as the **root** user.
6. On the ECS instance, paste and run the copied command.

**Verify the result**

1. After you install the EDAS Agent, go to the EDAS console. In the navigation pane on the left,
choose **Resource Management** > **ECS**.
2. On the **ECS** page, select the destination region from the top menu bar and a microservices
namespace. You can then view the status in the **Agent Status** column. A status of **Online** or **Online Docker** indicates that the EDAS Agent is installed. If the installation fails, the status is **Unknown**.

**Select from Existing Clusters**: In the current region, select a **microservices**

#### Kubernetes Configurations

##### Manage ConfigMaps

You can use ConfigMaps to store non-confidential configurations, such as Java Virtual Machine (JVM) heap memory, JVM properties, and Java agent parameters. This topic describes how to manage ConfigMaps.

**Prerequisites**

A Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) cluster has been created. A Kubernetes cluster has been imported into EDAS. For more information, see Create and import a Container Service for Kubernetes cluster.

**Background information**

nagement You can use ConfigMaps to store configurations that do not require encryption. These configurations can be injected into containers when you create or deploy applications. If you modify a ConfigMap, you must redeploy the application for the changes to take effect. You can use ConfigMaps in the following two scenarios: You can use configuration items to define environment variables for containers. For more information, see Configure environment variables. You can mount a configuration item as a file to a specified directory in a container. For more information, see Configuration Management.

**Create a ConfigMap**

1. Log in to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Resource Management > Container Service**
**K8s Clusters**.
3. In the cluster list, click the target cluster.
4. On the **Cluster Details** page, click the **Configuration Items** section.
5. In the **ConfigMaps** section, click **Create ConfigMap**.
6. In the **Create Configuration Item** panel, set basic parameters such as the name and
cluster.

| Configuration Item | Description |
|---|---|
| Name | The name of the configuration item. The name can contain lowercase letters, hyphens (-), and digits. It must start with a letter and cannot end with a hyphen (-). The name can be up to 63 characters in length. |
| Cluster Name | Select the target Kubernetes cluster from the drop-down list. |
| K8s Namespace | A Kubernetes namespace assigns internal system objects to different namespaces to form logically separate projects, groups, or user groups. This allows the different groups to be managed separately while sharing the resources of the entire cluster. default: The default namespace for objects that do not have a specified namespace. kube-system: The namespace for objects created by the system. kube-public: This namespace is automatically created and can be read by all users, including unauthenticated users. In this example, default is selected. |

7. In the **Create Configuration Item** panel, set the configuration item mapping, and then
click **OK**. You can set the ConfigMap mapping by manually adding key-value pairs or by importing a configuration. A single ConfigMap supports multiple mappings. Manually enter the ConfigMap mapping. Click **Add** and set the **Key** and **Value** for the configuration item. nagement

**Note**

You can click **Save As Template** to save the mapping configuration for future use.

| Configuration item | Description |
|---|---|
| Key | The key of the configuration. The key can contain letters, digits, underscores ( ), hyphens (-), and periods (.). _ |
| Value | The value of the configuration item. |

Import the ConfigMap mapping.

**Note**

You can import a ConfigMap mapping from a file or from a template. Import a ConfigMap mapping from a file: Click **Import Configurations > Import From File** and select the configuration item mapping file from your local computer. EDAS automatically parses the file and displays the content as key-value pairs. EDAS validates the file format. Only JSON, YAML, and Properties files are supported.

**Note**

Add key-value pairs to your file according to its format. The following examples show how to specify key-value pairs in different file formats. JSON format example `{`

```json
  "key1": "value1",
  "key2": "value2",
```

`}` YAML format example

```
key1: value1 key2: value2
```

Properties format example

```
key1=value1 key2=value2
```

nagement Import a ConfigMap mapping from a template: a. Click **Import Configuration > Import From Template**, select a template, and click **Use Template** in the corresponding Actions column. b. For templates that are not in KeyValue format, the **Parse The Imported Template**
**Or File Into Key-value Pair Data?** dialog box appears. You can select **Yes** or **No** as
needed.

**Note**

**Yes**: Parses the template or imported file into the key-value data format. Parsing
is supported only for JSON, YAML, and Properties formats. Files in other formats are parsed into a single key-value pair, where the value is the content of the imported file.
**No**: The original format is retained.

**View a ConfigMap**

1. Log in to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Resource Management > Container Service**
**K8s Clusters**.
3. In the cluster list, click the target cluster.
4. On the **Cluster Details** page, click the **Configuration Items** section.
5. In the **Configuration Items** section, click **Details** for the target configuration item.
You can filter for the target configuration item by **Configuration Item Name** or **K8s**
**Namespace**.
6. On the details page of the configuration item, you can view its basic information and data.

**Modify a ConfigMap**

1. Log in to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Resource Management > Container Service**
**K8s Clusters**.
3. In the cluster list, click the target cluster.
4. On the **Cluster Details** page, click the **Configuration Items** section.
5. In the **Configuration Items** section, find the target configuration item, and click **Edit** on
the right. You can filter for the target configuration items by **Configuration Item Name** or **K8s**
**Namespace**.
6. In the edit panel, modify the mapping name and value of the configuration item, and then
click **OK**.

**Note**

If an application uses the ConfigMap, you must redeploy the application after you modify the ConfigMap to apply the changes.

**Delete a ConfigMap**

1. Log in to the EDAS console.
nagement
2. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Resource Management > Container Service**
**K8s Clusters**.
3. In the cluster list, click the target cluster.
4. On the **Cluster Details** page, click the **Configuration Items** section.
5. In the **Configuration Items** section, find the target configuration item and click **Delete** on
the right. You can filter for the target configuration item by **Configuration Item Name** or **K8s**
**Namespace**.

You can filter for the configuration items by **Configuration Item Name** or **K8s**
**Namespace**.

##### Manage secrets

In an Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS) Kubernetes environment, you can use secrets to store sensitive information, such as passwords and certificates. This topic describes how to manage secrets.

**Prerequisites**

A cluster has been created in the Container Service for Kubernetes (ACK) console. The Kubernetes cluster has been imported into EDAS. For more information, see Use the console to manage Kubernetes clusters and Create and import a Container Service for Kubernetes cluster.

**Background information**

You can store sensitive information, such as passwords and certificates, in a secret. You can then inject the secret into a container when you create or deploy an application. If you modify the secret, the changes take effect after you redeploy the application. Secrets are used in the following scenarios: Use a secret to define environment variables for a container. For more information, see Configure environment variables. Mount a secret as a file to a specified directory in a container. For more information, see Configuration management. nagement Use a secret to provide HTTPS certificate information for an application Ingress. For more information, see Create an application Ingress.

**Create a secret**

1. Log in to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Resource Management > Container Service**
**for Kubernetes clusters**.
3. In the cluster list, click the target cluster.
4. On the **Cluster Details** page, click the **Secrets** module.
5. In the **Secrets** module, click **Create Secret**.
6. In the **Create Secret** panel, set the parameters and click **OK**.
nagement

| Configuration item | Description |
|---|---|
| Secret dictionary name | Enter a custom name for the secret. The name can contain lowercase letters, hyphens (-), and digits. It must start with a letter and cannot end with a hyphen. |
| Cluster name | Select the target Kubernetes cluster from the drop-down list. |
| Kubernetes n amespace | A Kubernetes namespace logically groups objects within the system into different projects, teams, or user groups. This allows different groups to share cluster resources while being managed separately. default: The default namespace for objects that do not have another namespace. kube-system: The namespace for objects created by the system. kube-public: This namespace is created automatically and can be read by all users, including unauthenticated users. |
| Type | Select the type of secret to create. You can createO paque or TLS Certificate secrets. Opaque: Arbitrary user-defined data. When you select this type, the Base64 Encoded Data check box appears. Select the Base64 Encoded Data check box to upload binary data that is already Base64 encoded. If you select this option, the data you provide must be Base64 encoded. EDAS will not encode the data again. TLS Certificate: Used to store a Transport Layer Security (TLS) certificate and its related key. This type is mainly used for Ingress scenarios. It supports a collection of routing rules that route external HTTPS requests to internal services. |
| Opaque | To create an Opaque secret, set the following parameters: Base64 Encoded Data: If you select this check box, the data you provide for the secret must already be Base64 encoded. EDAS will not encode the data again. Configuration Mapping: For more information about the configuration mapping parameters, see Create a configuration item. |
| TLS Certificate | To create a TLS Certificate secret, you can either Create A Self-signed Certificate or create one manually. Manual creation: Manually enter the Cert (public key of the TLS certificate) and the Key (private key of the TLS certificate). Create a self-signed certificate: Generate a certificate by configuring the Domain Names, Key Length, Certificate Start Time, and Certificate Expiration Time. |

**View a secret**

1. Log in to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Resource Management > Container Service**
**for Kubernetes**.
nagement
3. In the cluster list, click the target cluster.
4. On the **Cluster Details** page, click the **Secrets** tab.
5. In the **Secrets** module, locate the desired secret and click **Details**.
You can search for the secret by **Secret Name** or **K8s Namespace**.
6. On the secret details page, you can view its basic information and the data it contains.
For secrets that store TLS certificates, the details page also displays certificate information, such as the associated domain, certificate status, and service provider.

**Modify a secret**

1. Log in to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Resource Management > Container Service**
**for Kubernetes**.
3. In the cluster list, click the target cluster.
4. On the **Cluster Details** page, click the **Secrets** module.
5. In the **Secrets** module, find the secret that you want to edit and click **Edit** on the right.
You can filter secrets by **Secret Name** and **K8s Namespace**.
6. In the editing panel, modify the secret's key-value pairs and click **OK**.

**Note**

If an application uses the secret, you must redeploy the application after you finish editing. This ensures that the updated secret takes effect in the application.

**View associated Ingresses**

1. Log in to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Resource Management > Container Service**
**for Kubernetes**.
3. In the cluster list, click the target cluster.
4. On the **Cluster Details** page, click the **Secrets** tab.
5. On the **Secrets** tab, find the target secret and click **View Associated Applications** in the
right-hand column. You can search for secrets by **Secret Name** or **K8s Namespace**.
6. In the dialog box that appears, view the Ingresses associated with the secret. Click the
name of an Ingress to view its details.

**Delete a secret**

1. Log in to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Resource Management > Container Service**
**for Kubernetes**.
3. In the cluster list, click the target cluster.
4. On the **Cluster Details** page, click the **Secrets** module.
5. In the **Secrets** module, find the secret you want to delete and click **Delete**.
You can filter secrets by **Secret Name** and **K8s Namespace**.
6. In the confirmation dialog box, click **OK**.
nagement

**Note**

If an application uses this secret, you must disassociate the secret from the application before you delete it.
