### Manage resource groups

Resource groups in Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS) help you organize your resources. You can also use them to control account permissions. Grant a RAM user permissions on a resource group. The RAM user can then manage all resources in that group.

**Scenarios**

Your company uses EDAS to publish its application systems. Department A manages applications for the User Center, and Department B manages applications for the Product Hub. Two departments share an EDAS service that is provisioned by a root account, and each department uses a separate RAM user. Department A deploys the User Center application on its dedicated ECS and SLB instances, while Department B deploys the Product Hub application on its dedicated instances. You create two resource groups in EDAS. You attach the resources for Department A to one group and the resources for Department B to the other. Then, you grant permissions on these resource groups to the respective RAM users for each department. When Department A uses its RAM user, it can only manage resources in its assigned group. The same applies to Department B. This prevents conflicts when the departments manage their resources. Figure 1. Diagram of a resource group management scenario nagement

**Administrator:**

**Centralized**

Corresponds to an Purchase Alibaba Cloud account with EDAS activated Authorization Authorization Department A Department B corresponds corresponds to RAM user A to RAM user B Resource Resource Group A Group B ECS 1 SLB 1 ECS 2 SLB 2 EDAS

**Create a resource group**

1. Log on to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Resource Management > Resource Group**.
3. In the upper-right corner of the **Resource Group** page, click **Create Resource Group**.
4. In the **Create Resource Group** dialog box, enter a **Resource Group Name** and
**Resource Group Description**, and then click **OK**.

**Attach resources to a resource group**

You can attach ECS instances, SLB instances, and clusters to a resource group. The steps are simple and nearly identical for each resource type. This topic uses attaching an ECS instance as an example.
1. On the **Resource Group** page, find the resource group that you want to manage and click
**Attach ECS** in the **Actions** column.
2. In the **Attach ECS** dialog box, select one or more ECS instances, and then click **OK**.

**Grant resource group permissions to a RAM user**

You can grant permissions on a resource group to a RAM user. This ensures that the RAM user can only access the specified resource group.
1. Log on to the EDAS console using your Alibaba Cloud account.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **System Administration > RAM User**.
3. Find the user to whom you want to grant permissions and click **Grant Resource Group** in
the **Actions** column.
4. In the **Grant Resource Group** dialog box, select a resource group, and then click **OK**.

**Delete a resource group**

1. In the resource group list, find the target resource group. In the **Actions** column, click
**Delete**.
nagement
2. In the **Delete Resource Group** dialog box, click **OK**.

**Add a cluster to a resource group**

1. In the resource group list, find the target resource group. In the **Actions** column, click **Bind**
**Cluster**.
2. In the **Bind Cluster** dialog box, select a cluster and click **OK**.

**Edit a resource group**

1. In the resource group list, find the target resource group. In the **Actions** column, click **Edit**.
2. In the **Edit Resource Group** dialog box, change the name and description, and then click
**OK**.

### Manage a dedicated registry

**and configuration center**

In a Java microservices model, common registry centers, such as Eureka, ZooKeeper, and Nacos, are used for service registration and discovery. These centers effectively isolate and decouple dependencies between services, which simplifies the dynamic management of microservices. A dedicated registry and configuration center provides service registration and discovery and lets you create and use resources on demand. This helps avoid the single point of failure that can occur in a shared environment.

**Create a dedicated registry and configuration center**

1. Log on to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Resource Management > Dedicated**
**Registry and Configuration Center**.
3. On the **Dedicated Registry and Configuration Center** page, click **Create**.
4. On the **Create Instance** page, set the required parameters and click **Submit**. The
instance is created after its **Running Status** changes to **Running**.

| Configuration item | Description |
|---|---|

nagement

| Edition | Developer Edition Note The engine specification is Small (2C+4G) by default. Standard Edition Note You can set the engine specification to Small (2C+4G), Medium (4C+8G), or Large (8C+16G). |
|---|---|
| Region | The region where the instance resides. This cannot be changed. |
| Instance Name | Enter a name for the instance. |
| Engine Version | The default version is 2.0.3.3. This is not the latest version. You can manually upgrade it after you submit. |
| Engine Specification | If you select Developer Edition for Edition, the default value is Small (2C+4G). If you select Standard Edition for Edition, you can select Small (2C+4G), Medium (4C+8G), or Large (8C+16G). |
| Number Of Cluster Nodes | If you select Developer Edition for Edition, the default value is 1. If you select Standard Edition for Edition, you can select 3, 5, or 7. |
| Network Type | The default value is Virtual Private Cloud. |
| VPC | Select an existing VPC. For more information, see Sync a VPC. |
| VSwitch | Select a vSwitch. |

**View instance details**

nagement
1. Log on to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Resource Management > Dedicated**
**Registry and Configuration Center**.
3. Click the **ID/Name** of the target instance to open the **Instance Details** page.

**Basic information**

1. On the **Basic Information** tab, you can view the **Basic Information**, **Running**
**Information**, **Network Information**, and **Instance Nodes** sections for the instance.
2. In the **Basic Information** section, you can view details such as **Instance ID**, **Network**
**Connectivity Mode**, **Number of Cluster Nodes**, **Engine Specification**, **Engine Type**,
**Engine Version**, **Instance Name**, **Edition**, and **Region**.
3. In the **Running Information** section, you can view details such as the **Running Status**
and **Creation Time**.
4. In the **Network Information** section, you can view details such as **Internal Network**
**Address**, **Internal Network Port**, **VPC Information**, and **VSwitch**.
5. In the **Instance Nodes** section, you can view details such as **Node Name**, **Health Status**,
and **Operation Time**.

**Microservices namespace**

1. On the **Microservices Namespace** tab, you can view a list of microservices namespaces.
The list includes details such as **Microservices Namespace ID**, **Microservices**
**Namespace Name**, **Number of Configurations**, and **Number of Active Services**.
2. In the Actions column, click **Configuration List** to open the **Configuration List** page. For
more information, see Create a configuration.
3. In the Actions column, click **HSF** to open the **HSF > Service Search** page. For more
information, see Query HSF services.
4. In the Actions column, click **DUBBO** to open the **Dubbo > Service Search** page. For more
information, see Query Dubbo services.
5. In the Actions column, click **Spring Cloud** to open the **Spring Cloud > Service Search**
page. For more information, see Query Spring Cloud services.

**Restart an instance**

1. Log on to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Resource Management > Dedicated**
**Registry and Configuration Center**.
3. Click the **ID/Name** of the target instance to open the **Instance Details** page.
4. On the **Basic Information** tab, click **Restart Instance** in the upper-right corner of the
**Basic Information** section.
5. In the **Restart Instance** dialog box, review the information and click **OK**.

**Upgrade or downgrade an instance**

1. Log on to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Resource Management > Dedicated**
**Registry and Configuration Center**.
3. In the Actions column of the target instance, click **Upgrade/Downgrade**. The
**Microservices Engine (MSE) (Subscription) | Upgrade/Downgrade** page appears.
nagement

**Note**

Only the **Standard Edition** supports instance upgrades or downgrades.
4. In the **Current Configuration** section, view the instance information. You can upgrade or
downgrade the **Engine Specification** and adjust the **Number of Cluster Nodes**. Then, click **Submit**.

**Note**

After you change the configuration, the instance automatically restarts for the change to take effect. The network configuration feature is no longer available on the instance upgrade or downgrade page. To change network settings, use the Set Internal Network and Set Internet operations on the Basic Information page of the instance in the console.

**Release an instance**

1. Log on to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Resource Management > Dedicated**
**Registry and Configuration Center**.
3. Click the **ID/Name** of the target instance to open the **Instance Details** page.
4. On the **Basic Information** tab, click **Release Instance** in the upper-right corner of the
**Running Information** section.
5. In the **Release Instance** dialog box, review the information and click **OK**.

**Important**

After you release the instance, all service registration and configuration information on the instance is removed and cannot be recovered. If your client is still connected to this instance, a connection error will occur, which will cause the microservice application to fail. Before you proceed, carefully verify the instance that you want to release. enter

## Component center

### Batch operations

In the EDAS console, run commands to perform batch operations on ECS instances that have the EDAS agent installed.

**Procedure**

1. Log on to the EDAS console.
2. In the left navigation pane, choose **Component Center > Batch Operations**.
3. On the **Batch Operations** page, select a **microservices namespace**. Then click **By**
**Cluster**, **By Application**, or **By Instance** to specify the execution dimension.

**Note**

This document uses the cluster dimension as an example. The procedures for the other two dimensions are similar.
4. To the right of **Select Cluster**, click **Add**. In the **Select Cluster** dialog box, select the
target clusters in the left pane. You can also search for clusters by keyword. Click the **>** button to move the selected clusters to the **Selected** area. Then click **OK**.
5. In the text box to the right of **Command**, enter a command.

**Note**

After you enter a command, the system executes it on all instances in the ECS cluster by default. This setting cannot be changed.
6. Click **Execute**.

**Results**

View operation results and details After the command runs, a new **Execution Results** tab appears on the current page. The command execution results for all ECS instances appear in the **Execution Results** tab. enter Click the record for an ECS instance to view detailed information about the command execution on that instance. View execution records On the **Batch Operations** page, click **Execution Records**. On the **Execution Records** tab, view the batch execution records. Each record includes the **Operator**, **Creation Time**,
**End Time**, **Command**, and **Status**.
If you are logged on with an Alibaba Cloud account, you can view all batch operation commands executed by the account and all Resource Access Management (RAM) users that belong to the account. If you are logged on as a RAM user, you can view only the batch operation commands that you executed. The records are sorted by creation time in descending order. You can also sort them by end time or status. In the **Details** column, click **View** to open the **View Details** page. nistration

## System administration

### Profile

If you set a Resource Access Management (RAM) user as an alert contact, you must update the user's profile.

**Update your profile**

1. Log on to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **System Administration > Profile**.
3. On the **Profile** page, update the information in the **Account**, **Contact**, **Mobile Phone**, and
**Email** fields, and then click **OK**.

### Permission assistant

The EDAS Permission Assistant is a tool that generates Resource Access Management (RAM) permission policies. This tool helps you quickly create EDAS-related permission policies in RAM and migrate permission management from built-in EDAS RAM users to standard RAM users.

**View EDAS system policy templates**

The Permission Assistant page in the EDAS console provides eight default permission policy templates.
1. Log on to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **System Management > Permission**
**Assistant**.
3. On the Permission Assistant page, you can view the system policy templates provided by
EDAS. If the **Policy Type** is **System Policy**, the policy is a template provided by EDAS. You can perform the following operations: In the rightmost column of the policy, click **Clone**. In the **Create Permission Policy** panel, edit the details to create a custom permission policy. In the rightmost column of the policy, click **View Details**. In the **View Details** dialog box, click **Copy**. Then, log on to the RAM console to use the copied policy to create a custom policy and grant the permissions to the corresponding RAM user. For more information about the eight built-in EDAS system policy templates, see Introduction to EDAS system policy templates.

**Create a custom policy template**

In addition to using the built-in system policy templates, you can create custom policy templates in the Permission Assistant.
1. Log on to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **System Management > Permission**
**Assistant**.
3. On the **Permission Assistant** page, click **Create Permission Policy**.
4. On the **Create Permission Policy** page, on the **Create Custom Permission Policy** tab,
set the **Policy Name** and **Remarks**. nistration
5. Click **Add Permission Statement**. After you add the statement, click **Confirm**. On the
**Create Custom Permission Policy** tab, click **Next**.

**Important**

When you add a permission statement, you can select only one effect type: Allow or Deny. A permission policy can contain multiple permission statements. If one statement sets a permission to **Allow** and another sets it to **Deny**, the deny rule takes precedence.
6. On the **Policy Preview** tab, preview the permissions and then click **Finish**.
The console displays the message New policy granted successfully. Click **Back To List** to return to the **Permission Assistant** page and view the new policy template. In the rightmost column of the policy, click **View Details**. In the **View Details** dialog box, click **Copy**. Then, log on to the RAM console to use the copied policy to create a custom policy and grant the permissions to the corresponding RAM user.

### License consumption details

EDAS is a cloud-native Platform as a Service (PaaS) that hosts distributed applications and manages microservices. It provides comprehensive solutions that cover application development, deployment, monitoring, and O&M. A license is consumed when an application is created successfully. No license is consumed if the application fails to be created.

**Authorization consumption logic**

The number of authorized vCPUs consumed is calculated using the following formula: Number of vCPUs in the nodes of the application or service hosted on EDAS × License feature coefficient. For example, a distributed application node with 4 cores and 8 GB of memory (4C8G) has a feature coefficient of 1 and consumes 4 vCPUs. An AliEE application server node with 8 cores and 16 GB of memory (8C16G) has a feature coefficient of 2 and consumes 16 vCPUs.

**View License consumption details**

1. Log on to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **System Administration > License**
**Consumption Details**.
3. In the **License Consumption Details** area, you can view the following information.

| Consumption | Description |
|---|---|
| Consumed Licenses | A purchased license can be consumed by multiple EDAS feature modules at different rates. |
| EDAS Consumption | Consumption is measured by the vCPUs of the pods for the hosted application or service. For example, a 4C8G node consumes 4 vCPUs. |
| AliEE Consumption | Consumption is measured as 2 × the number of vCPUs of the application server pods. For example, a 4C8G node consumes 8 vCPUs. |
| MSE Consumption | Consumption is measured as 10 × the number of vCPUs of the instance's DPI engine specification. For example, a 2C4G node consumes 20 vCPUs. |

4. In the **Details** area, you can filter the list by selecting **AliEE**, **EDAS**, or **MSE** from the
**Feature Module** drop-down list. To perform an advanced search, click **Advanced Filter**,
select a **Feature Module**, and enter a **Name**. The consumption details list displays the **Feature Module**, **Name**, **Actual Application**
**VCPUs**, **License Feature Coefficient**, and **Actual License Consumption**.

On the **Basic Information** page, you can view the **Application Information** and
**Application Settings**.

## Permission management

### Overview of Permission

**Management**

Applications hosted on Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS) can contain multiple services or subsystems that are developed and maintained by different teams. EDAS provides an enterprise-level permission management system that uses an account framework and various permission management operations. This system helps you ensure security by isolating applications, resources, and data, and controlling access to them.

**Built-in EDAS permission management and RAM permission**

**management**

EDAS has a built-in permission management system and also integrates with Resource Access Management (RAM) permission management. To manage EDAS permissions in a unified way, you can use RAM permission management. The built-in EDAS permission management requires an Alibaba Cloud account to log on to the EDAS console and assign EDAS permissions and resources to a RAM user. After you integrate with RAM permission management, you can configure roles and access policies for RAM users to enable more fine-grained permission management.

**Why use RAM permission management**

You can set access policies to control which resources users can access. For example, you can grant users read-only permissions for a specific EDAS application.

**Finer-grained Authorization**

| Built-in EDAS permission management | RAM permission management |
|---|---|

anagement

| After an Alibaba Cloud account assigns resources to a RAM user, all permissions apply to these resources. For example, if you assign resources APP1 and APP2 to a RAM user and then grant the permissions to deploy and stop applications, the RAM user has permission to deploy and stop both APP1 and APP2. The resource granularity is coarse and does not allow for precise permission control. | Compared to the built-in EDAS permission management, RAM provides finer-grained access control. You can configure resources for each permission. For example, an Alibaba Cloud account can grant a RAM user the permissions to deploy and stop applications. At the same time, the deploy permission is configured with resources APP1 and APP2, and the stop permission is configured with resources APP2 and APP3. In this case, the RAM user can deploy APP1 and APP2, but not APP3. The user can stop APP2 and APP3, but not APP1. |
|---|---|

**More Powerful Syntax**

RAM permission management provides a richer syntax than the built-in EDAS permission management. It supports features such as fuzzy matching with wildcard characters and combinations of multiple authorization policies, which lets you implement more complex authorization logic. Take the following RAM policy as an example: `{`

```json
    "Statement": [
```

`{`

```json
        "Action": [
          "edas:ReadApplication"
```

`],`

```json
        "Effect": "Allow",
        "Resource": ["acs:edas:*:*:namespace/*/application/*"]
```

`},` `{`

```json
        "Action": [
          "edas:ReadApplication"
```

`],`

```json
        "Effect": "Deny",
        "Resource": ["acs:edas:*:*:namespace/*/application/12345678"]
```

`}` `],`

```json
    "Version": "1"
```

`}` This RAM policy has two statements: The first statement is an **Allow** statement. The action **edas:ReadApplication** grants the permission to **view applications**, and the resource is the wildcard character *, which represents **all applications**. As a result, the first statement grants the RAM user permission to view all applications in EDAS. The second statement is a **Deny** statement. The resource is the application with the ID 123 4567812345678. This statement denies the permission to view this application. When combined, these two statements grant the RAM user permission to view all applications except for the one with the ID 12345678.

**Mapping between built-in EDAS permissions and RAM**

**permissions**

anagement Built-in EDAS permissions and RAM permissions do not have a one-to-one mapping and therefore cannot be directly replaced. EDAS provides a policy transformation feature that converts built-in EDAS permissions into the most consistent RAM permissions possible. By default, EDAS resources, such as applications and clusters, that are associated with a RAM user are available to all permissions assigned to that user. Table 1. Permission mapping

| Built-in EDAS permission | RAM permission | RAM resource |
|---|---|---|
| Super Admin(All privileges) | edas:* | acs:edas:*:*:* |
| Proxy for Alibaba Cloud account | edas:ManageSystem | acs:edas:*:*:* |
| System administration - Operation logs | edas:ReadOperationLog | acs:edas:*:*:* |
| Application Management - Edit microservices namespace | edas:ManageNamespace | acs:edas:*:*:namespace/${nam espaceId} |
| Application Management - Query microservices namespace | edas:ReadNamespace | acs:edas:*:*:namespace/${nam espaceId} |
| Resource Management - Create cluster | edas:CreateCluster | acs:edas:*:*:namespace/* |
| Resource Management - View cluster | edas:ReadCluster | acs:edas:*:*:namespace/*/clust er/${clusterId} |
| Resource Management - Manage and delete cluster | edas:ReadCluster edas:ManageCluster | acs:edas:*:*:namespace/*/clust er/${clusterId} |
| Application Management - Create application | edas:CreateApplication | acs:edas:*:*:namespace/* |
| Application Management - Deploy, start, scale out, and delete application | edas:ManageApplication edas:ReadApplication | acs:edas:*:*:namespace/*/appli cation/${applicationId} |
| Application Management - View application information | edas:ReadApplication | acs:edas:*:*:namespace/*/appli cation/${applicationId} |
| Application Management - Configure container and edit application JVM parameters | edas:ConfigApplication edas:ReadApplication | acs:edas:*:*:namespace/*/appli cation/${applicationId} |
| Application Management - Set log path | edas:ManageAppLog edas:ReadApplication | acs:edas:*:*:namespace/*/appli cation/${applicationId} |

### Account systems

EDAS provides a built-in account system and integrates with Alibaba Cloud Resource Access Management (RAM) to enhance security and simplify enterprise-level account management.

**Concepts**

anagement Account systems include concepts such as Alibaba Cloud accounts, RAM users, sub-accounts, and roles. Alibaba Cloud account In EDAS, an Alibaba Cloud account has permissions for all of its resources and all EDAS operations. RAM user EDAS supports the RAM account system. An Alibaba Cloud account can log on to the Apsara Uni-manager Management Console to create RAM users and assign the least privilege to them as needed. This practice supports efficient enterprise management by assigning specific duties to each user. In the EDAS console, on the **System Management > Sub-account** menu, you can perform the following operations: An Alibaba Cloud account can log on to the console to view a list of all its sub-accounts. In the upper-right corner of the page, click **Sync Sub-account** to sync RAM users. Sub-accounts that are configured with EDAS built-in permissions and have not been migrated to RAM authorization can manage roles and grant permissions for applications and resource groups. Sub-account A sub-account is created by an Alibaba Cloud account. The Alibaba Cloud account can use built-in access policies to assign permissions and resources to the sub-account. The account can also configure RAM roles and access policies for the sub-account. The RAM permission management method is recommended. Role A role is a virtual user with a specified set of permissions. A role does not have a permanent access key. A trusted entity must assume the role to use its permissions. You can create roles in EDAS or use roles from RAM. Access policy An access policy is a set of permissions described using a specific syntax. An access policy precisely defines the authorized resources, operations, and conditions for access. You can create access policies only in RAM. The built-in access control of EDAS supports only granting permissions for applications or resource groups to sub-accounts.

**Scenarios**

The following scenario explains how to use the EDAS account systems. After the required resources are prepared, three departments, each with an Alibaba Cloud account, create their own sub-accounts or RAM users to assign and manage permissions and resources. Account A grants all ECS resources and all permissions to sub-account or RAM user a. Account B creates two roles: application administrator and operations administrator. It grants these roles to sub-accounts or RAM users b1 and b2, respectively. Account C creates a role to view applications and grants it to sub-account or RAM user c. anagement B A Assign resources and Assign resources and Assign resources and permissions permissions permissions b2 c b1 a

### EDAS built-in permission

**management**

#### RAM users

When you use EDAS, different roles are often required for different tasks. To separate duties, an Alibaba Cloud account can assign specific roles and resources to RAM users. This permission model is similar to the relationship between system users and regular users in Linux, where a system user can grant permissions to or revoke permissions from a regular user. The relationship between an Alibaba Cloud account and a RAM user is as follows: In EDAS, an Alibaba Cloud account can attach RAM users to avoid sharing account keys. By assigning the least privilege to RAM users, you can efficiently manage your enterprise and ensure that each user has specific duties. When an Alibaba Cloud account is attached to a RAM user, a mapping relationship is created that is valid only within EDAS. In other environments, the Alibaba Cloud account and the RAM user are independent accounts. An Alibaba Cloud account can function as a primary account with attached RAM users. The same account can also be a RAM user of another Alibaba Cloud account.

#### Manage EDAS built-in permissions

Manage EDAS built-in permissions using your Alibaba Cloud account. This includes creating roles, granting roles to RAM users, authorizing applications for RAM users, and authorizing resource groups for RAM users.

**Create Roles**

You can define different operation permissions by creating roles in your Alibaba Cloud account.
1. Log on to the EDAS console.
anagement
2. In the left navigation pane, choose **System Administration > Roles**.
3. On the **Roles** page, click **Create Role** in the upper-right corner.
4. On the **Create Role** page, enter a **Role Name**. Select permissions from the **Available**
**Permissions** list on the left. Click **Add >>** to move them to the **Selected Permissions**
list on the right. Then click **OK**. Return to the **Roles** page. The created role appears in the role list. In the **Operation** column of the target role, click **View Permissions**, **Manage**
**Permissions**, or **Delete** to perform related operations.

**Grant Roles to RAM Users**

Grant an appropriate role to a RAM user to give the RAM user operation permissions for applications.
1. Log on to the EDAS console.
2. In the left navigation pane, choose **System Administration > RAM Users**.
3. In the **Operation** column of the target RAM user, click **Manage Roles**.
4. In the **Manage Roles** dialog box, select roles from the **Unselected** list on the left. Click **>**
to move them to the **Selected** list on the right. Then click **OK**. Return to the **RAM Users** page. The authorized roles appear in the **Roles** column of the RAM user. To adjust the authorized roles, repeat the authorization steps. In the **Manage Roles** dialog box, adjust the roles in both lists.

**Authorize Applications for RAM Users**

Authorizing an application grants a RAM user access to that application. However, specific operations—such as starting or deleting the application—require role-based permissions. Therefore, after authorizing an application, you must also grant the RAM user an appropriate role to enable those operations. anagement
1. Log on to the EDAS console.
2. In the left navigation pane, choose **System Administration > RAM Users**.
3. In the **Operation** column of the target RAM user, click **Authorize Applications**.
4. In the **Authorize Applications** dialog box, select applications from the **Unselected** list on
the left. Click **>** to move them to the **Selected** list on the right. Then click **OK**. Return to the **RAM Users** page. The authorized applications appear in the **Authorized**
**Applications** column of the RAM user.
To adjust authorized applications, repeat the authorization steps. In the **Authorize**
**Applications** dialog box, adjust the applications in both lists.

**Authorize Resource Groups for RAM Users**

1. Log on to the EDAS console.
2. In the left navigation pane, choose **System Administration > RAM Users**.
3. In the **Operation** column of the target RAM user, click **Authorize Resource Groups**.
4. In the **Authorize Resource Groups** dialog box, select resource groups from the
**Unselected** list on the left. Click **>** to move them to the **Selected** list on the right. Then
click **OK**. Return to the **RAM Users** page. The authorized resource groups appear in the **Authorized**
**Resource Groups** column of the RAM user.
To adjust authorized resource groups, repeat the authorization steps. In the **Authorize**
**Resource Groups** dialog box, adjust the resource groups in both lists.

### RAM Permission

**Management**

#### Introduction to RAM users

When you use EDAS, different users often perform different tasks. An Alibaba Cloud account can assign specific roles and resources to Resource Access Management (RAM) users to separate responsibilities. anagement

**Account relationships**

The relationships between an Alibaba Cloud account and RAM users are as follows: In EDAS, an Alibaba Cloud account can attach RAM users. This practice avoids sharing account keys and lets you assign the least privilege to RAM users. This enables efficient enterprise management with clearly defined responsibilities. When an Alibaba Cloud account attaches a RAM user, a mapping is created. This mapping is valid only within EDAS. Outside of this environment, the Alibaba Cloud account and the RAM user are independent accounts. An Alibaba Cloud account can be a primary account that attaches RAM users. It can also be a RAM user attached to another Alibaba Cloud account.

#### Create users and user groups

An Alibaba Cloud account can create users and assign roles to them. This helps meet the system's access control requirements.

**Create an organization**

An organization administrator can create only subordinate organizations under the organization to which the organization administrator belongs.

**Variables in the Resource element of an access policy**

The following variables can be included in the Resource element of an access policy statement: $namespace: The tenant ID of the microservices namespace. You can find this ID on the Microservices Namespace page. The part circled in the following screenshot is the tenant ID. $clusterId: The cluster ID, for example, 8c349f69-505c-436f-8dc7-**********. You can find this ID on the Cluster Details page. $applicationId: The application ID, for example, ec8e38a3-3dca-47a7-b6f9-5**********. You can find this ID on the Basic Information page of the application.

### View all permissions

You can view all permissions in the EDAS console.

**Procedure**

1. Log on to the EDAS console.
2. In the left-side menu bar, choose **System administration > All permissions**.
3. Click a level to view its permissions.

### Use Permission Assistant to

**grant permissions to applications**

**by cluster**

Your business may involve multiple developers. Each developer's account can be mapped to the same namespace, but they use different clusters to create resources and deploy applications. Managing permissions for each application individually is time-consuming and error-prone. The EDAS Permission Assistant lets you grant permissions to applications by cluster. This simplifies and accelerates the management process.

**Procedure**

1. Log on to the EDAS console.
2. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **System Administration > Permission**
**Assistant**.
3. On the **Permission Assistant** page, click **Create Access Policy** or click **Edit** to the right
of the policy that you want to modify.
4. On the **Edit Access Policy** page, click **Add Permission Statement**. The **Add**
**Authorization Statement** page appears.
5. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Manage Applications**. In the following figure, ①
is the cluster name and ② is the application name. After you make your selections, click
**Confirm**.
anagement
6. Click **Next**. Review the policy preview. If the preview is correct, click **Finish**.
7. Find the access policy that you configured. Click Edit to view the permissions that you
added.

## FAQ

This topic describes the common problems and solutions during product development and use.

### Known issues and solutions

This topic describes known issues in this version of the product and their solutions.

**Why does the application monitoring data page appear gray and fail to open**

**correctly?**

Cause: This issue occurs if you have not purchased a certificate. If an Application Real-Time Monitoring Service (ARMS) page uses a self-signed or invalid certificate over HTTPS, the browser blocks access to the page. Solution: Open the blocked ARMS page in a separate browser tab. After the page opens successfully, open it again in EDAS.

**Why is no monitoring data available after an application upgrade?**

Cause: The monitoring solution for Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS) changed in version 3.9.0. Because of this change, you must manually restart the application to enable monitoring after an upgrade. Solution: To view infrastructure monitoring and service monitoring data, restart applications that were hot-upgraded. If you cannot restart the application, you can connect to the Elastic Compute Service (ECS) instance remotely and perform the following steps: i. Reinstall EDAS Agent. For more information, see Use a command script to manually install EDAS Agent. ii. Switch to the admin user and run the `edas refresh-apm` command.

**Why do I receive an HTTP 503 error when accessing an application after**

**unbinding an SLB instance?**

Cause: When you unbind a Server Load Balancer (SLB) instance from an application group in the EDAS console, EDAS does not delete the forwarding rules of the SLB instance. However, this action also detaches the instances in the vServer group. This causes SLB traffic forwarding to fail and results in an HTTP 503 error. Solution: Manually delete the corresponding forwarding rules in the SLB console.

**Why does access to an application using an SLB IP address fail after I enable**

**traffic shaping?**

Cause: After you enable traffic shaping for an application that is bound to an SLB instance over HTTP, the SLB instance sends a `HEAD / HTTP/1.0` message to perform a health check on the backend nodes. Tengine returns an HTTP 400 response, which causes the health check of the SLB listener to fail. As a result, a 502 Bad Gateway error occurs when you try to access the application. Solution: For applications that do not require traffic shaping, you can disable the feature on the application's basic information page in the EDAS console. This operation uninstalls Tengine, modifies the application configuration, and restarts the application. If you must use this feature, go to the health check settings of the SLB instance and select 4xx as an expected HTTP status code for health checks.

**What should I do if a deployment task gets stuck?**

If a deployment gets stuck, you can restart the two EDAS EAM containers and then retry the deployment.

**Why does the previous content of a mount script remain after I clear it?**

As a workaround, modify the script to print an empty statement, such as `echo ""`.

**Canceling an HTTP Rule in Traffic Shaping Settings and Clicking Save Causes an**

**'Execution Failed' Error**

This error may occur on your first attempt to cancel a rule. To successfully cancel the rule, save the configuration again on the same page.

**Why do I see a "no Permission" error when I delete an application as a RAM user,**

**even though the deletion succeeds?**

This error message is misleading. You can safely close the error dialog box. The application is deleted, and this error will not appear on subsequent attempts.

**As a RAM user, why can I see ECS instances in the cluster list but not on the ECS**

**management page or in the application scale-out list?**

The cluster list displays all ECS instances in the cluster, regardless of permissions. However, the ECS management page and the application scale-out list show only the instances that the RAM user is explicitly authorized to access. If an ECS instance is not authorized for the RAM user, the user cannot view or manage that instance from these pages.

**How can I specify the IP address for starting an instance that has multiple**

**network interface controllers (NICs)?**

You can add the startup parameter **-Daddress.server.ip={accessible_IP_address}** to the `startup.bat` or `startup.sh` script.

**Customizing the IP address of a service provider**

When you publish a service, you may need to publish it to a virtual IP address that is not a physical IP address on the local machine, such as an Elastic IP Address (EIP) of an ECS instance. If you specify this virtual IP address using the `-Dhsf.server.ip` parameter, an error occurs when the service starts and the service fails to be published. This issue occurs because the system cannot find the virtual IP address on the network interface controllers (NICs) of the local machine during the publishing process. To solve this problem, EDAS lets you customize the IP address for the service provider. This way, you do not need to specify IP addresses when you publish a service from the provider to the configuration center. After the service is published, you can modify the IP address of the service provider and republish the service. No changes are required on the service consumer. Follow these steps: i. After the service is published, find the service in the **Configuration List** and click
**Update** in the column on the right.
You can also find the published service in the **service list**. ii. On the **Edit Configuration** page, modify the IP address in the Content field.

**Important**

To prevent service invocation errors, do not change the content that follows the IP address unless it is necessary. iii. Click **OK**. iv. You can restart the service. The service is then re-registered with the new address. After the modification, the service consumer can directly call the service. You can view the logs in the {user.home}\logs\configclient\config-client.log directory to check the actual IP address called by the service. Check the content next to the keyword **Data-received** in the logs to view the complete information about the called service.

#### HSF FAQ

**Locate and solve HSF problems**

High-speed Service Framework (HSF) records error information in the /home/admin/logs/hsf/hsf.log file. If an HSF-related error occurs, you can check this file to locate the error. HSF errors typically have corresponding error codes that you can use to quickly find a solution.

**How to set the HSF timeout period?**

You can set the timeout period using the HSF tags: methodSpecials and clientTimeout.
**methodSpecials**: Configures the timeout period for a specific method. Unit: ms.
**clientTimeout**: Configures a uniform timeout period for all methods in an interface. Unit:
ms. The timeout settings are prioritized in the following order from highest to lowest: Consumer methodSpecials > Consumer clientTimeout > Provider methodSpecials > Provider clientTimeout The following code shows an example of the consumer tag configuration:

```xml
<hsf:consumer id="service" interface="com.taobao.edas.service.SimpleService" version="1.1.0" group="test1" clientTimeout="3000" target="10.1.6.57:12200?_TIMEOUT=1000" maxWaitTimeForCsAddress="5000"> <hsf:methodSpecials>
    <hsf:methodSpecial name="sum" timeout="2000" ></hsf:methodSpecial>
</hsf:methodSpecials> </hsf:consumer>
```

**HSF invalid call is removed**

**Error message**:

```
 invalid callis removed because ofconnection closed
```

**Cause**:
Transient disconnection: A consumer establishes a connection with a provider and initiates a call request. This error occurs if the consumer closes the connection due to network issues or other reasons while the provider is still processing the request and before the consumer-side timeout is reached. Provider restart: A consumer sends a request and waits for a response from the provider. If the provider restarts, the socket connection is terminated. As a result, the consumer receives a "connection closed" callback from the operating system and reports an error.

**Solution:**

If the operation is idempotent, you can implement a retry mechanism in your application. You should also check the server network because this error is typically caused by a transient disconnection.

**Failed to bind IP and port on HSF startup**

**Problem:**

The following error occurs during HSF startup:

**Java.net.BindException: Can't assign requested address**

**Cause:**

The application failed to retrieve the current IP address and port.

**Solution:**

You can set the following Java Virtual Machine (JVM) parameter to resolve this issue.

```
 -Dhsf.server.ip=IP_address_of_your_local_NIC -Dhsf.server.port=12200
```

**How to prevent user logs from being overwritten**

**Problem:**

After an application is deployed using EDAS, its log4j logs cannot be output.

**Cause:**

The log4j configuration is overwritten, which prevents logs from being output.

**Solution:**

You can set the JVM parameter `-Dlog4j.defaultInitOverride=false` to ensure that user logs are output.

**Other HSF issues**

**Error message**:
The following error is reported during startup:

```
 java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: HSFApiConsumerBean.ServiceMetadata.ifClazz is null
```

**Solution**:
This error indicates that the class corresponding to the interface failed to load. Confirm that the interface class can be loaded from the classpath.
**Error message**:

```
 failure to connect 10.10.1.1
```

**Solution**:
Confirm that the applications are in the same virtual private cloud (VPC) and region. Applications cannot connect if they are in different VPCs or regions. Confirm that the applications are in the same security group. If they are in different security groups, you must open port 12200. You can run the `telnet 10.10.1.1 12200` command to check whether the port is reachable. If the port is not reachable, check the firewall settings of the server at **10.10.1.1**.

#### HSF error codes

**Error code: HSF-0001**

**Error message**:
HSFServiceAddressNotFoundException: The destination address of the service to call was not found. Description: The service to be called is xxxx, which is in the xxxx group.
**Solutions**:
1. Name mismatch. Check that the service name, version number, and group are identical for
the publisher and the consumer. These values are case-sensitive and cannot have leading or trailing spaces.
2. Tomcat container startup error. Check the `/logs/catalina.out` and `localhost.log.YYYY-MM-
DD` log files in the Tomcat installation directory for exceptions. Resolve any exceptions that you find.
3. The service group is not created. Log on to the EDAS console. In the navigation pane on the
left, choose **Microservices Governance > HSF**. On the **HSF** page, click **Service Groups** in the navigation pane to check whether a service group is created for the application. For example:

```
<hsf:provider
          id="sampleServiceProvider" interface="com.alibaba.edas.SampleService"
ref="target"
          version="for-test" group="your-namespace" ></hsf:provider>
```

**group:**your-namespace must exist in the service group list.
4. Authentication failed. Check the /home/admin/configclient/logs/config.client.log file on the
**provider** machine for a **spas-authentication-failed** error. This error can occur for the
following reasons: The service group is not created. The AccessKey ID and AccessKey secret used to install the EDAS Agent are incorrect. This can happen if you install the agent using a web terminal. a. Run `cat /home/admin/.spas_key/default` . b. Log on to the EDAS console. In the navigation pane on the left, choose **Resource**
**Management > Microservices Namespace**.
c. On the **Microservices Namespace** page, check whether the AccessKey ID and AccessKey secret in the **AccessKey** column for the target microservices namespace match the ones used to install the EDAS Agent. The values are case-sensitive. Using a web terminal can cause case mismatches. d. The provider address cannot be pinged. This can happen if the machine has multiple network interface cards (NICs) and publishes an IP address that the client cannot access. Use **-Dhsf.server.ip** to specify the server's IP address.
5. The service is called too early. The call is initiated before the ConfigServer pushes the
address, which causes an error. To resolve this, add the `maxWaitTimeForCsAddress` configuration to the service consumer.
6. Data push is abnormal. Contact a developer to resolve this issue.

**Error code: HSF-0002**

**Error message**:
Consumer error: HSFTimeoutException.
**Solutions**:
Check the network health of the machine. You can ping the server's IP address to check for connectivity. The server processing time is greater than 3 s. Search the `hsf.log` file on the server for timeout logs to locate the specific class and method. Serialization error on the server. Check the code. Stream types, files, or oversized objects can cause serialization errors. Do not transfer these types of data. Low code performance. Perform code refactoring and make improvements. The server logic is complex and requires more than 3 s of processing time. You can modify the timeout period. Occasional timeouts occur, and garbage collection (GC) happens on both the client and the server. Check the server and client GC logs. A long-running GC process can cause a timeout. The client load is high. This causes client requests to fail, which results in a timeout. To resolve this, add more client machines.

**Error code: HSF-0003**

**Error message**:
Consumer error: java.io.FileNotFoundException: /home/admin/logs/hsf.log. This error message indicates that the specified path is not found.
**Solution**: The default HSF log path cannot be found, or you do not have the required
permissions to access it. You can add the **-DHSF.LOG.PATH=xxx** parameter at startup to change the default path.

**Error code: HSF-0005**

**Error message**:
Startup error: java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: The object to be published as a service is not configured. Service name: com.taobao.hsf.jar.test.HelloWorldService:1.0.zhouli.
**Solutions**:
The target attribute is missing from the bean of the provider. Check the configuration file. The implementation class of the service specified by the target attribute does not exist. Check the configuration file.

**Error code: HSF-0007**

**Error message**:
Startup error: java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: unsurpport serialize type.
**Solutions**: The serializeType or preferSerializeType attribute for the bean of the provider is
invalid. Check the configuration file. We recommend that you use Hessian or Hessian 2.0 for serialization.

**Error code: HSF-0008**

**Error message**: java.lang.IllegalArgumentException. This error message is returned when
the service type specified in ProviderBean is not the interface [com.taobao.hsf.jar.test.HelloWorldServiceImpl].
**Solutions**: serviceInterface configured in the bean of the provider is not an interface.
serviceInterface must be set to an interface. Check the configuration file.

**Error code: HSF-0009**

**Error message**: java.lang.IllegalArgumentException. This error message is returned when
the interface [com.taobao.hsf.jar.test.HelloWorldService] is not implemented in the actual service object [com.taobao.hsf.jar.test.HelloWorldServiceImpl@10f0a3e8].
**Solutions**: No interface is implemented in the bean that is specified by the target attribute of
the provider. Check whether the corresponding interface is implemented in the implementation class.

**Error code: HSF-0014**

**Error message**: java.lang.IllegalArgumentException. This error message is returned when
the interface class [com.taobao.hsf.jar.test.HelloWorldService1] specified in ProviderBean does not exist.
**Solution**: The provider's `serviceInterface` property is configured incorrectly because the
specified interface does not exist.

**Error code: HSF-0016**

**Error message**:
Startup error: Failed to start the HSF server.
**Solutions**:
Check for conflicts on port 12200. A server bind failure is a common cause of a startup failure. If the machine has multiple NICs and a public IP address, use **-Dhsf.server.ip** to specify the local IP address.

**Error code: HSF-0017**

**Error message**:
Startup error: java.lang.RuntimeException: [ThreadPool Manager] Thread pool allocated failed for service [com.taobao.hsf.jar.test.HelloWorldService:1.0.zhouli]: balance [600] require [800].
**Solution**: The allocated thread pool is not large enough. The default maximum size of an HSF
thread pool is 600. To change the default global maximum size, you can configure the JVM parameter **-Dhsf.server.max.poolsize=xxx**.

**Error code: HSF-0020**

**Error message**:
WARN taobao.hsf - HSF service: The error message com.taobao.hsf.jar.test.HelloWorldService:1.0.zhouli is returned if you repeatedly initialize the HSF service.
**Solutions**: In an HSF service process, the service is uniquely identified by the service name
and version. Services that have the same name and version but belong to different groups cannot be published or subscribed to in a single process. Check the configuration file. For example, the service com.taobao.hsf.jar.test.HelloWorldService cannot be published or subscribed to in a single process if the following two configuration items exist in the configuration file: com.taobao.hsf.jar.test.HelloWorldService 1.0 groupA com.taobao.hsf.jar.test.HelloWorldService 1.0 groupB

**Error code: HSF-0021**

**Error message**:
Startup error: java.lang.IllegalArgumentException. This error message is returned when the interface class [com.taobao.hsf.jar.test.HelloWorldService1] specified in ProviderBean does not exist. java.lang.IllegalArgumentException. This error message is returned when the interface class [com.taobao.hsf.jar.test.HelloWorldService1] specified in ConsumerBean does not exist.
**Solutions**: The serviceInterface attribute of HSFSpringProviderBean is incorrectly configured.
The specified interface does not exist (HSF-0014) or the interface specified by interfaceName in HSFSpringConsumerBean does not exist (HSF-0021).

**Error code: HSF-0027**

**Error message**: [HSF-Provider] HSF thread pool is full.
**Solutions**:
The processing speed of a service on the HSF server is slow, and requests from the consumer cannot be processed in time. As a result, the number of threads for service execution in the thread pool on the HSF server reaches the maximum value. By default, the HSF server dumps the file /home/admin/logs/hsf/HSF_JStack.log. You can view the **HSFBizProcessor-xxx** thread stack information in the file and analyze the performance bottleneck. By default, the maximum number of threads in the thread pool on an HSF server is 600. To increase the number, change the value of the JVM parameter **-**
**Dhsf.server.max.poolsize=xxx**.

**Error code: HSF-0030**

**Error message**: [HSF-Provider] does not find a method to call the service.
**Solutions**:
The server does not provide this method. Log on to the EDAS console. In the navigation pane on the left, select **Application List**. Click the name of the application. On the application details page, click **Service List** in the navigation pane on the left to check whether the corresponding service was published successfully. New and old versions coexist, and the call is made to an incorrect version of the service. Check the service as described in the previous step. The provider and consumer interfaces are inconsistent. For example, the provider's parameter is `java.lang.Double`, but the consumer uses `double` for the call. The server and client loaded inconsistent interface classes. Compare the MD5 values of the interface JAR packages on the server and the client to check for consistency.

**Error code: HSF-0031**

**Error message**: [HSF-Provider] takes xxx ms to execute the xxx method of the xxx HSF
service. The time approximates the timeout period.
**Solutions**: The provider prints out an error log when **the timeout period minus the actual**
**time elapsed is less than 100 ms**. By default, the timeout period is 3s.
If the timeout period is very short, such as less than 100 ms, this log is printed for every call. You can ignore this log. If the timeout period is long and this log is still printed, the business logic execution is slow. Analyze the performance bottleneck of the business logic.

**Error code: HSF-0032**

**Error message**: Please check log on server side that unknown server error happens.
**Solutions**: An error that is not captured occurs when the provider processes a request. Check
the hsf.log file of the provider for troubleshooting.

**Error code: HSF-0033**

**Error message**: Serialization error during serialize response.
**Solutions**:
An error occurs when the provider returns data during serialization. Check the hsf.log file of the provider for troubleshooting. If the log file contains "must implement java.io.Serializable", implement a serializable interface on the DO.

**Error code: HSF-0038**

**Error message**: The HSF server has multiple NICs, and an invalid IP address is bound to the
HSF server.
**Solutions**: Add -Dhsf.server.ip=xxx.xxx.xx.xx to the JVM startup parameters to specify the
desired IP address.

**Error code: HSF-0035**

**Error message**: RPCProtocolTemplateComponent invalid address.
**Solutions**: A TCP connection cannot be established between the current instance and the
corresponding address. Check whether the corresponding remote address and port can be connected.

### Usage FAQ

Common problems during development are related to accounts, resources, application lifecycle, and monitoring and alarms.

#### Account management

Q: Can I create multiple RAM users? A: Yes. Q: Who can grant application operation permissions for RAM users? EDAS allows you to grant application operation permissions to RAM users only by using the primary account.

#### Resource management

This topic describes common issues and solutions related to resource management.
**Problem**: The EDAS Agent does not report data and its version number is not displayed on
the interface after installation.
**Answer**: Troubleshoot the issue as follows:
1. Log on to the ECS instance and view the /home/admin/edas-agent/logs/agent.log file. If a
UnAuthorizedException error occurs, check the following items: The AccessKey ID and AccessKey secret used to install the EDAS Agent are incorrect. This issue can occur if you installed the agent from a web terminal. a. Run the `cat /home/admin/.spas_key/default` command. b. Log on to the EDAS console. In the upper-right corner, click your profile picture and then click **Personal Information**. c. On the **Personal Information** page, view the **AccessKey ID** and **AccessKey Secret** in the **AccessKey** section. d. Check whether the AccessKey ID and AccessKey secret on the ECS instance are the same as those on the **Personal Information** page.

**Important**

The values are case-sensitive. Using a web terminal can cause case inconsistencies. The region script used for installation is incorrect.
2. View the /home/admin/edas-agent/logs/std.log file. If a "Java not found" error or another
exception occurs, run the `java -version` command to check the Java version. The required version is 1.8. If the version is 1.5, run the `rpm -e <rpm_package_name>` command to remove the incorrect version, and then reinstall the agent.
**Problem**: The agent status is "Unknown" or "Abnormal" after installation.
**Answer**: Check the std.log and agent.log files in the /home/admin/edas-agent/logs directory
on the ECS instance: std.log contains logs from the agent installation process. agent.log contains the running logs of the agent. Troubleshoot the problem based on the error. The following possible causes are provided: If the log contains `Permission denied` or `No such file` , the cause might be insufficient file directory permissions. Confirm that the admin user has permissions for all files in the /home/admin directory, and then reinstall the agent. Check whether the ECS hostname is consistent with the entry in the /etc/hosts file. If they are inconsistent, modify the file and restart the agent:

```
/home/admin/edas-agent/bin/shutdown.sh /home/admin/edas-agent/bin/startup.sh
```

**Problem**: Which Java version does EDAS use? Can I choose the version?
**Answer**: EDAS provides Java 7 and Java 8. By default, Java 7 is used. You can also select the
Java version during the EDAS Agent installation. The usage is as follows:

```
install.sh -ak -sk [-java <7(default)|8>]
```

**Problem**: What happens if the agent's heartbeat process stops?
**Answer**:
If no application is deployed on the corresponding ECS instance, there is no impact. If an application is deployed, the **Real-time Status** of the corresponding ECS instance changes to **AGENT ABNORMAL**. You can view the list of ECS instances where the application is deployed on the **Instance Deployment Information** tab of the application's
**Basic Information** page. In this case, commands to deploy, start, or stop the application
on this ECS instance become invalid. You need to perform the following operations: i. Log on to the machine and run the `sudo -u admin /home/admin/edas-` `agent/bin/startup.sh` command to start the agent. Then, troubleshoot the cause of the unexpected exit. ii. Check the /home/admin/edas-agent/logs/agent.log file for error messages. iii. Confirm that the system has enough memory. Insufficient memory can cause the system `Linux oom kill`. If to trigger an out-of-memory (OOM) kill. For more information, search for an `oom kill` occurs, check the system memory usage and adjust the memory allocation.
**Problem**: What should I do if an Ali-Tomcat container exits unexpectedly?
**Answer**: Log on to the EDAS console and restart the application. Then, troubleshoot the
cause of the unexpected exit by checking the following items: Check the /home/admin/tomcat(installation directory)/logs/catalina.out file for error messages. Confirm that the system has enough memory. Insufficient memory can cause the system to trigger an out-of-memory (OOM) kill. For more information, search for linux oom kill. If an oom kill occurs, check the system memory usage and adjust the memory allocation.
**Problem**: The EDAS Agent does not start automatically after the system restarts.
**Answer**: Automatic startup of the agent is supported on CentOS 6.5 but has not been tested
on other operating systems. If the agent does not start automatically, you can run the following script to start it manually:

```python
sudo -u admin /home/admin/edas-agent/bin/startup.sh /usr/alisys/dragoon/bin/DragoonAgent
```

**Problem**: Why can a RAM user view ECS instances in the cluster list, but not on the ECS page
or in the application scale-out list?
**Answer**: The cluster list displays all ECS instances in the cluster, regardless of permissions.
However, the ECS list and the application scale-out list check whether the RAM user has been granted permissions for each ECS instance. If a RAM user has not been granted permissions for an ECS instance, that instance is not displayed in those lists.

#### Application lifecycle class

**Question:** Does the EDAS Agent restart automatically after the server restarts?
**Answer:** Yes. The EDAS Agent restarts automatically after the server restarts. However,
Tomcat does not restart automatically.
**Question:** Why can't I start the EDAS Agent?
**Answer:** First, run the following ping command on the server to check if the EDAS console is
reachable:

```
ping edas-internal.console.aliyun.com
```

Second, check if your security token file is set up correctly:

```
cat /home/admin/.spas_key/default
```

**Question:** Does EDAS support deploying multiple applications on the same server?
**Answer:** No. In EDAS, you can deploy only one application on a single ECS instance.
**Question:** Can I use any URL for the deployment package during application deployment?
**Answer:** The URL must be accessible from your server to allow the application deployment
package to be downloaded.
**Question:** Why do application operations, such as starting, stopping, or deploying an
application, fail?
**Answer:** Application operation failures usually occur because the EDAS Agent is not running
correctly. On the server where the failure occurred, check if the EDAS Agent is running.
**Question:** When I create an application, why don't my servers appear in the server selection
dialog box?
**Answer:** This issue can occur if the EDAS Agent is not installed correctly on the server. Verify
that the agent is installed correctly. For more information, see Import ECS instances.

**Important**

When you install the agent, make sure to select the correct region and namespace.
**Question:** Why is the status of an ECS instance "Unknown" in the EDAS console?
**Answer:** The EDAS Agent periodically reports heartbeat data to the EDAS console. If the
agent stops reporting data for a certain period, the instance status changes to Unknown. This issue usually occurs because the EDAS Agent has stopped running.
**Question:** Services can be called correctly, but the service list does not appear. Why?
**Answer:** The API contains generics, but a specific type is not assigned to the generics. This
causes the service list parsing to fail. Modify the corresponding code to fix this issue.
**Question:** The service list is displayed correctly, but service calls fail. What should I do?

**Answer:**

1. Check if the group for the service provider is created. If the group is not created,
authentication fails.
2. Check the /home/admin/logs/hsf/hsf.log file for the specific error code. Then, look up the
error code in the HSF FAQ.
**Question:** Can I restore an application after deleting it?
**Answer:** No, you cannot. Deleting an application is an irreversible operation, and all
application data is purged after deletion.
**Question:** How do I perform a phased release or a beta release?

**Answer:**

If an application runs on multiple ECS instances, you can perform a phased release by setting the number of batches to a value greater than 1. If an application runs on multiple ECS instances, you can designate some instances as beta instances. During a release, you can choose to deploy the application only to the beta instances. Only the instances marked as beta are updated.
**Question:** After my application is deployed on multiple instances, how are cluster sessions
shared?
**Answer:** EDAS does not provide a distributed session management feature. You can use a
distributed cache system, such as ApsaraDB for Memcache or Redis, to manage sessions.
**Question:** How do I set the health check URL?
**Answer:** When you deploy an application, the provided WAR file is automatically deployed to
the Tomcat directory. Therefore, the health check URL must include the WAR package name by default. The file specified in the URL must return an HTTP status code from 200 to 400. For example, if your WAR package is named order.war and it contains an index.jsp file, you can set the health check URL to http://127.0.0.1:8080/order/index.jsp.
**Question:** After my application is deployed on multiple servers, how can I implement load
balancing? Can I use SLB?

**Answer:**

1. For web applications in EDAS that provide HTTP services, you can use Server Load Balancer
(SLB) for load balancing. You can configure SLB on the application's configuration page in EDAS.
2. You do not need to configure load balancing for applications that are RPC service providers.
EDAS provides native load balancing support for these applications.

#### Troubleshoot EDAS Agent issues

**Symptoms**

Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS) Agent becomes abnormal or a container exits.

**Causes**

EDAS Agent becomes abnormal. The system time of the Elastic Compute Service (ECS) instance is not synchronized with that of EDAS Agent, which has a deviation of 30s. The network resolution times out.

**Solutions**

1. Log on to the ECS instance where the application is deployed and go to the
/home/admin/edas-agent/ directory. View the agent.log log to check whether the ECS instance where EDAS Agent is deployed is properly connected to EDAS.
2. Check whether the system time of the ECS instance where the application is deployed is
synchronized with that of the components such as edasServer, Dauth, edasConsole, and edasAdmin.

**Important**

Components typically use a multi-node deployment. An issue can occur if the system time is not synchronized between the nodes of a component.
3. Check the AccessKey ID and AccessKey secret.
i. Log on to the ECS instance. Run the `cat /home/admin/.spas_key/default` command to view the AccessKey ID and AccessKey secret. ii. Log on to the EDAS console. In the upper-right corner, click your profile picture and select
**Personal Information** from the list.
iii. On the **Personal Information** page, view the **AccessKey ID** and **AccessKey secret** in the **AccessKey** section. iv. Check if the AccessKey ID and AccessKey secret on the ECS instance match those on the
**Personal Information** page.

**Important**

The values are case-sensitive. Web terminals can cause case inconsistencies.

| on to the ECS instance. Run the | dmidecode -s system-serial-number \| grep -v '^#' |   |
|---|---|---|
| dmidecode \| grep -i uuid \| awk '{print tolower($2)}' |   |   |
|   |   | commands to check if the |

UUIDs are consistent. If they are consistent, no further action is required. If they are inconsistent, run `cp /usr/sbin/staragent_sn /usr/sbin/staragent_sn.bak &&`

```
dmidecode | grep -i uuid | awk '{print tolower($2)}' > /usr/sbin/staragent_sn , and
```

then run `pkill -9 staragent && /home/staragent/bin/agent.sh start` . Then, execute the following SQL statement to verify the result.

```
-select * from ecs where serial-num=""; /home/staragent/conf/staragent.conf
```

#### Troubleshoot change process issues

**Symptoms**

An application deployment is stuck and cannot proceed to the next step.

**Causes**

Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS) Agent that is deployed on an Elastic Compute Service (ECS) instance becomes abnormal and the client fails to deliver commands. This results in a failed job whose execution is dependent on EDAS Agent. A job of a service type fails to run because the management components of EDAS become abnormal. The following jobs are of a service type: Bring Tegine online or offline. Update Tegine. Bring Server Load Balancer (SLB) online or offline. Set the weight for load balancing. A health check reports an error because the application package is abnormal.

**Solutions**

1. Failed online health checks account for more than half of all failed tasks. A health check
typically fails because of an incorrect health check configuration or an issue with the application package. If a URL health check fails, first confirm that the health check URL is configured correctly. If the health check configuration is invalid or an issue exists in your application package, configure the URL for the health check again or fix the issue of the application package. If you verify that this issue is not caused by the health check configuration or application package, proceed to the next step.
2. Log on to the ECS instance where the application is deployed. Check the startup logs of
Tomcat and application logs to troubleshoot the issue.
3. Start the change process again and check whether a command delivery timeout results in
this issue.

#### Troubleshoot issues in a change

**process**

When you deploy, start, scale out, or scale in an application in Enterprise Distributed Application Service (EDAS), you can use change records to visualize the entire process and monitor its progress. If a change fails, you can review the change details to identify the failed steps and the reasons for the failure.

**Troubleshoot change failures**

After an application change fails, you can troubleshoot the failure by reviewing the change process on the application details page.
1. On the application details page, click **Change Records** in the navigation pane on the left.
If a change fails, **Execution failed** appears in the **Change Status** column.
2. On the **Change History** page, click **View** in the Actions column of a failed change record.
3. On the **Change Details** page, on the **Batch 1 Deployment** tab, click a failed stage, such
as Execute Deployment. View the logs of the failed step for the instance on the right to identify the problem. The tabs that appear depend on the number of batches that you set for deployment. For example, if you set two batches, a Batch 1 Deployment tab and a Batch 2 Deployment tab appear.

**Typical application change exceptions and solutions**

This section describes how to use the change process to troubleshoot and resolve typical exceptions that occur during application changes.

**Change Failure Due to a Port Health Check Exception**

Port 65000 is inaccessible. The application requires this port to be open when it starts. The Tomcat container did not start correctly.

**Solution**

Check the application logs for exceptions.

**Change Failure Due to a URL Health Check Failure**

If you configure a health check URL, the application checks whether the URL is accessible at startup. The deployment continues only after an HTTP 200 response is received. The URL health check fails if a response code other than 200 is returned within the 3-minute health check period. The application may have failed to start. Check the application logs to verify. Check whether the URL is configured correctly. Check whether the application has an interceptor that blocks requests to the HTTP health check URL. After you resolve the issue, deploy the application again.

**Change Failure Because the Disk Is Full**

If the disk is full, the application may hang at a stage in the change process for a long time.

**Error Message**

```
 [EDAS-10000] No space left on disk  or  No space left on device. Free space (for
```

`/home/admin) in bytes: 0exit 1` . This message indicates that the machine's disk is full. This is usually because the application's business logs have filled the disk space. To resolve this issue, you must clear the application logs.

**Solutions**

For an application in an ECS cluster, log on to the ECS instance to clear the logs from the disk. For a Docker application in a Swarm cluster, **Reset The Application**. After the reset, the container is stopped, deleted, and then rebuilt. This process releases the disk space.
